live-002: The New Jersey Supreme Court on July 20, 2026 affirmed the Appellate Division's reversal of trial court orders that had allowed Jackson Township to condemn Lots 84 and 90, owned by Bellevue Jackson, LLC and Getzel Bee, LLC. Chief Justice Stuart Rabner wrote for a unanimous court. According to the opinion, the township adopted an ordinance in February 2023 to exchange land, including the two privately owned lots, with a developer, Bellevue Estates, LLC (unrelated to Bellevue Jackson), which would transfer its own land to the township for open space. The early ordinances did not say how the two lots would be used or identify a public purpose. The township told the owners in March 2023 that it was acquiring land "for open space purposes," filed condemnation complaints in June 2023, and only in a September 2023 ordinance indicated the lots would be exchanged. The trial court found a public purpose in October 2023; the Appellate Division reversed in January 2025, calling the lots, "in essence, currency, to exchange for open space." The Supreme Court held that neither the Local Lands and Buildings Law nor the Eminent Domain Act, nor federal or state case law, authorizes condemning someone's land only to exchange it for another's property that will be put to public use. The condemned lots were left to the developer's discretion, not restricted to public use; it was the developer's land that would become open space. The court also found the township's shifting ordinance language fell short of its duty to "turn square corners" with property owners. Because the township's counsel said the exchange had already been completed, the court remanded to the trial court to determine what relief the owners should receive.
live-003: Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB, as trustee for the Benchmark 2026-B43 CMBS trust, sued Milton 90 Pleasant Valley Street LLC and Development Associates of Benton Harbor LLC on July 28, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, Mortgage Professional America reported. According to the article, Barclays Capital Real Estate made the $34.4 million loan around April 14, 2026 at a 6.4% fixed rate, maturing May 6, 2036, and it was assigned to the trust effective May 20, 2026. CWCapital Asset Management is the special servicer. The loan is secured by about 46 acres at 90 Pleasant Valley Street in Methuen, Massachusetts and the Fairplain Plaza shopping center in Benton Township, Michigan. The trustee alleges two guarantors filed Chapter 11 in New Jersey around June 4, 2026, and the borrowers then missed the first payment due June 6, raising the rate to an 11.4% default rate. A default letter followed on June 16 and an acceleration letter on July 15. The borrowers leased nearly all of each property to affiliated companies under 99-year leases, and those affiliates have also filed Chapter 11. The trustee alleges the borrowers are not enforcing those leases, conduct the filing calls "affiliate atrophy," and that collecting from the affiliates would cover the loan payments. The complaint seeks foreclosure of the mortgages, foreclosure on personal-property collateral under the UCC, and appointment of a receiver to take possession, collect rents and step into the affiliate leases and the related bankruptcy cases. One guarantor is named as a defendant to pursue any shortfall after a sale; the other two are not, because the bankruptcy stay bars joining them. The allegations have not been tested, and no court has ruled on them.
live-004: FitFactariDC LLC, a commercial tenant, sued CoStar Group and five large brokerages, CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Newmark, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois on June 12, 2026. The proposed class action says CoStar gathered and passed along sensitive lease data, while the brokerages supplied that data and got access to competitors' information in return. The tenant says the arrangement made it pay "artificially inflated" rent on a lease in Denver, The Real Deal reported, citing Bisnow. According to the complaint, seeing rivals' final lease terms almost as soon as they were signed let the defendants keep asking rents in step, give smaller concessions and hold firm in negotiations with tenants. CoStar general counsel Gene Boxer called the lawsuit "frivolous" and said the company expected a "swift and complete victory," according to the report. The other defendants declined to comment or did not respond. The court docket shows the tenant voluntarily dropped Colliers International Group Inc. on Aug. 7, 2026; its U.S. unit, Colliers International USA, LLC, remains a defendant. Judge Joan H. Lefkow set a briefing schedule on Aug. 13, and CoStar and the brokerages filed separate motions to dismiss on Aug. 17. The tenant's response was due Oct. 1 and replies Nov. 2, and the court canceled the Aug. 19 initial status hearing. The case follows years of litigation against RealPage and apartment landlords over rent-setting software, including a Justice Department suit that RealPage settled in November 2025 without paying penalties or admitting wrongdoing, in exchange for changes to its platform and independent oversight, The Real Deal noted. This suit applies a similar theory to commercial lease data.
live-005: The SEC filed SEC v. RAD Diversified REIT, Inc., et al., No. 8:26-cv-02186, in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida on July 29, 2026 against the Tampa-based REIT, its two founders and relief defendant The Seminar Solution, LLC. According to the SEC's litigation release, the REIT raised at least $152 million from more than 5,500 retail investors nationwide. The complaint describes it as a non-traded REIT that has never been registered with the Commission, and says it filed for Chapter 11 in the Middle District of Florida on March 1, 2026. The SEC alleges that from November 2019 through March 2024 the defendants misled investors about the REIT's profitability, stock valuation practices and liquidity, using unregistered sales agents and high-pressure tactics. The complaint alleges the defendants said the stock price rested on independent valuations when the properties were not independently valued, and did not update the price after July 2023 despite widespread foreclosures; it says the REIT faced at least 166 foreclosure actions totaling about $47 million before its bankruptcy. It also alleges that a bank declined a $15 million line of credit in February 2023 after reviewing the REIT's financial statements, and that redemptions were frozen in February 2024. According to the SEC, about $54 million of investor funds went to The Seminar Solution, an entity owned by the founders, who then allegedly misappropriated millions for personal expenses; the release puts their combined misappropriation at nearly $5 million. The SEC charges violations of the registration and antifraud provisions of the Securities Act and the Exchange Act and seeks injunctions and disgorgement with prejudgment interest against all defendants, plus civil penalties and officer-and-director bars against the founders. The case is assigned to U.S. District Judge Kathryn Kimball Mizelle. On October 23, 2026 the SEC filed an unopposed motion to approve a consent judgment as to the REIT, attaching the REIT's consent, a proposed judgment and an exhibit titled "Order Approving Partial Settlement with SEC." The CourtListener docket, last updated November 3, 2026, shows a case management and scheduling order entered that day but no ruling on the consent-judgment motion.
live-006: Silver Star Properties REIT filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on May 28, 2026, Bisnow reported, citing a June 5 shareholder update filed with the SEC. The Houston-based REIT said it aims to reorganize its obligations and preserve "tangible and intangible assets." It reported $75 million in liabilities and $100 million in assets, warned shareholders that the proceedings might cancel their equity, and said four loans are in default, along with a $5.75 million promissory note on a self-storage property that moved to foreclosure on June 2. The company previously filed for Chapter 11 in September 2023, with a plan to liquidate legacy office assets, reposition others into a new entity and resolve $217 million in outstanding debt. It planned to sell its retail, office and industrial holdings and move fully into self-storage, and bought nine properties in 2023 through an acquisition of Southern Star Self-Storage. According to the shareholder update, ongoing litigation, tight finances and lending constraints led to a review of strategic alternatives. Bisnow reported that the pivot was slowed by an SEC investigation, litigation and blocked deals to sell properties. In a 2023 lawsuit, Silver Star accused founder and former CEO Allen Hartman, who left in October 2022, of fraud, breach of fiduciary duty and interfering with asset sales; that case is still ongoing. Bisnow corrected its article on June 11 to clarify the status of that case and the date of Hartman's departure.
live-007: Via Mizner Lender 1 LLC, the administrative agent for a group of lenders, sued in Palm Beach County Circuit Court on July 17, 2026 to foreclose a mortgage on the Mandarin Oriental condominium project under construction on Federal Highway in Boca Raton, according to The Coastal Star. The borrower is Via Mizner Owner III, the Penn-Florida Companies affiliate building the condos, which gave the mortgage in August 2023. The lenders seek $417.7 million to repay the original $270 million loan plus interest, advances and fees, and allege Penn-Florida stopped making interest payments in June 2024 and failed to pay the full amount in September 2025 as promised. The complaint seeks to cut off claims by what it calls 'purported junior lienholders,' including construction manager Strategic Group Builders, and 'purported contract purchasers' of condo units, arguing that the mortgage is superior to other interests arising from the borrower. Strategic Group filed its own suit on July 6, seeking $24.1 million it says it was not paid, plus interest, costs and fees, and seeking to foreclose a lien it recorded against the property. It named Via Mizner Owner III and four project lenders, which it says stopped making monthly payments to it without notice. The Coastal Star also reported that unit buyers have pursued their deposits in separate cases, and that at least nine have settled. Separately, in a case concerning the adjoining Mandarin Oriental hotel, Penn-Florida affiliates Via Mizner Owner II and Via Mizner Pledgor II filed for Chapter 11 in December 2025 after failing to repay about $210 million to lenders at maturity, The Coastal Star reported. The auction of that property was moved to August 14, 2026, with a sale hearing set for August 21. The Coastal Star did not report a response from Penn-Florida to the foreclosure complaint.
live-008: CommunityAmerica Federal Credit Union filed two lawsuits in Hennepin County District Court against the owners of two office buildings in the Metropoint business park in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, the Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal reported, according to Connect CRE's July 23, 2026 roundup. The buildings are Metropoint 300, at 300 Highway 169 S., and Metropoint 400, at 400 Highway 169 S. The credit union is seeking to recover roughly $46 million in loans tied to the properties. Both buildings were scheduled to be sold at a foreclosure auction in September 2026. The report did not name the owners or say why the loans went into default.
live-009: U.S. District Judge Melissa R. DuBose on July 28, 2026 granted the landowners partial summary judgment on one count of their suit against the Town of Johnston, a ruling the Rhode Island Current described as finding the town's attempted seizure of a 31-acre property for a proposed apartment complex unlawful. The owners' companies planned a 252-unit affordable housing complex on the site on George Waterman Road. The dispute dates to December 2024, when Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr. issued a public letter opposing the project and warned the town would 'fight back' using 'all the power of government' available, the Current reported. Polisena said he wanted the land for a new public safety complex and town hall. On March 10, 2025, after an appraisal valued the property at $775,000, the Town Council voted 5-0 to begin condemning the site, and the owners sued the same night, arguing the taking was pretextual. DuBose issued a temporary restraining order on March 19, 2025, followed by a preliminary injunction. On August 4, 2026, the owners moved for contempt, arguing that two resolutions passed at a July 31 special council meeting, one putting a charter amendment on the November ballot to expand the town's condemnation authority and one creating a Municipal Public Building Authority, violated the injunction. DuBose ordered the town to show cause and to produce the meeting's agenda, minutes and resolutions; a town spokesperson told the Current that 'motions cannot be ignored.' On August 11, after reviewing the town's response, DuBose found the town's actions on and around July 31 did not violate the April 2, 2025 injunction and canceled the show-cause hearing, according to the docket. On August 28 she denied the town's request for a separate final judgment on the count it lost, and the case is in discovery.
live-010: The New York Court of Appeals on May 28, 2026 reinstated an implied-covenant claim by 111 West 57th Investment LLC, which the dissent identifies as AmBase Corporation's investment vehicle, against Apollo lending entities including ACREFI Mortgage Lending, LLC. Chief Judge Rowan D. Wilson wrote for a 4-3 majority; Judge Garcia, joined by Judges Singas and Cannataro, dissented in part, and Judge Halligan took no part. According to the opinion, the plaintiff invested $65 million in a joint venture to develop a luxury residential tower at 111 West 57th Street. The venture borrowed $725 million, including a $325 million Apollo mezzanine loan that fell out of balance because of budget overruns. In a March 2017 forbearance, that loan was split into a $300 million senior and a $25 million junior mezzanine loan secured by the venture's equity. Apollo gave Spruce Capital Partners models showing about $600 million in cash flow to equity if Spruce took the collateral by strict foreclosure, and on June 28, 2017 assigned the junior loan to a Spruce entity at its $25 million par value. Spruce sent a notice of default two days later and, on July 7, 2017, notified the venture it would take the equity by strict foreclosure absent objection; the foreclosure went forward and the venture's equity was wiped out. The plaintiff alleges Apollo, Spruce and the project's sponsor arranged a "backroom deal" to cut it out. The Appellate Division had dismissed the claim against Apollo in 2023 on the ground that Apollo's discretion to assign the loan could not be overridden by the implied covenant. Assuming without deciding that Apollo had sole discretion, the majority held that such discretion does not exempt a party from the covenant and that the complaint sufficiently alleged Apollo used the assignment as part of a scheme to strip the plaintiff of the equity the forbearance was meant to protect. Whether the plaintiff can prove those allegations is for later proceedings. The court affirmed dismissal of the tortious interference claims as insufficiently pleaded. Judge Garcia's dissent argued the majority used the covenant to rewrite a negotiated commercial loan agreement and that the decision would make rights under billions of dollars of outstanding loan agreements uncertain. The opinion notes that related litigation continues, including a surviving claim against Spruce.
live-013: A federal judge in New Jersey has allowed investors to pursue a putative class action alleging that the directors and advisers of three non-traded Lightstone Value Plus REITs did not disclose their chairman's conflict of interest before shareholders voted to remove the funds' liquidation deadlines, AltsWire reported. U.S. District Judge Michael A. Shipp ruled on August 5, 2026 that the plaintiffs adequately alleged that the proxy statements and related solicitor calls omitted a material conflict involving David Lichtenstein, the REITs' chairman and chief executive, who through affiliated entities owns the funds' external advisers. According to the complaint, Lichtenstein held subordinated participation interests through three special-purpose entities, potentially worth more than $59.8 million, that would have had no value if REIT II and REIT III had liquidated by the deadlines in their original charters, September 2024 and March 2025. The plaintiffs allege the 2022 proxies disclosed that the interests existed but not that they depended on extending the REITs' lives, which the court found could have significantly changed how a reasonable shareholder viewed the vote. The court also found that phone solicitors made misleading statements between a December 2022 meeting, where the amendments failed, and a January 2023 reconvened meeting, where they passed; investors allege solicitors called a "yes" vote "the most likely path to liquidity." The charter amendments, presented as a single item, also eliminated board fiduciary duties to shareholders, cut quorum requirements to as little as 33% of votes entitled to be cast, restricted shareholder access to investor lists and expanded indemnification for officers and directors, according to AltsWire. All four counts survive, including breach of fiduciary duty claims against the director defendants and the advisory entities. Lightstone did not respond to AltsWire's request for comment. The case, filed in November 2024, is now in initial scheduling before Magistrate Judge Tonianne J. Bongiovanni.
live-015: The New Jersey Supreme Court on July 13, 2026 unanimously modified the test, set in its 1992 decision in Sica v. Board of Adjustment of Wall, that governs use variances for 'inherently beneficial' uses such as hospitals, senior housing, schools and child care centers, the New Jersey Globe reported. Justice Anne M. Patterson wrote for the Court. The case arose from Monarch Communities' proposal for a 165-unit senior living facility on residentially zoned property in Montville Township. Senior housing is an inherently beneficial use under state law, but the township's zoning board denied the application, finding that it conflicted with the zoning plan and would have significant negative impacts, according to the Globe. The trial court and the Appellate Division both reversed the board. The Court held that Sica no longer fully reflects a 1997 amendment to the Municipal Land Use Law that requires inherently beneficial use applicants to satisfy both of the statute's 'negative criteria.' Under the revised fourth step, a board must first decide whether the applicant has shown that the variance would not substantially impair the intent and purpose of the zone plan and zoning ordinance; if not, the variance must be denied before any balancing of public benefits against detriments. These applicants remain exempt from the heightened Medici proof standard that applies to ordinary use variances. The Court reversed the Appellate Division and remanded to the zoning board to reconsider under the new standard, expressing no view on whether the project should be approved.
live-017: Travelers Property Casualty Company of America and St. Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Company, which issued excess policies under Travelers, filed a declaratory judgment action in Marion Superior Court on Nov. 26, 2025 against Washington Shoppes LP and The Broadbent Company, Inc. (No. 49D01-2511-CE-056363), The Indiana Lawyer reported. The insurers ask the court to declare that they owe no defense or indemnity coverage for cleanup at the shopping center at 10021 E. Washington St. in Indianapolis. Washington Shoppes has owned the site since 1998; The Indiana Lawyer describes Broadbent as owning the retail area that Washington Shoppes operates. Sunrise Dry Cleaners operated at or around the address from 1987 to 1996. A 2023 site investigation requested by the shopping center found tetrachloroethylene (PCE) and its degradation products in the soil and groundwater. The Indiana Department of Environmental Management later identified the property owner as potentially responsible for the contamination, and the center sought coverage for defense and cleanup costs. The insurers say each of their primary and excess policies excludes coverage for pollutants such as tetrachloroethylene. They also argue that, even if Washington Shoppes shows it qualifies as an insured, coverage may be barred if it knew of actual or potential contamination before acquiring the site or before the policies were issued. Attorneys for both sides did not respond to The Indiana Lawyer's requests for comment.
live-019: The United States, at EPA's request, and the State of Montana, through its Department of Environmental Quality, sued Columbia Falls Aluminum Company, LLC on July 2, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Montana, Missoula Division, under CERCLA and Montana's state cleanup law. The complaint describes CFAC as the successor to the company that owned and operated the aluminum reduction plant at the roughly 1,340-acre site northeast of Columbia Falls. A proposed consent decree was lodged the same day. According to the Justice Department's Federal Register notice, CFAC will reimburse EPA $1.8 million in past response costs, pay future response costs, and perform the remedy in EPA's January 2025 Record of Decision, work EPA estimates at $57,634,528. EPA's July 6, 2026 announcement said the cleanup will address arsenic, cyanide, fluoride and polyaromatic hydrocarbon contamination, including low-permeability caps on landfills and a slurry wall around the main source of groundwater contamination to stop migration toward the Flathead River. The plant operated from 1955 to 2009, and EPA said spent potliner stored in unlined landfills leached contaminants into groundwater. EPA quoted the president of CFAC's parent company, Glencore Ltd., as calling the cleanup a positive step. The notice opened a 30-day public comment period ending August 6, 2026. The plaintiffs moved to approve the consent judgment on August 31, the case was reassigned to Judge William W. Mercer on September 3, and on November 12, 2026 the court entered an order on the motion and the consent judgment.
live-022: RealPage, which licenses revenue-management software to owners and managers of residential rental properties, sued Attorney General Letitia James in the Southern District of New York in November 2025 (No. 1:25-cv-09847), challenging General Business Law § 340-B, which New York enacted on October 16, 2025 as an amendment to its antitrust law, the Donnelly Act. Section 2 of the law bars facilitating agreements between competing landlords not to compete, including by operating software that performs a "coordinating function," which the law defines as collecting pricing and lease data from two or more unaffiliated landlords, analyzing it by computer, and recommending rents or lease terms. Section 3 makes it unlawful for landlords to set or adjust rents based on such software's recommendations. RealPage moved for a preliminary injunction, the state agreed not to enforce the law until that motion was decided, and the attorney general moved to dismiss. While the motions were pending, RealPage filed notices of supplemental authority, including, on August 10, 2026, the Second Circuit's August 5 decision in DoorDash, Inc. v. City of New York, which held that a New York City rule requiring delivery platforms to share customer information with restaurants violated the First Amendment. In an August 13 letter, reported by Law360, the attorney general's office said that case involved a compelled disclosure of customer data, while the New York statute regulates anticompetitive conduct. In her September 29 opinion, Judge Caproni found that RealPage's recommendations, which it now generates mostly from customer-supplied and public data under its consent decree with the U.S. Department of Justice, are commercial speech subject to intermediate scrutiny, and that Section 3, as drafted, "probably does not" survive that review. She found that Section 2 targets conduct that is already illegal and does not restrict protected speech. She denied the motion to dismiss on both jurisdictional and pleading grounds. The attorney general answered the complaint and moved for reconsideration on October 13, 2026, and briefing on that motion closed on November 3. Under an October 23 scheduling order, fact discovery is due by February 22, 2027, and the case will be tried without a jury.
live-023: U.S. Bank National Association filed a complaint in Denver District Court on Monday, August 10, 2026, on behalf of lenders, seeking appointment of a receiver for Republic Plaza after a loan default in March, the Denver Gazette reported. A receiver would protect and maintain the property to ensure the lender's debt is repaid. The complaint says the defendant, "being a sophisticated commercial borrower, has failed to make payments as required by the Loan Documents," and that the plaintiff has "reasonable concern" that the property will not be properly operated or maintained. The 56-story tower at 370 17th St. is owned and managed by Brookfield Properties, which recently rebranded as BGRE, and MetLife Investment Management is also an owner. Brookfield declined to comment to the Gazette. The building narrowly avoided foreclosure in 2023 under a deal that gave its owners until March 2026, 9News reported at the time, according to the Gazette, which also reported that Bank of America's Colorado office was set to move out of the building in October. Reported loan figures differ. Connect CRE, citing the Denver Business Journal, described an approximately $130 million defaulted loan, while a later Connect CRE roundup citing Morningstar Credit listed the loan at $230.1 million, held in two CMBS trusts. That roundup said Trigild has been appointed receiver and plans to sell the property in 2027, that the loan moved to special servicing ahead of its March maturity, and that the property was appraised at $136.0 million after the transfer.
live-024: U.S. Bank, acting for two lender groups, has sued to foreclose on the retail portion of Brightline's MiamiCentral station, The Real Deal reported, citing the South Florida Business Journal. The defendants are Brightline Investment Holdings, the Brightline-affiliated owner of the 124,000 square feet of retail at 600 Northwest First Avenue, one of its subsidiaries, and property manager FECI Realty. The case does not involve the train station, the rail company or the station's office buildings, which Blackstone-managed funds bought in 2021 for $230 million, and the retail space and station remain open. The retail property was financed in 2022 with a $128.5 million loan split into two pieces. The $65 million senior piece is held by XYQ Cayman Ltd., which the lawsuit identifies as an affiliate of Boston-based Bracebridge Capital; four EB-5 funds for foreign investors seeking U.S. green cards hold the remaining $63 million. The senior piece is paid first, and the foreclosure suit concerns only that piece. The lender alleges the borrower failed to make a $16 million principal payment due Dec. 26, 2025 and a $6 million payment due March 15, 2026, and stopped making quarterly interest payments in December 2025. It says the full $65 million senior balance is now due and asks the court to foreclose, enforce guarantees from Brightline Investment Holdings and its subsidiary, and appoint a receiver to oversee the property. The report did not include a response from Brightline. The retail space is 65 percent leased, with 41,000 square feet available, according to an online listing cited by The Real Deal. Tenants include AT&T, Starbucks, Chick-fil-A, Rosetta Bakery, Joe & The Juice and Wolf of Tacos. The suit follows Fitch's July downgrade of bonds issued by the separately owned rail operator, Brightline Trains Florida; the rating agency cited a "very high probability" that the operator will miss coming debt payments.
live-026: Acres Loan Origination LLC, an affiliate of commercial mortgage lender Acres Capital, has filed a foreclosure complaint in New York state Supreme Court against the Auden Buffalo student housing community at 2915-2949 N. Forest Road in Amherst, Buffalo Business First reported, according to Connect CRE's roundup for the week of August 13, 2026. The defendant is an affiliate of DMG Investments, a New York City real estate developer. In the complaint, Acres says it made two loans totaling $32.5 million in early 2021 to finance construction of Auden Buffalo, and that the loan matured in January 2024 with all of the principal still unpaid. The filing came days after a group of lenders represented by Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. began foreclosure proceedings against Air Buffalo, an apartment building at 1265 Sweet Home Rd. that is also owned by a DMG affiliate, according to the same report. Connect CRE's summary did not include a response from DMG.
live-028: The Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project is a planned 67-mile transmission line through rural parts of Baltimore, Carroll and Frederick counties that New Jersey-based PSEG is building at the behest of grid officials, according to Maryland Matters. To complete its application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity, PSEG needed field surveys: the Fourth Circuit's opinion says Maryland's Power Plant Research Program deemed the application incomplete until certain field-based studies were done. PSEG sued in the District of Maryland on April 15, 2025 against landowners who refused access, invoking Real Property Section 12-111(a), which lets a 'body politic or corporate having the power of eminent domain' enter private land for surveys after a bona fide effort to notify the owner in writing. Judge Adam B. Abelson granted a preliminary injunction on June 20, 2025. On appeal, 117 parties argued that letting PSEG survey would amount to exercising eminent domain before it holds a certificate. The panel disagreed. If that were required, Judge Berner wrote, PSEG would have 'no viable path' to obtaining a certificate, and delaying the permitting process 'could exacerbate the very energy crisis' the project was meant to address. The panel found no abuse of discretion in the injunction, agreed with the district court that the brief access the statute allows is not a taking under the federal or Maryland constitutions, and rejected the argument that PSEG's in-service deadline could not be met. Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III joined the opinion; Judge Julius N. Richardson concurred. PSEG said it appreciated the court's 'careful consideration' and would keep engaging with property owners. The president of the opposition group Stop MPRP said she was 'deeply disappointed' and noted the ruling does not approve the line or let PSEG acquire land, questions still before the Public Service Commission. Maryland Matters reported that Abelson had held one resident in contempt in July for obstructing surveyors and had allowed U.S. marshals to accompany surveyors onto a handful of properties. On November 4, 2026, 60 landowners, represented by a public interest law firm, asked the U.S. Supreme Court to hear the case, arguing the Fourth Circuit allowed entry without first establishing that PSEG holds the eminent domain power its right of entry depends on, Maryland Matters reported.
live-029: The developer of the Mandarin Oriental-branded Residences in Boca Raton has sued its lender, an affiliate of Madison Realty Capital, in New York state court, days before a scheduled UCC foreclosure auction of the developer's ownership interests, The Real Deal reported. Via Mizner Owner III LLC and Via Mizner Pledgor III LLC, led by Penn-Florida Companies president and CEO Mark Gensheimer, filed the suit on Aug. 13, 2026 against Via Mizner Lender 1 and Via Mizner Lender 2 LLC and seek more than $500 million in damages. They ask for declaratory judgments on the parties' relationship and on alleged violations of New York's Uniform Commercial Code, and for an order stopping the sale. On Aug. 17, Justice Andrew Borrok signed an order temporarily halting the auction and set a hearing for Oct. 1. According to the complaint, Madison led more than $300 million in financing for the project in 2023 and, months later, stopped funding, saying the loans "were out of balance." The developer says it then could not pay vendors, and that Madison took control of construction, replaced the project manager with Straticon LLC, began paying vendors directly and put a lawyer without construction experience in charge of decisions. The complaint also alleges Madison told a consultant's employee to go "scorched Earth" on the project, and that all work stopped once Madison stopped paying vendors. It accuses Madison of "gross mismanagement and gross negligence" and of manufacturing the defaults behind its enforcement. Madison did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In July 2026 the lender filed a nearly $418 million foreclosure suit against the developer, alleging missed payments beginning in 2024 and a failure to repay the loan when it matured. By late 2024 the two sides had signed restructuring agreements confirming Madison's control over the condo portion of the project, including its completion, according to the report. The 1.5-acre site at 105 East Camino Real is planned for a 164-key Mandarin Oriental-branded hotel and an 88-unit condo, linked by a sky bridge, which remain unfinished after years of delays; the project was first announced in 2015. Buyers, contractors and subcontractors have also sued the developer in separate cases over the years.
live-031: U.S. Bank National Association, as trustee for the registered holders of the Morgan Stanley Bank of America Merrill Lynch Trust 2016-C28, filed suit on August 12, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against Lenox Drive Office Park LLC, a Delaware company that owns office buildings on Lenox Drive in Mercer County, Mortgage Professional America reported. Greystone Servicing Company handles the loan. Lenox Drive Office Park LLC bought Princeton Pike Corporate Center in Lawrenceville in early 2016, NJB Magazine reported at the time. According to the complaint as reported, Morgan Stanley Bank, N.A. made a $130 million loan to the borrower in December 2015, split across several promissory notes and secured by a mortgage on the office park along with cash-management agreements and UCC filings on rents and fixtures. The loan matured on January 1, 2026, and the trust says it was not repaid. As of July 1, 2026, the trust says $141,767,219.75 was owed, including principal, interest at the note and default rates, late fees and servicing charges, with interest still accruing. The trust seeks an order foreclosing and selling the property and the appointment of a receiver to run the office park during the case and conduct the sale. The federal docket shows a clerk's entry of default on October 8, 2026, an amended complaint on October 29, and an entry titled "Appoint Receiver" on November 6. No court has ruled on the merits.
live-035: The developer and 9 New York Ave LLC filed the suit in the Circuit Court of Cook County, where JLL is headquartered, Law360 and Bisnow reported. Bisnow reported that the developer, a Maryland-based investor who had put money into multifamily deals before but is not a specialist in the sector, delivered the 115-unit Pinnacle in the NoMa neighborhood in 2024 and sold it in April 2026 to July Residential for $30.5 million. The complaint asserts breach of contract, fraud, fraudulent inducement, negligent misrepresentation and breach of fiduciary duty. According to Bisnow's account of the complaint, JLL projected stabilized NOI of $1.65 million in March 2021 and said construction lenders would require a minimum 8.5% debt yield, which that figure did not meet. JLL allegedly raised its projection to $1.94 million in December 2021 despite what the suit calls no material change in the property, then to $2.04 million in January 2022 and $2.07 million in the model given to the lender's appraiser, a level that cleared the threshold and implied a $51 million stabilized value. The suit attributes the increases to higher assumed rents, lower payroll, lower vacancy and no rent concessions. The appraisal for the lender, Hingham Institution for Savings, projected NOI of $1.85 million, and an appraisal the developer obtained in December 2020, before hiring JLL, projected $1.4 million. The suit says the developer invested more than $13.3 million and lost more than $7.4 million; the damages claim adds fees, interest and $4.3 million in lost opportunity. Hingham made a $23.7 million construction loan in May 2022, according to D.C. land records cited by Bisnow. The suit also says the developer tried in June to arbitrate under an April 2021 project management agreement, but JLL declined, arguing the claims did not fall under that agreement. JLL did not respond to Bisnow's requests for comment.
live-036: Wilmington Trust, a Delaware-based affiliate of M&T Bank Corp., sued Philadelphia-based Rubenstein Partners on June 7, 2024 in the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas to foreclose on the office tower at 312 Elm St. in downtown Cincinnati, the Cincinnati Business Courier reported in an article republished by Colliers. The complaint said Rubenstein owed $39.6 million in principal, interest, late charges and fees on a $46.1 million note executed in 2015, when Rubenstein bought the building. In an answer filed August 12, 2024, Rubenstein admitted each of the allegations, including that it had defaulted. Judge Lisa Allen appointed a managing director of Colliers Real Estate Management Services as receiver on July 30, 2024, with authority to collect rents, lease vacant space with the lender's consent and, with court approval, sell the building. The Business Courier said 312 Elm was the third office building in Cincinnati's central business district to go into receivership; the Netherland Plaza Hotel and the tower at 600 Vine St. were also in receivership. The tower, completed in 1992, has more than 378,000 square feet and was about 45.7% occupied. On December 30, 2024, Wilmington Trust filed a similar foreclosure suit against Rubenstein over 312 Plum St., a nearby office tower that Rubenstein bought in a deal that closed the same day as its 312 Elm purchase, the Business Courier reported. That complaint alleged Rubenstein owed $16.2 million on an $18.4 million mortgage loan and was delinquent on debts to vendors, and said the lender terminated a June 2024 discounted payoff agreement in October 2024 after Rubenstein allegedly failed to comply with it. In May 2026, the Business Courier reported that the foreclosure cases over both towers were resolved and that the 26-story 312 Elm tower and the 312 Plum tower were listed for an online Hamilton County sheriff's auction starting June 17, 2026, a process it said would likely see them revert to their lenders.
live-037: The lender on a $37.5 million commercial mortgage-backed securities loan has sued in federal court to foreclose on 10 East 34th Street, a 10-story, 55,000-square-foot office building between Fifth and Madison avenues, across the street from the Empire State Building. The complaint, filed August 14, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (No. 1:26-cv-06952), names the borrower, 10East34th, LLC, and asks the court both to foreclose and to appoint a receiver to run the property. According to The Real Deal, Caerus Group bought the building for $51.7 million in 2016, and it soon changed hands again. The current owner took out a 10-year, $37.5 million mortgage from Morgan Stanley in 2018, according to court documents cited by The Real Deal, and the loan was packaged into the BANK 2018-BNK13 CMBS trust. Caerus is not the owner or a party to the case. The complaint alleges that the owner stopped making monthly payments on April 1, 2026. Servicer Trimont sent a letter on May 6 asking for more than $500,000 to cover the missed April and May payments; June and July passed without payments, and the lender's lawyers sent another letter on June 30. The lender alleges that occupancy has fallen sharply over the past two years and that the lead tenant stopped paying rent for several months. The ground-floor retail tenant, a virtual reality venue, has closed, and the two remaining tenants occupy less than 30 percent of the building, The Real Deal reported. The case is before Judge Ronnie Abrams. In October the parties submitted a proposed stipulation and consent order on the appointment of a receiver, and the court asked them to propose the amount of the receiver's undertaking. After an October 30 status conference, the court ordered a joint status letter by December 1, 2026.
live-038: UMB Bank N.A., as bond trustee, has sued the Public Finance Authority and managers of a bond-financed cancer treatment center in Delray Beach, Florida, seeking receivership and foreclosure of the property, The Bond Buyer reported on July 29, 2026. According to the South Florida Business Journal, as summarized by Connect CRE, UMB, acting as trustee for investors in two bond funds, filed the leasehold foreclosure suit on July 13 against Public Finance Authority, a Wisconsin-based conduit issuer that issued bonds to finance the proton therapy center, which is mostly used for cancer treatment. The Business Journal reported that the South Florida Proton Therapy Institute and its equipment at Delray Medical Center could be seized in the $81.32 million suit. The complaint also names Tenet Healthcare Corp., Proton International LLC and Varian Medical Systems as parties that may claim an interest in the center but are not guarantors.
live-039: The owner of 148 State St., a Financial District office building, sued the City of Boston in Suffolk Superior Court on December 17, 2025, in a proposed class action alleging that the Assessing Department retaliated against commercial owners who appealed their assessments to the state Appellate Tax Board. The Pioneer New England Legal Foundation represents the owner. According to the foundation, the complaint alleges assessors overrode the city's CAMS valuation software and added back value under a "discretionary adjustment" for appealed properties. The suit asserts four claims: failure to determine fair cash value under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 59, Section 2A(a); retaliation for petitioning in violation of the First Amendment; denial of free access to the courts under Articles XI and XVI of the Massachusetts Constitution; and violation of Amendment Article CXII, which requires property within a class to be taxed proportionally and equally. It seeks to stop the practice, a declaration that it is unlawful, and repayment of excess taxes for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. The city argued the case should be dismissed because the plaintiff had not exhausted its administrative appeals, Banker & Tradesman reported. In a ruling issued May 11, 2026, Judge Peter B. Krupp allowed the suit to proceed to "at a minimum, some limited discovery," noting the plaintiff's allegation that at least 60 commercial taxpayers had been subject to the policy. He also noted that the chairman of the Assessing Department's Board of Review had said the city "stabilized" the values of properties with open appeals to align with prior years. On August 18, 2026, the foundation said data the city voluntarily provided on commercial properties valued at $6 million or more showed 150 properties and 182 instances in which taxes rose after an appeal, with disputed payments of about $19 million, Banker & Tradesman reported. The foundation's president said the practice appeared designed to limit the revenue lost to falling commercial assessments. The foundation sent its fourth request asking Department of Revenue Commissioner Geoffrey Snyder to investigate; a DOR spokesperson did not respond to Banker & Tradesman.
live-040: The New Jersey Supreme Court ruled on August 10, 2026 that a municipality condemning property does not have to state, in the ordinance authorizing the taking, the public use it intends. The 6-1 decision in Borough of Seaside Park v. Shree Jyoti, LLC (A-2-25) resolves the borough's effort to acquire the Desert Palm Inn, a motel it moved to condemn in April 2022, the New Jersey Monitor reported. According to the opinion, the borough council passed a resolution authorizing an appraisal and acquisition by eminent domain on November 15, 2021, and on April 14, 2022 passed an ordinance saying the taking would 'promote and protect the health, safety and welfare' of residents. The opinion notes that the record documented extensive code violations and a history of police incidents at the property. The borough's first condemnation complaint, filed July 19, 2022, was dismissed without prejudice because the ordinance did not specify a public use; its amended complaint identified a public parking lot with electric vehicle charging, and the borough later added a public drinking water well. The trial court and Appellate Division ruled for the borough. 'No law requires a municipality to articulate the intended public use in the ordinance itself,' Justice Michael Noriega wrote for the majority. The court also observed that the matter 'likely could have been resolved by simply disclosing the intended public use at the earliest reasonable point,' the Monitor reported. Justice John Hoffman agreed the statutes do not require a stated public use but would have blocked the acquisition under the 'square corners' doctrine, which requires government to deal forthrightly with the public. He wrote that Seaside Park knew its plans at least a month before moving to condemn but declined to tell the owner when asked, and that 'the majority degrades the square corners doctrine.' He contrasted the ruling with a recent decision blocking Jackson Township's use of eminent domain where its stated public purpose was found false.
live-041: In December 2018 the trustee of 100 Norfolk Street Realty Trust leased part of a warehouse building in Boston's Roxbury section to Chen's Food Enterprise, Inc. for ten years at $9,000 a month, according to the Appeals Court's opinion. In October 2023 the landlord brought a summary process case for nonpayment, seeking possession and $193,581. At the January 2024 trial, the judge granted the tenant's motion for involuntary dismissal at the close of the landlord's case because the landlord had not proved it sent the notice of termination the lease required; judgment of dismissal entered February 2, 2024. The landlord sent a notice of termination on February 12, 2024 and filed a new summary process case in the Roxbury Division of the Boston Municipal Court on February 26, claiming nonpayment of rent and wrongful transfer of the lease and seeking $205,267.50 and possession. The tenant's principal was later added as a defendant. After a three-day bench trial in June 2024, the same judge, Kenneth J. Fiandaca, rejected the tenant's claim-preclusion defense and awarded the landlord possession and $198,000 plus interest and costs. The Appellate Division of the Boston Municipal Court reversed, reasoning that the involuntary dismissal of the first case was an adjudication on the merits that barred the second. The Appeals Court (Shin, Ditkoff and Tan, JJ.) reversed. It did not resolve the parties' arguments over the elements of claim preclusion. It held instead that G. L. c. 239, § 7, which provides that a summary process judgment "shall not be a bar to any action thereafter brought by either party to recover the land or tenements in question," authorized the second case, and that the statute controls over the civil procedure rule treating an involuntary dismissal as on the merits. The court rejected the tenant's argument that reading the statute literally would let a landlord sue again until it wins, explaining that issue preclusion still bars relitigating issues actually decided. Because the Appellate Division had not reached the tenant's other appeal arguments, the Appeals Court remanded the case to the Appellate Division to address them. The $198,000 trial judgment is therefore not yet final.
live-045: Wells Fargo Bank, representing a commercial mortgage-backed securities trust, filed foreclosure lawsuits in multiple states in August 2026 over the portfolio backing a $1.28 billion loan to Workspace Property Trust, Bisnow reported on August 24, 2026. A suit filed in Hennepin County, Minnesota puts the unpaid principal at about $1.23 billion, and the lender says it is owed that balance plus interest, special servicer fees and attorney expenses. KeyBank National Association is the special servicer and attorney-in-fact for the lender, according to the new suits. Workspace obtained the CMBS loan in 2018, backed by 146 office and industrial properties totaling nearly 10 million square feet across four states. The portfolio now includes 143 properties in Arizona, Florida, Minnesota and Pennsylvania and is valued at $1.24 billion, down from $1.63 billion at issuance, according to Morningstar Credit. Occupancy is about 75%, down from nearly 89% at origination and 81% in 2022. The loan moved to special servicing in May 2023. It was scheduled to mature in July 2023 without extension options, but Workspace obtained a two-year extension that month; CEO Thomas Rizk told Bisnow in 2023 that existing investors had put significant new money into the company as part of the deal. Trigild was appointed receiver for the entire portfolio after Wells Fargo filed suit in Maricopa County, Arizona, in September 2025. Workspace Property Trust declined to comment, and Wells Fargo and KeyBank did not respond to Bisnow by press time.
live-046: On Monday, Aug. 17, 2026, Judge Kimberly Fitzpatrick of the 342nd District Court in Tarrant County signed a temporary restraining order barring the Town of Westlake from "holding a vote on, approving, adopting, or taking any action to implement Resolution 26-25 concerning the Circle T Data Center," including at a special meeting set for that day, The Dallas Express reported. The order took effect once the plaintiffs, the Lakes at Marshall Ridge Homeowners Association Inc. and two residents, posted a $5,000 bond. They allege Westlake failed to provide legally required public notice in connection with earlier zoning action affecting the project, and the order notes their contention that approving the resolution would authorize immediate grading, site work and construction. The judge struck four broader proposed provisions that would have barred approval of a development agreement, permits and site work, and the order did not resolve the merits. The project, by Virginia-based developer PowerHouse, consists of four buildings totaling about 1.1 million square feet on an 87.9-acre site along Denton Highway, Newsweek reported. Westlake has said the property has carried commercial and industrial zoning since 1998, that a data center is an allowed use, and that the project would expand its tax base while meeting local noise, water and landscaping rules, according to The Dallas Express. Newsweek, citing CBS News, reported that the plaintiffs also contend the site plan omits a setback and landscaped buffer the town's zoning ordinance requires between the data center and single-family homes. The judge heard arguments on Aug. 26 and left the order in place pending a decision on extending it. The restraining order expired on Sept. 25 after the judge declined to extend it, saying she needed more time to review documents delivered that morning, and set a further hearing for Oct. 23, Fox 4 reported. The neighboring City of Keller, which had sought its own temporary injunction, signed a $1.876 million settlement with Circle T Owner LP on Nov. 5, The Dallas Express reported. It provides $1.5 million for a noise mitigation fund, $300,000 for fire protection and $76,000 toward Keller's legal and consultant costs, along with nighttime and daytime noise limits, quarterly noise monitoring, a landscaped berm and emissions controls on backup generators; the payments depend on a separate Keller-Westlake settlement and dismissal of Keller's claims against the town. The status of the homeowners association's own claims was not reported.
live-047: On August 26, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit affirmed a Northern District of Georgia summary judgment holding the guarantor of a $56.33 million loan from Access Point Financial, LLC personally liable for $3,954,244.04. In an unpublished per curiam opinion, Judges Newsom, Lagoa and Brasher held that a borrower's voluntary Chapter 11 petition, filed the day before a scheduled foreclosure sale, was a full-recourse event under the guaranty. According to the opinion, Access Point lent $56,330,000 in October 2021 to three borrowers owning properties in Houston, Austin and Dallas, Texas; Bisnow reported in 2023 that the loan covered three former Crowne Plaza hotels and that the borrower was tied to Lockwood Development Partners. The guarantor, who managed the borrowers' parent entities, agreed to be personally liable for the full debt if, among other events, a borrower filed a voluntary bankruptcy petition or made a transfer the lender had not permitted. In September 2022 he replaced himself with DDI Equities, Inc. as the borrowers' manager without Access Point's consent. The Austin property was sold in 2022 for $30,739,480.22, which paid down the loan. After the borrowers defaulted, Access Point scheduled foreclosure of the Houston and Dallas properties for September 5, 2023. The day before, the Houston borrower transferred all its membership interests to 3 Big MMM, LLC without Access Point's consent and, under new management, filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition in the Southern District of Florida, which the bankruptcy court later dismissed as a skeletal petition. Access Point bought the Dallas property with a $10 million credit bid on September 5 and later the Houston property with a $7,846,000 credit bid, leaving about $3 million plus interest unpaid. It sued the guarantor on September 18, 2023, and the district court granted summary judgment on two grounds: the bankruptcy filing and the change of manager. On appeal, the guarantor argued that 3 Big MMM had no authority to file the petition, so the borrower had not filed one within the guaranty's meaning. Applying Georgia law, which construes guaranties strongly against the guarantor, the panel held that the guaranty did not require an 'authorized' or 'successful' petition, and it was undisputed that the Houston borrower had filed one. Having affirmed on that ground, the court did not decide whether the manager change or the transfer to 3 Big MMM was also a full-recourse event.
live-048: Held Properties, a family-owned company, has sued WealthStone, a tenant at its 1880 Century Park East office tower in Century City, over unpaid rent, The Real Deal reported. WealthStone is a real estate firm run by brothers Andres and Jean Paul Szita, who also started the development company Laurus Corporation and its fundraising arm, Ethika Investments. The early August complaint says WealthStone "fell behind on payments" and "has failed and refused" to pay rent. This is the landlord's second suit against the tenant. Held Properties was awarded $393,000 in an earlier case and now says it is owed another $708,000 in back rent, other charges and interest. It is also suing Andres Szita personally as the lease's guarantor and says he is liable for the full $1.1 million, including the earlier award; it appears to want the total from WealthStone, Szita or both. Neither Robert Held, the company's CEO, nor Szita responded to requests for comment. According to the five-year lease attached to the complaint, the 2019 deal covered about 4,400 square feet on the 10th floor. Rent started at $3.75 per square foot a month and rose each year to $4.22 in 2024, or roughly $197,000 in the first year and $222,000 in the last. The Real Deal noted that Class A space in Century City now rents for about $7.75 per square foot a month. The 15-story building has more than 300,000 square feet of offices.
live-049: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court on Aug. 19, 2026 affirmed a Superior Court judgment allowing Boston's rebuild of White Stadium in Franklin Park to continue, WBUR reported. The project is a public-private partnership that splits its $325 million cost between the city and Boston Legacy FC, which is paying $190 million. The suit (SJC-13865) was brought by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and 20 individual plaintiffs, who argued that the rebuild illegally privatizes public parkland and would require an act of the Legislature. Writing for the court, Justice Gabrielle R. Wolohojian first held that the plaintiffs have no cognizable individual interest in the George Robert White Fund, the public charitable trust that owns the stadium, and so lack standing to challenge alleged violations of its terms. The plaintiffs urged a more relaxed standing test because the Attorney General had decided not to bring an enforcement action. The court declined, holding that membership in an organization whose mission is in harmony with a trust's purpose, or recreational use of trust land as a member of the public, is not enough. On the main issue, the court held that the stadium parcel is not subject to Article 97 of the state constitution, which requires a two-thirds vote of the Legislature to dispose of parkland or convert it to another use. The city took the land by eminent domain for a public park in 1883, but a 1947 statute authorized conveying the parcel to the White Fund and a 1950 statute designated the stadium as a school building and yard. Together, the court held, those statutes removed the parcel from parkland status more than 20 years before Article 97 was ratified in 1972. The court also rejected the plaintiffs' challenges to planned uses of areas of Franklin Park outside the stadium parcel. Mayor Michelle Wu praised the decision and said construction was on track for a planned summer 2027 opening. The Conservancy's president said the group was disappointed and repeated its call for a smaller, fully public project, and Boston Legacy FC called the ruling a "tremendous victory," according to WBUR. The suit was filed in Superior Court on Feb. 20, 2024; after a three-day bench trial, the trial judge entered judgment for the defendants, and the SJC transferred the appeal from the Appeals Court on its own initiative.
live-050: Cushman & Wakefield has replaced SL Green Realty as property manager of Worldwide Plaza, the 49-story Midtown Manhattan office tower at 825 Eighth Ave., according to court filings reported by Bisnow on Aug. 10, 2026. A judge approved transferring management away from SL Green by July 1. Hilco Global was appointed temporary receiver in March, and as part of the transition the receiver set up new bank accounts, obtained other insurance coverage and hired a new tax consultant and leasing brokers. Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank and a trustee for CMBS bondholders, together responsible for the $940 million senior mortgage, sued in New York State Supreme Court in Manhattan to foreclose, Commercial Property Executive reported in February 2026, citing Bisnow. Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Bank have since been removed as plaintiffs, leaving Wilmington Trust representing the bondholders. According to the lawsuit as described by CPE, the 2017 loan was split into a $705 million CMBS loan and a $235 million companion loan, and beginning in 2025 the borrowers repeatedly missed or only partly made interest payments, including a payment of more than $2.9 million due Dec. 8, and did not pay $6.5 million of a $21.6 million tax bill in January. An SL Green spokesperson told Bisnow at the time that the suit was a procedural step and that all parties were working toward a resolution. Law firm Cravath, Swaine & Moore left its 617,000 square feet at the tower in 2024, and an appraisal the next year cut the property's valuation by $1.4 billion, Bisnow reported. SL Green's earnings statement put occupancy at 61% as of June 30, while the receiver's June report put it at 51%. The receiver also reported monthly net operating income of negative $484,000, said WNET was preparing to leave when its 95,000-square-foot lease expired, and said default and eviction proceedings were under way against three retail tenants. On SL Green's July 23 earnings call, Chairman and CEO Marc Holliday said the asset needed to be recapitalized after Cravath's move-out. Extell Development acquired the property's $190 million senior mezzanine loan in October 2025, about a year after the owners defaulted on that debt, and scheduled its own UCC foreclosure auction. SL Green and RXR sued to block it, but Justice Andrea Masley denied their request for a preliminary injunction; they appealed, and that case is ongoing. A $70 million junior mezzanine loan is also in monetary default, according to an SEC filing by New York REIT Liquidating LLC, which holds a 49.9% interest in the property; the SL Green-RXR venture owns 50.1%. Bondholders stand to lose up to $488 million, Bloomberg reported, according to Bisnow. Representatives for SL Green, RXR and Cushman did not immediately respond to Bisnow's requests for comment.
live-051: U.S. District Judge Nitza I. Quiñones Alejandro of the Eastern District of Pennsylvania on Aug. 17, 2026 granted receiver CBRE's motion to approve the private sale of Centre Square, Philadelphia's largest office property, to affiliates of Dean Adler and PMC Property Group for $70 million, ahead of an Oct. 16 deadline for the transaction, Bisnow reported, citing the Philadelphia Business Journal. According to the PBJ, she wrote that there was "no just reason for delay" and that the order was final immediately for purposes of appeal. The two-tower, 2.2-million-square-foot complex at 1500 Market St. has been in foreclosure since 2023. Wells Fargo Bank, as trustee for a CMBS trust, filed the foreclosure complaint against owner NG 1500 Market St. LLC on Jan. 12, 2023, and the court appointed CBRE as receiver on April 14, 2023, according to the court docket. Nightingale Properties and InterVest Capital Partners bought the property in 2017 and refinanced it two years later with a $390 million loan from JPMorgan Chase before stopping payments, Bisnow reported. Occupancy was 36% when CBRE listed the property for sale as a potential conversion in August 2025. The $70 million price is 21% of what Nightingale and InterVest paid. Adler and PMC went under contract with CBRE in March 2026 with plans for a partial mixed-use redevelopment including apartments and a hotel. Later that month, CSC Coliving and Universal Group Co. challenged the sale, saying they had submitted higher bids; CSC Coliving later withdrew its challenge. Adler and PMC then sought to get out of the purchase despite a $5 million nonrefundable deposit, with Adler telling The Philadelphia Inquirer in July that the buyers needed to do more homework. The court denied Universal Group's motion to intervene on July 27 and its motion for reconsideration on Aug. 7, according to the docket. Universal filed a notice of appeal to the Third Circuit on Aug. 26.
live-052: Wilmington Trust National Association, acting as trustee for a Redwood Trust Inc. subsidiary that holds the loans, has sued in the Circuit Court of Cook County to foreclose on 137 condominium units spread across seven Chicago buildings, along with the rents those units produce. According to documents The Real Deal obtained from the court, the lender seeks nearly $51 million in principal and accrued interest, plus late charges, attorneys' fees and other costs that are not included in that figure. The loans were originated by CoreVest, Redwood's San Francisco-based lending arm. The debt consists of two revolving credit lines, extended in November 2021 and January 2023, that together total $85 million. The borrowers are two entities for which Yitzy Klor, head of Strategic Properties of North America (SPNA), is the registered agent under state records, and Klor personally backs the debt. The complaint alleges Klor drew at least $51 million that remains unpaid. It dates the first default to Nov. 10, 2023, and describes a forbearance agreement reached in March 2024 and later extended to January 2026, followed by a loan modification in May 2026, before the lender filed suit. SPNA's model is the condo deconversion: buying units one at a time, then offering to buy the rest in bulk so the building can be run as a rental. Chicago lets a buyer force out holdouts once owners holding a set share of the building agree; The Real Deal noted the city raised that threshold from 75 percent to 85 percent of a building's value in 2019. The largest block in the suit, 47 units, is at 200 North Dearborn Street, a 309-unit high-rise. SPNA offered $95 million for that building in 2022, and two more offers made this year through an entity called YK Investments were rejected, The Real Deal reported. The other units are at 1850 North Clark Street, 70 West Huron Street, 33 West Delaware Place, 211 East Ohio Street, 3660 North Lake Shore Drive and 440 North Wabash Avenue. The Real Deal also reported that SPNA's Skokie office, the borrowers' registered address, is the subject of a separate $340,000 foreclosure suit filed earlier this year, and that attorneys for Byline Bank have brought litigation involving that building. Klor did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the publication said.
live-053: A New York Supreme Court judge has ordered a foreclosure auction of 500 and 512 Seventh Avenue, two Midtown office buildings, to satisfy a $356 million debt, The Real Deal reported on Aug. 24, 2026. According to court documents cited by the publication, the borrower agreed not to oppose the lender's foreclosure motion. The lender filed its foreclosure suit in July 2025. The borrower, 500-512 Seventh Avenue Limited Partnership, is a partnership of brothers Meyer and Joseph Chetrit, Joseph Moinian and Edward Minskoff. It bought the leasehold for $140 million in 1999 and borrowed $375 million against the buildings in 2018. The loan also covers 228 West 38th Street. No. 512 is a 45-story tower with 544,300 rentable square feet, and No. 500 is an 18-story building with 676,500 rentable square feet. The Chetrit Group has its offices in No. 512. The lender's case centers on that office lease. It says the Chetrit Group ran up more than $1 million in unpaid rent, and an attorney for the lender told the court the failure was "evidence of self-dealing or, at a minimum, severe negligence and mismanagement," given that the guarantor is an insider of the borrower. In a deposition this spring, Meyer Chetrit said the Chetrit Group held a 56 percent stake and had never paid the $42,000 rent on its offices in the "four or five" years it had been there, The Real Deal reported. The lender had earlier accused the borrower of moving $1 million in tenant security deposits to outside funds, including $300,000 to other Chetrit Group projects or associates, and of missing monthly payments. Representatives for the Chetrits, Moinian and Minskoff did not immediately respond to The Real Deal's request for comment. Asked in the deposition where the foreclosure stood, Meyer Chetrit answered: "About to lose it already."
live-054: On August 6, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a judgment for Nassau County in The Retail Property Trust's challenge to a $4.8 million fine for failing to file income and expense statements for Roosevelt Field in Garden City, which the court described as the second-largest shopping mall in New York State, with over 2 million square feet of leasable space. The Trust, a Massachusetts business trust, is listed as a subsidiary of Simon Property Group in Simon's annual reports filed with the SEC. Judge Richard J. Sullivan wrote for the panel, which also included Judges Richard C. Wesley and Steven J. Menashi. According to the opinion, Nassau County's Annual Statement of Income and Expense (ASIE) Law requires commercial property owners to report financial data so assessors can value properties accurately; the county, which alone pays refunds when properties are overvalued, faced tax certiorari refunds of roughly $100 million a year. In late 2013, the county replaced a $500 penalty with fines of 0.25% to 0.75% of a property's fair market value, depending on how long an owner takes to comply. The Trust did not file statements for 2013 and 2014, and in 2016 the county imposed $4,753,209 in penalties. The Trust says it never received the preliminary notice letters the law requires. Rather than use the law's remedies or a state Article 78 petition, it sued in the Eastern District of New York in 2017. Judge Joanna Seybert, adopting a magistrate judge's recommendation, granted the county summary judgment, denied the Trust's sanctions motion and dismissed its state-law claims without prejudice. The panel first held that the Excessive Fines Clause shields business entities, including trusts and corporations. Applying the Bajakajian factors, it then found the fine not grossly disproportional: the Trust knowingly and willfully failed to comply over years, it was the kind of income-producing owner the law targets, the penalty scaled with the property's value and was lower than New York City's 5% penalty, and the noncompliance undermined accurate assessment. The court wrote that the owner of a multi-hundred-million-dollar property fined 'a fraction of one percent of the property's value' for willful, repeated refusal to comply cannot claim gross disproportionality. It also held that Article 78 review gave the Trust adequate procedural due process, that the law has a rational basis, and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in denying sanctions. Judge Wesley concurred, arguing that the court did not need to decide whether the Excessive Fines Clause applies to business entities, or to a Massachusetts business trust, because the fine was not excessive in any event. The majority responded that the question was squarely presented and that resolving it gives district courts needed guidance.
live-055: The Atlanta City Council on August 18, 2025 unanimously approved a measure to acquire the Magnolia Park and Azalea Gardens apartment complexes on the city's Westside by eminent domain, Bisnow reported. The resolution, introduced by Council Member Byron Amos, says the properties have long suffered from neglect and unsafe conditions with little sign of reinvestment by their owners, and calls for a public-private partnership to redevelop them as "deeply affordable, high-quality housing." The city has 60 days to draft a plan covering the acquisition timeline, financing, redevelopment and tenant relocation. Azalea Gardens, a nine-building, 92-unit property, has been owned for 15 years by TYTA LLC, a New Jersey-registered entity. A manager at the company told Bisnow the property had negative cash flow for at least five years, that it is now vacant after the company relocated residents, and that TYTA plans to file demolition permits for an affordable housing project once it finds a financial partner. He said the company would ask the city to hold off on an eminent domain suit and would try to work with the city. Magnolia Park, with 300 units in 20 buildings on a 22-acre site, is owned by John Eagan Homes I and II LP, entities tied to two Florida addresses according to Fulton County records; Bisnow could not reach that owner. The council also unanimously approved a separate Amos resolution directing staff to identify multifamily properties where at least 10% of units have been blighted for 10 or more consecutive years and to prioritize acquiring them for long-term affordable housing. The measures add to the city's "blight tax," which lets Atlanta charge owners of blighted properties a higher tax rate until they are fixed or redeveloped, and to Mayor Andre Dickens' earlier proposal to use eminent domain against commercial and multifamily blight.
live-056: Harbor Custom Development, founded in Gig Harbor in 2014 as Harbor Custom Homes, filed for Chapter 11 protection in December 2023 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Washington, listing $172.5 million in debt and $224 million in assets across four states, The News Tribune reported. In February 2024 the company said it had found no viable plan and would wind down by selling four apartment properties and assets in three other states. One of those properties was Pacific Ridge Apartments, an 80-unit complex at 8445 Pacific Ave. S. in Tacoma's Fern Hill area, completed in 2022. The chief restructuring officer said in a June 13, 2024 declaration that the property was worth well below what was owed. Court filings put Sound Capital's construction loan balance at about $20.3 million as of June, and Pierce County assessed the property at more than $17.5 million. Harbor Custom's second amended Chapter 11 plan, filed in late June 2024, named Sound Capital Construction Fund, LLC as the recipient of the property under a settlement agreement and provided that the related lien would be extinguished and the loan deemed satisfied. Sound Capital NW Holdings LLC, affiliated with Bellevue-based Sound Capital Loans, took possession through a $5 million credit bid on August 21, 2024. Sound Capital did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.
live-057: Charlotte Hawkins LLC sued Bar One Lounge South End LLC and its two owners in Mecklenburg County Superior Court, alleging they defaulted on a 10-year lease for a nearly 2,400-square-foot space, the Charlotte Business Journal reported in April 2025. The Business Journal describes Charlotte Hawkins as tied to Atlanta-based Portman Holdings, which owns the 24-story Linea apartment tower at 2161 Hawkins St. in South End, a building with ground-floor space for shops and restaurants. Bar One announced plans in January 2023 to invest $10 million in locations in South End and Mooresville, including a roughly 2,400-square-foot space at Linea. In March 2025, one of the owners said he was not moving forward with the Mooresville location, and the Business Journal reported that the future of the South End restaurant is undetermined. The report does not state the amount sought or include a response from the defendants.
live-058: Oakworth Capital Bank, an Alabama lender, sued RC Nashville Development Partners, LLC and its principal on October 28, 2023 in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, alleging default on a $10 million note that matured and came due on August 9 and seeking $10,470,772.90 plus interest, the Nashville Post reported. The loan was tied to a planned two-tower development at 401-417 Seventh Ave. S.: a building for a Ritz-Carlton hotel, condominiums and a rooftop restaurant, alongside a 32-story apartment tower, in a $585 million project. The developer told the Post the project remained viable, cited inflation and rapid interest-rate increases, and said he was talking with two other lenders. On April 11, 2024, the triangular 1.2-acre lot at 727 Korean Veterans Boulevard, planned for a 46-story Ritz-Carlton tower, was sold at a foreclosure auction at the Metro Nashville Courthouse to R Squared Properties LLC of Washington for $35 million, the same price the site sold for in March 2020, the Tennessean reported. According to the docket, the court entered default against RC Nashville in April 2024, granted Oakworth summary judgment against the principal on October 30, 2024, entered a default judgment against RC Nashville on January 7, 2025, and entered an order dismissing the case on August 4, 2025.
live-062: A federal judge in North Carolina has entered settlements between LivCor, LLC, a multifamily landlord affiliated with Blackstone, and both the U.S. Justice Department and nine states over claims that LivCor used RealPage's revenue-management software and competitors' data to set apartment rents. Judge William L. Osteen Jr. of the Middle District of North Carolina entered the federal final judgment on May 19, 2026, and the states' final consent judgment and dismissal with prejudice on June 26, 2026, according to the court docket. LivCor was added to the government's antitrust case against RealPage in an amended complaint filed January 7, 2025, which named several large landlords. The Justice Department filed its proposed settlement with LivCor on December 23, 2025, and in April 2026 moved for its entry, certifying compliance with the Antitrust Procedures and Penalties Act. LivCor and the states filed a joint motion for their consent judgment on June 18, 2026. Attorney General Jeff Jackson announced the state settlement that day, ABC11 reported. His office said the settlement amount was $7 million and that LivCor controls about 3,500 apartments in North Carolina. LivCor will stop using non-public data from other landlords, through RealPage's software or by other means, to set rents. The attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Oregon and Tennessee joined North Carolina. LivCor admitted no wrongdoing and did not respond to ABC11's request for comment. Jackson said Greystar and Cortland, the state's two largest landlords, had already settled. On September 30, 2026, Judge Osteen denied motions to dismiss filed by RealPage, Camden Property Trust, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company, and denied LivCor's and Greystar's motions as moot. Those four defendants answered the amended complaint on November 11, 2026. The Justice Department has separately filed proposed settlements with Willow Bridge and Pinnacle.
live-063: New York-based J. Safra Real Estate, which acquired the ground lease for Faneuil Hall Marketplace from Ashkenazy Acquisition Corp. in 2024, has sued seven current and former tenants since 2024 for more than $2 million in unpaid rent, Bisnow reported on August 6, 2026, citing court filings first reported by the Boston Business Journal. live-064: On June 29, 2026, Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Glenn H. Yamahiro granted C.D. Smith Construction's motion for default judgment and ordered a money judgment of $11,301,704.63 against The Edison Project LLC and The Edison SPE, LLC, plus costs, expenses and reasonable attorneys' fees, according to the order in Case No. 26-CV-2091. Edison St., where a partially completed foundation sits for what was planned as a 31-story, 353-unit apartment tower. Smith filed its construction lien and foreclosure suit in March 2026 against Neutral and its project affiliates, after work stopped in September 2025. live-065: The Wells Fargo Tower at 90 S. Cascade Ave. and the FirstBank Building at 2 N. Cascade Ave., the two tallest buildings in Colorado Springs and part of the downtown Palmer Center, have fallen into foreclosure, The Gazette reported on August 25, 2026, citing El Paso County Public Trustee's Office records.
