The court rendered judgment for ATC on breach of contract, found a fact issue on whether MM CCM 48M Leasing is a proper party, and remanded ATC's fee claim and its claims against MM CCM 48M Leasing. The mandate issued April 15, 2026. For buyers of retail properties, the ruling is a reminder that specialty leases such as antenna, rooftop and signage agreements can survive a mall's closing, and that assuming and performing such a lease makes it hard to argue later that the property's decline excuses performance.
live-122: The case concerns the Holiday Inn Club Vacations Galveston Seaside Resort. According to the court's opinion, the original owner, Silverleaf Resorts, Inc., contracted with CBRE to oversee and manage construction, with T&G as general contractor and with ACI for construction administration and oversight. Construction began in April 2014, Holiday Inn says it took control when it acquired Silverleaf in transactions ending in August 2016, and the City of Galveston issued a certificate of occupancy on October 13, 2016. During construction, a testing firm found water penetration at many tested windows and parts of the curtain wall; after repairs the windows passed retesting in May 2016, though the tester warned that some windows might leak later. Holiday Inn says it noticed water intrusion in fall 2019 and spring 2020, and an April 2020 consultant report attributed leaks to defective work on the pool terrace, parking garage, roof, exterior cladding and stucco, elevated walkways and windows. Holiday Inn sued CBRE in state court on October 8, 2020 and sued T&G and ACI in federal court the next day. The federal court dismissed that case for lack of diversity jurisdiction on May 5, 2023, and Holiday Inn refiled against T&G and ACI in state court on May 9, 2023. The 405th District Court of Galveston County granted summary judgment for all three defendants and signed a take-nothing judgment on December 4, 2023. In a memorandum opinion by Justice Kevin Jewell, the appeals court reversed. On limitations, it held that the discovery rule can apply to construction-defect claims, that Holiday Inn's pleading was not a judicial admission that it knew of the defects it sued over, and that CBRE had not shown that the leaks found during construction, or leaks reported in 2017 and 2018, were related to the damage in the 2020 report. T&G and ACI, which relied on CBRE's arguments, likewise failed to negate the discovery rule, and Holiday Inn raised fact issues on tolling for the period its claims were in federal court. The court also found fact issues on Holiday Inn's standing and capacity to sue CBRE as Silverleaf's assignee, and on the economic loss rule, citing expert evidence of moisture damage to structural components and mold that went beyond the subject of the CBRE contract. The court denied rehearing on March 20, 2025. The Supreme Court of Texas denied review on October 24, 2025, and the mandate issued on December 5, 2025, returning the case to the trial court for further proceedings.
live-124: According to DTSC, Halford's Cleaners operated a dry-cleaning business at 941 McHenry Avenue in Modesto from about 1948 to 2025 and allegedly discharged significant volumes of hazardous substances, mainly tetrachloroethylene (PCE), into the soil, contaminating groundwater and nearby sewer lines. The site, now called the Modesto Groundwater Contamination site, was placed on the U.S. EPA's National Priorities List in March 1989 after a city water supply well was contaminated with PCE from the site. DTSC said it took over operating the groundwater extraction and treatment system in 2012 and the monitoring well network in 2024. On February 26, 2026, DTSC and the Toxic Substances Control Account sued the property's owners in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, seeking recovery of response costs under CERCLA section 107(a) and declaratory relief. The complaint alleges the owners bought the property in 1974 and leased it to dry-cleaning operators from 1974 to 2025. It also states that the EPA sued the owners and a former operator in 2007, and that the owners resolved the EPA's claims in a 2011 consent decree to which DTSC was not a party. Under the consent decree, signed by Judge Mendez on July 7, 2026, the owners will pay a total of $2 million in installments. The decree states that the settling defendants do not admit liability. The court's order made the decree its final judgment and closed the case. DTSC announced the settlement on July 15, 2026.
live-125: The Mission LLC has proposed a 270-unit, eight-story housing development behind the Santa Barbara Mission, with 54 below-market units and three stories of underground parking, using California's "builder's remedy" provision to bypass zoning, the Santa Barbara Independent reported. The paper noted concerns about the site including flood zones, wetlands, a historic graveyard, known archaeological resources, an underground creek, landslide potential and traffic on a narrow exit road from a very high fire-risk area. In October 2025, state legislators passed SB 158, a budget trailer bill that removes builder's-remedy projects from an environmental-review exemption when they meet a set of criteria: a city of 85,000 to 95,000 people in a county of 440,000 to 455,000, a property of four acres or more, FEMA-identified floodways, state-identified wetlands and adjacency to a state historic landmark. The Independent reported that The Mission LLC's project appears to be the only one the law affects. The company sued the state and the city in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on October 24, 2025, alleging the law illegally singles out its project and that the city lacks a compliant housing element. After a March 5, 2026 hearing on the motions to dismiss, Judge Vera ruled on June 2, 2026 that the case was not ripe because the project application remains under review, calling the complaint "woefully short" on specifics, and that the company had not met the requirements for an exception to the state's sovereign immunity, according to the Independent. He expressed no view on the merits but said SB 158 raises "serious constitutional questions," called the ripeness defects "eminently curable," and gave the company until June 22 to amend. The company did not respond to the Independent's request for comment. The CourtListener docket shows an amended complaint filed July 10, 2026, a renewed motion to dismiss filed July 24, 2026, and further entries on that motion in October and on November 2, 2026.
live-127: The Anchorage Community Development Authority filed a complaint on July 21, 2026 in state Superior Court against Hughes Family LLC and Anchorage Innovation District LLC, seeking a court-ordered sale of the former Nordstrom building at Sixth Avenue and D Street, the Anchorage Daily News reported on August 12. The three-story building has been vacant since 2019, when Nordstrom closed after 44 years there. ACDA owns 80% of the building, four of its five lots, according to the Daily News. The fifth lot belongs to Hughes Family LLC, which is owned by four individuals, and which has an agreement with Anchorage Innovation District LLC to develop its share. Anchorage Innovation District is owned and managed by entities tied to developer Mark Pfeffer. The complaint says ACDA is at "an impasse" with the two companies over how to redevelop the property and argues that the building cannot be divided with a party wall or partition. It asks the court to order all five lots sold and the proceeds split proportionally. In February 2026, Mayor Suzanne LaFrance's administration announced plans to convert the building into an "iconic development that would anchor downtown." At a July 17 Assembly committee presentation, ACDA director Mike Robbins said the project was more than a year from starting and that construction could begin next fall. Neither ACDA nor its attorney responded to the Daily News, and Hughes and Pfeffer Development did not respond to requests for comment. As of the article's publication, no further court action was scheduled. The Daily News later updated the article to clarify aspects of the Nordstrom and JCPenney garage projects.
live-129: LDG proposed Prospect Cove, a four-story, 198-unit affordable apartment complex for seniors in Prospect, a Louisville suburb, in 2016. According to LDG's counsel, Louisville Metro Council denied the project in 2017 after strong opposition from the City of Prospect and local residents. LDG sued Prospect and Metro that year, arguing, as Louisville Public Media summarized it, that the city opposed the project because of its association with low-income, senior, disabled and racial-minority residents. Louisville Metro settled with LDG, in a settlement LDG's counsel announced in December 2025, agreeing to pay $6 million and to make changes that include a smaller Metro Council role in zoning changes the Planning Commission approves unanimously, longer approval windows for affordable housing projects, and Fair Housing Act training for council members and staff. The claims against Prospect went to trial on August 10, 2026. After a two-week trial, the jury found for LDG on five of eight counts, including violations of the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Protection Clause, and awarded $36.3 million. Law360 reported that the jury found the suburb's officials conspired to block the project. Prospect Mayor Doug Farnsley said the city "disagrees with the jury's decision" and is evaluating its next steps. LDG has said it plans to break ground at the end of 2026 or early 2027. Louisville Public Media reported that the Kentucky Housing Corporation awarded LDG $26 million in tax-exempt bonds in August 2026, and an LDG spokesperson said construction costs have doubled since the suit began.
live-130: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruled on September 3, 2026 that the Town of Nahant may proceed with taking conservation and access easements over roughly 12 acres of Northeastern University's property on East Point, a 28.7-acre peninsula where the university runs its Marine Science Center. The unanimous opinion by Justice Elizabeth Dewar reversed a Superior Court judgment for Northeastern; the case reached the SJC on direct appellate review. According to the opinion, the federal government took East Point by eminent domain in 1941 for a military installation and later transferred 20.4 acres to Northeastern; the town bought the remaining 8.3 acres in 1975 and keeps a public park there. In 2018 Northeastern presented plans to expand its campus with a new 55,000-square-foot building. After local opposition, town meeting voters in May 2021 authorized the board of selectmen to take easement interests in the Northeastern parcel and appropriated $1.5 million toward the cost. The easements would bar new buildings in the easement areas, which would prevent the planned building, and would give the public access to Canoe Beach. The town filed its petition in Superior Court in September 2021. Northeastern argued the taking was in bad faith because its real aim was to block the project, and on cross motions for summary judgment a Superior Court judge agreed. In May 2025 he entered judgment dismissing the petition and awarding Northeastern more than $1 million in attorney's fees, expert fees and costs. The SJC held that conservation, open space and public access are proper public purposes, consistent with the town's earlier actions showing interest in the area, including placing East Point in a natural resource zoning district in 1991 and listing the Northeastern parcel in town open space plans. The extreme circumstances of Pheasant Ridge, where a town's stated purposes were a pretext it never intended to carry out, were not present. The court acknowledged it was undisputed that the town acted in response to Northeastern's announcement and that the taking would block the project, but said preventing development is the very purpose of a conservation easement and that a town's eminent domain vote is a legislative act entitled to a presumption of validity. It also rejected arguments that private funding of the taking, including a $3 million gift from the Nahant Preservation Trust, made it invalid, and that the Dover Amendment's limits on zoning educational uses barred it. The court remanded for entry of an order establishing the town's right to take and for further proceedings, noting that the town may take the easements only upon paying just compensation. Town Administrator Alison Nieto told CommonWealth Beacon the town was 'pleased' with the decision. A Northeastern spokesperson told The Boston Globe the university was 'deeply disappointed' given what it called evidence of improper motive, and urged town officials to pursue a collaborative path forward.
live-131: Jovia Financial Federal Credit Union, based in Westbury, New York, has sued to foreclose on a 10-story office building in Chicago's South Loop, The Real Deal reported. The September 4, 2026 complaint, filed in Cook County Circuit Court, names S Indiana Avenue LLC, an entity controlled by Lakewood, New Jersey investor Reuven Y. Rivlin, and seeks $17.1 million. Jovia alleges the borrower defaulted on a $17.5 million mortgage on the 129,200-square-foot building, built in 1996 at 1911-1921 South Indiana Avenue, after a three-month forbearance agreement expired in June. Neither Rivlin nor Jovia's attorneys responded to The Real Deal's requests for comment. The complaint also seeks to hold Rivlin personally liable under an unlimited guaranty he signed in 2022 as part of the loan, which would let the credit union pursue him for the full $17.1 million balance whatever the foreclosure produces. Rivlin's entity bought the building on December 31, 2021 for $14 million and took the $17.5 million loan from Jovia on January 5, 2022. The Real Deal noted that court filings do not say how the loan proceeds above the purchase price were used. The default traces to the Illinois Department of Central Management Services, which leased 129,126 square feet on behalf of the Department of Children and Family Services. According to the lender's court filings, the state stopped paying rent after December 2025. A CMS spokesperson told The Real Deal that 'this lease was terminated for cause per the terms of the lease.' City records show more than three dozen open code violations at the building since 2024 and several failed inspections, and the City of Chicago sued the landlord in August 2024 seeking more than $39,000 in fines and penalties, a case still pending in the circuit court's municipal division. After the lease ended, the borrower filed a claim against CMS in the Illinois Court of Claims seeking unpaid 2026 rent and property tax escalation payments for 2024 and 2025. In January, the property tax appeal firm Schmidt Salzman & Moran filed a lien of nearly $52,000 against the property over unpaid legal fees, according to county records. The Real Deal also reported that three days before the foreclosure was filed, Rivlin's company ABS Management announced a nationwide office and retail acquisition strategy.
live-132: Portland Music Holdings LLC, the company behind a proposed 3,300-seat concert venue at the corner of Cumberland Avenue and Myrtle Street next to Merrill Auditorium, sued the City of Portland in federal court on June 9, 2026, the Portland Press Herald reported. The company had told the city in May that it planned to sue, less than a month after the City Council's April vote to create a buffer between large music venues. The court docket lists the case as a civil-rights claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The complaint alleges that the "actual reason" councilors voted for a 180-day moratorium before passing the buffer was that some members had a "personal animosity" toward the company and Live Nation and were trying to shield other venues from competition, the Press Herald reported. It calls the retroactive zoning changes "fundamentally unfair and an abuse of power" and notes the Planning Board had unanimously opposed the buffer. The project had drawn opposition from local musicians, independent venues and residents concerned about traffic and pedestrian safety near City Hall. Live Nation, which said in May it no longer had an interest in the venue or the company, is not part of the suit. A city spokesperson said officials do not comment on pending litigation. Councilor Wes Pelletier, who sponsored the buffer, said he was confident in the city's legal standing, and Councilor Ben Grant had argued at the April vote that the council had authority to adopt the retroactive moratorium and zoning changes. The city moved to dismiss the complaint on July 21, 2026; the parties consented to have Magistrate Judge John C. Nivison decide the case, and he heard oral argument on the motion on September 30, 2026, according to the docket.
live-133: In June 2024, KKR Real Estate Finance Trust lent Lubert-Adler Real Estate Funds and Keystone Development + Investment $83.7 million to buy Philadelphia's 131-year-old Bourse building and convert part of it into a hotel, and to buy 400 Market St., which was converted into apartments as planned, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported. The loan required the hotel project to be near completion by the end of May 2026. KKR says 400 Market is not part of its lawsuit. On July 28, 2026, KREF Capital LLC sued LAK Bourse Owner, LLC and LAK Bourse Master HTC Landlord, LLC in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. According to the Inquirer, the complaint says the development team "abandoned its plans" for the hotel and stopped conversion work earlier in 2026, defaulting the mortgage with more than $24 million in principal outstanding, and that the owners missed mortgage payments starting in June. It sought a $24.2 million judgment plus interest and fees and a public auction of the building. At least five contractors had filed more than $2 million in liens for unpaid work, the paper reported. The suit followed a breakup between real estate investor Dean Adler and Keystone. Adler decided to scrap the hotel and event-space plan and, according to the Philadelphia Business Journal, planned to work with PMC Property Group on a multifamily conversion. Keystone sued Adler in Delaware Chancery Court for breach of contract, alleging he failed to provide promised funding, and Adler countersued, accusing Keystone of unauthorized spending and "gross negligence." In a March ruling reported by Law360, a judge rejected Adler's attempt to oust Keystone and kept Keystone in control of the project, the Inquirer said. Keystone declined to comment on the lawsuit but said it remained "confident" it would prevail against Adler in Delaware. Adler told the Inquirer he believed the Keystone case was near resolution, that KKR's potential foreclosure would follow, and that the Bourse would be revitalized as 400 Market was. On October 12, 2026, KREF Capital filed a notice voluntarily dismissing the federal case under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i); the notice gives no reason.

live-136: Former owners of a 474-unit apartment complex in College Park, Georgia have sued Arbor Realty Trust, alleging the lender kept them on a high-interest bridge loan by promising a later refinancing and then foreclosed, The Real Deal reported. live-138: The Wyoming Supreme Court on February 2, 2026 revived a $14 million lawsuit by Gunwerks, LLC, a maker of custom guns and optics, over the manufacturing facility built for it in Cody, Cowboy State Daily reported. Because only a community could receive money from the Wyoming Business Council's Business Ready Communities program, Gunwerks worked with the City of Cody and Forward Cody, a nonprofit economic development group, to obtain a $3 million grant and a $3 million loan for the building, according to the opinion and Cowboy State Daily. live-146: Blue Sky Towers IV LLC, suing on its own behalf and for the benefit of Cellco Partnership d/b/a Verizon Wireless, filed suit on September 11, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine against the Town of Waldoboro, its Board of Appeals and its Planning Board, Wireless Estimator reported on September 15. live-147: On May 13, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed a grant of summary judgment to Circle K Stores Inc. in a premises-liability suit by a customer who fell in the parking lot of a Circle K in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. In a published opinion by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, joined by Judges Julius N. Richardson and Toby Heytens, the court held that a jury, not a judge, must decide whether the hazard was 'open and obvious,' and that the customer did not need expert testimony to connect his fall to his injury. According to the opinion, on October 19, 2022, a store employee was sweeping outside the entrance with water and a powdered concrete cleaner. He was not wearing the yellow reflective vest that company policy required, and no signs or cones warned that cleaning was under way. The customer, leaving after paying for gas, stepped on a wet painted line, slipped and ruptured his patellar tendon; the court said he incurred about $430,000 in medical expenses. He sued in state court in November 2022, and Circle K removed the case to the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, which granted summary judgment on three grounds: the wet surface was open and obvious, Circle K could not have foreseen the specific danger, and there was no expert testimony on causation. Circle K defended two of those grounds on appeal, and the Fourth Circuit rejected both. It reasoned that visible wetness on concrete does not by itself make a surface an obvious danger, because the real hazard was the unannounced use of a chemical cleaner that a customer could not reliably detect by sight. To win summary judgment, the court said, a store owner must show either that the hazard was so obvious no reasonable invitee would encounter it or that it took sufficient steps to flag the danger, and Circle K showed neither. On causation, the court held that a slip-and-fall is within jurors' ordinary experience, although either side may offer experts, including on the customer's earlier tendon injury. The court also vacated the district court's rulings on the customer's Daubert motion and on his spoliation motion, which concerned a contractor's restriping of the lot before his expert could inspect it. On remand, the district court ruled on pretrial matters in October 2026, granting the spoliation motion in part, and a jury was selected on October 21 for a trial set to begin October 27. On October 26, the court cancelled the trial and dismissed the case under a 60-day settlement order, without prejudice to reopening if the settlement is not completed, according to the docket on CourtListener. The docket entries do not disclose the settlement terms.

live-149: An affiliate of Miami developer OKO Group, led by billionaire Vlad Doronin, has sued four insurers for $22.4 million it says they still owe on a builder's-risk claim for the Missoni Baia condo tower in Edgewater, The Real Deal reported. live-150: The Idaho Supreme Court has affirmed the dismissal of business-damages claims arising from the State of Idaho, Idaho Transportation Board's condemnation of part of Triple Crown Development, LLC's land in Canyon County for a highway interchange. The opinion, by Justice Colleen D. Zahn in Docket No. 52872-2025, was filed September 2, 2026; Mealey's reported on it September 14. The State and Triple Crown had stipulated to the value of the condemned land, and they also stipulated to let four companies intervene: Thueson Construction, Inc.; Americrete Ready Mix Concrete, Inc., which does business as G&B Redi-Mix; Americrete Land Holding LLC; and River Rock Sand & Gravel LLC. According to the opinion, Triple Crown and the intervenors are all controlled by the same person. The claims rested on a plan to mine gravel from the condemned parcel. Americrete Land Holding owns land next to Triple Crown's property, and G&B runs a concrete plant there. According to the opinion, the plan was for River Rock to mine gravel on the condemned land and for Thueson Construction to haul it to the G&B plant, but no permits were obtained and mining never began. Canyon County District Judge Gene A. Petty granted the State summary judgment, finding no evidence that Triple Crown owned a business operating on the condemned property and that the intervenors did not do business on land Triple Crown owned. On appeal, the companies argued that a joint venture among them, or their common owner, held a beneficial interest in both parcels and the businesses. The Court rejected that argument. Reading section 7-711(2) together with the rest of Idaho's eminent domain chapter, it held that "owned" means fee title ownership: a qualifying business must be owned by the fee owner of the condemned land, or must operate on adjoining land that fee owner also owns. Triple Crown did not own the intervenors' businesses, those businesses were not on the condemned property, and Americrete, not Triple Crown, holds title to the adjoining land. The Court found the ownership issue dispositive and did not reach the State's other arguments, and it distinguished an earlier decision involving a closely held corporation owned by the condemnee. The State asked for attorney fees on appeal under Idaho Code section 12-117. The Court declined, finding that the companies' arguments were supported by legal authority and that the appeal was not frivolous, unreasonable or without foundation. Chief Justice Bevan and Justices Brody, Moeller and Meyer concurred.
live-151: Florida's Second District Court of Appeal affirmed a final judgment entered on a jury verdict against Wal-Mart Stores East, LP on June 24, 2026 (No. 2D2025-0567), the Tampa Free Press reported. The appeal came from the Hillsborough County Circuit Court, where Judge Christopher C. Nash presided. Judge Sleet wrote for a unanimous panel that included Chief Judge Lucas and Judge Rothstein-Youakim. According to the opinion, the plaintiff, a service technician for D.H. Pace Door Company, went to a Walmart store in July 2020 to replace a manual door with an automatic one in the order pick-up area. The new door had to be connected to an existing metal junction box in a restricted room that a store manager opened with a key card. The technician could not find the right breaker because about 200 breakers in the breaker room were unlabeled, so he decided to check the wires with a voltmeter. When he touched the loosened metal cover of the box, he was shocked, fell from his ladder to the concrete floor and injured his head. He then found the wires uncapped and the grounding wire unsecured. Experts for both sides agreed the box did not comply with the National Electrical Code, which Florida has adopted as part of its building code. Walmart argued that a property owner owes no duty to an independent contractor's employee injured while doing the work he was hired to do, and that neither exception to that rule applied. The court disagreed. It held that the evidence supported constructive knowledge: Walmart built the store and installed its junction boxes, the box sat in a locked area only Walmart personnel could enter, and the condition had existed for an extended period. Because the hidden danger was not inherent in installing a door, the court held, the trial court properly denied Walmart's motions for summary judgment and directed verdict.
live-154: Simon Property Group co-founder Herb Simon has sued the family of his late nephew, David Simon, over the restructuring of a private real estate company, according to The Real Deal, citing Inside Indiana Business. Sturgeon leased the building to the City of Portland for $18,000 a month for the NW Northrup Shelter, a 200-bed overnight shelter that opened in September 2025 despite neighborhood opposition over livability concerns. live-162: South Union Township sued Namdar Realty Group and Uniontown Mall Realty in November 2025 over conditions at the 689,585-square-foot Uniontown Mall, the Observer-Reporter reported. live-163: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court on September 18, 2026 affirmed a Superior Court judgment dismissing the Town of Marshfield's challenge to the MBTA Communities Act, G. L. c. 40A, § 3A. The 2021 law requires municipalities served by the MBTA to have zoning that permits multifamily housing as of right in at least one district of reasonable size; noncompliant communities lose eligibility for certain state grants. According to the opinion, Marshfield town meetings rejected proposed compliant zoning in April and December 2024, the select board voted in February 2025 not to approve an interim action plan, and the state housing office notified the town it was not in compliance. The town and board sued on February 27, 2025. Writing for the court, Justice Serge Georges, Jr. held that the complaint did not plausibly allege an unfunded local mandate under G. L. c. 29, § 27C: it did not show that the town's costs of drafting and presenting zoning proposals were mandatory and beyond incidental local administration expenses, and its claim of future costs was too conclusory and speculative. Letters from the State Auditor's Division of Local Mandates calling the Act an unfunded mandate, issued to three other communities, did not fill that gap and do not bind the court. The court did not decide whether compliance costs are categorically excluded from the mandate law. The court held that the town and its select board lack standing to assert a constitutional voting rights claim on behalf of town meeting voters. Although it found the Home Rule Amendment claim waived, it reached it because of its public importance and held the Act is a valid general law on a matter of statewide concern, the housing crisis. It also found no conflict with the Zoning Act, G. L. c. 40A, § 5: town meeting keeps its power to approve or reject proposals, but the consequence of rejection is noncompliance with the Act. In a statement, Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell said the decision "reaffirms that the Law is constitutional and compliance is mandatory." Her office said 168 MBTA communities have taken steps to comply and that more than 10,000 units are being developed as a direct result of the law. The ruling follows the SJC's January 8, 2025 decision in Attorney General v. Milton, which held the Act enforceable but found the state's original compliance guidelines invalid because they were not issued under the Administrative Procedure Act; the housing office issued emergency guidelines in January 2025 and final guidelines on April 11, 2025.
live-164: Developer NSI, A.1 LLC filed a 31-page, six-count petition against the City of Springfield, Missouri in Greene County Circuit Court on September 17, 2026, according to the Springfield Business Journal. live-165: A developer and its company, NSI6 LLC, asked a Benton County, Missouri judge for a temporary restraining order after county commissioners adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers on Aug. 10, 2026, KY3 reported. live-166: Cole County Circuit Judge Cotton Walker has ruled that Preserve Montgomery County, an advocacy group opposed to data centers in Montgomery County, Missouri, can continue its lawsuit over the county's handling of an Amazon data center project, the Columbia Missourian reported in a story published by KBIA through the Missouri News Network. live-168: U.S. Bank National Association sued 1592 Boston Street LLC on September 10, 2026, seeking to foreclose on the Bostonian Apartments at 1592 Boston St. in Aurora, Colorado, according to BusinessDen's weekly roundup of real estate lawsuits. live-169: The Hendersonville City Council voted unanimously on January 7, 2026 to deny Advenir Azora Development LLC's request to rezone a 21-acre site on Haywood Road east of Blythe Street for a 180-unit development, after the planning board had unanimously recommended denial, the Hendersonville Lightning reported. live-170: A judge on the 19th Judicial District Court signed a temporary restraining order on Monday, July 13, 2026, barring the City of St. George from adopting or enforcing a proposed ordinance that would rezone a nearly 60-acre parcel near the Pecue Lane interchange with Interstate 10, The Advocate reported. live-171: The Supreme Court of Ohio ruled on Tuesday, September 15, 2026, that Sheetz may pursue a second lawsuit seeking damages from the City of Centerville over its rejected plans for a store at 6318 Far Hills Avenue near Interstate 675, the Dayton Daily News reported. The unanimous decision, Sheetz, Inc. v. Centerville, 2026-Ohio-3531, answered a question of state law certified by the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, where Sheetz's damages suit is pending. The court held that a party need not bring damages and declaratory-relief claims in an R.C. Chapter 2506 administrative appeal to avoid a res judicata bar, because those claims cannot be brought in such an appeal. The dispute began in 2023, when Centerville City Council, citing public opposition from groups including Epiphany Lutheran Church and Bethany Village Senior Living, overturned a major site plan for the store that the city's planning commission had approved unanimously. Sheetz filed an administrative appeal and, in early 2024, a separate damages suit that was moved from Common Pleas Court to federal court. In January 2025, Montgomery County Common Pleas Judge Angelina Jackson ruled that the council exceeded its authority by rejecting a plan that complied with all local development codes and ordered the city to approve it. The Second District Court of Appeals upheld that ruling, and the city appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court in December 2025, the Daily News reported. U.S. District Judge Michael J. Newman certified the question to the Ohio Supreme Court and stayed the federal case in May 2025, the federal docket shows; the damages case will now proceed there. A city spokesperson said the decision "addresses a procedural legal issue related to the separate federal litigation involving Sheetz and does not affect the status of the proposed development," and that while the city's position has not changed, it respects the courts' decisions. live-172: The California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, Division Two, on Aug. 26, 2026 granted a writ petition by warehouse owner Schurman Family Company TIC and directed the Alameda County Superior Court to enter summary judgment in its favor, Business Insurance reported. The trial court had allowed a worker's negligence and premises liability claims against the landlord to proceed. Schurman owned an Oakland warehouse and leased portions of it to Verizon for communications equipment. Verizon hired L.D. Strobel as an independent contractor to work on the site. In June 2021, a Strobel employee sent to check equipment in an enclosure on the roof left a steel walkway, stepped onto a sloped section of roof and fell through a skylight, suffering serious injuries, according to the report. He sued Verizon and Schurman. The trial court granted summary judgment to Verizon under the Privette doctrine, which generally shields those who hire independent contractors from liability for the contractors' workplace injuries, but refused to extend it to Schurman because the landlord had not hired Strobel. In an opinion by Justice Desautels, the appeals court held that the doctrine reaches non-hiring parties within the "chain of delegation." It found that Schurman's lease expressly allowed Verizon to install, operate and maintain equipment at the property, that Verizon hired Strobel to do that work, and that Strobel knew about the skylights before the accident. The court said it would be "anomalous and inequitable" to potentially impose greater liability on Schurman, which did not control the worker's activities, than on Verizon or Strobel. It held that when a lease contemplates work by an independent contractor and the tenant hires one to do it, the landlord is protected unless a recognized exception applies.
live-173: The lender behind a $48.5 million loan on Atlantic City's Showboat hotel has filed a foreclosure suit alleging the owner defaulted on payments and violated multiple terms of its financing, the Press of Atlantic City reported on August 7, 2026. A judge was scheduled to rule on November 6, 2026 on the lender's motion for summary judgment; the outcome had not been reported in the sources reviewed.
live-174: Cogent Bank has filed a foreclosure suit in Monroe County Supreme Court over the Wyndham Rochester Downtown hotel on State Street, 13WHAM News reported on September 1, 2026. live-175: U.S. District Judge George H. Wu has dismissed a proposed securities class action against Alexandria Real Estate Equities, the largest owner of U.S. lab buildings, and three of its executives, Bisnow reported on September 14, 2026. live-176: Citibank, acting as trustee for holders of commercial mortgage-backed securities, and special servicer LNR Partners have sued in Cook County to foreclose on 625 North Michigan Avenue, a 28-story office building on Chicago's Magnificent Mile. live-177: A downtown Seattle retail property owned by an entity linked to Unico Properties has been placed in receivership after a default on a $14.5 million loan that matured two years earlier, the Puget Sound Business Journal reported, according to Connect CRE's September 24, 2026 lender roundup. live-178: Developer Charles Cohen satisfied a $187 million judgment owed to Fortress Investment Group in June 2026, but the two sides are still fighting. In a letter to the court on Thursday, June 25, Cohen's attorney wrote that Cohen "is committed to pursuing his defenses and counterclaims against Fortress for substantial damages," Bisnow reported. live-179: In April 2018, Marketplace Home Mortgage, LLC, a mortgage-loan company, signed a three-year lease for space in the Pinnacle North Office Center, owned by Pinnacle North, LLC. It defaulted on rent that summer. MHM sold its assets to New American Funding in a deal that closed December 31, 2018; the buyer assumed some liabilities but not the lease, and MHM was insolvent by then. In January 2019 MHM told the landlord it was no longer operating and had no revenue or employees. In December 2019 its sole member and president had MHM write him a $50,000 check. Pinnacle North later obtained a default judgment against MHM for $52,548.24 plus interest, costs and attorney fees. Unable to collect, Pinnacle North sued the principal in Oakland Circuit Court to pierce MHM's veil and to avoid the $50,000 payment under Michigan's voidable-transfer statute, MCL 566.31 et seq. After a two-day bench trial, the court ruled for the landlord in 2023, holding him liable for the full default judgment plus costs, fees and interest, and later awarded about $92,000 in attorney fees covering both lawsuits. A panel of Judges Patel, Swartzle and Mariani affirmed. It rejected the principal's late request to apply Minnesota law, where MHM was organized. On veil-piercing, the court pointed to evidence that he personally borrowed money to capitalize MHM, which MHM then repaid through a $193,000 payment in 2018; that MHM kept paying a $270,000 American Express debt ahead of other creditors because of his potential personal liability; and that he wrote himself the $50,000 check while MHM was insolvent. On the voidable-transfer claim, the court held MHM received no reasonably equivalent value for the payment, which the trial court found was a return of a prior capital contribution rather than a loan repayment. The court also upheld the fee award under the lease clause covering suits to collect rent.
live-184: 100 Summer St., a 32-story, 1.1-million-square-foot office tower at Summer and Devonshire streets near South Station, went to a foreclosure auction after its lender, Wells Fargo, foreclosed in September 2026, the Boston Globe and Bisnow reported. live-186: The $49.7 million commercial mortgage-backed securities loan on the Embassy Suites by Hilton Portland Airport, a 251-key hotel next to Portland International Airport, moved to special servicing after missing its August 2026 maturity date, Connect CRE reported in its September 24, 2026 lender roundup. live-187: The Granary District office campus formerly known as Industry SLC has been renamed Foundry43, Building Salt Lake reported on September 24, 2026. The parking structure and retail space are complete, and work continues on more than 64,000 square feet of creative office space and a 34,000-square-foot fitness center. live-188: A nonprofit group, Joliet Residents For Responsible Growth, and three members who live near the project sued the City of Joliet in Will County Circuit Court on May 18, 2026, seeking to void the City Council's 8-1 vote on March 19 approving an annexation agreement for the $20 billion, 795-acre Joliet Technology Center, The Herald-News (Shaw Local) reported. The other defendants are Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, HW Technology Park Development and American Real Estate Partners. The approvals annexed the site and rezoned it from agricultural to light industrial for a 24-building, 1.8-gigawatt data center campus. The complaint alleged that a Feb. 18 Plan Commission notice did not disclose that the proposal involved a data center, that residents were denied a right to cross-examine the developers' witnesses at a March 16 council meeting, that the March 19 meeting violated the Open Meetings Act, and that the rezoning bore no substantial relation to public health, safety or welfare.
