live-267: According to the opinion, Stradtman Park, LLC borrowed $3.6 million from KeyBank National Association in July 2014 on a commercial property valued at about $7 million. In October 2014 KeyBank assigned the loan to Wilmington Trust, National Association, as trustee for JPMBB Commercial Mortgage Securities Trust 2014-C24, and it was placed in a CMBS under a pooling and servicing agreement the borrower did not sign. LNR Partners, LLC was to act as special servicer if the loan became distressed or defaulted. The borrower paid as required from 2014 into early 2020: $18,779.30 a month in principal and interest and $20,300.39 a month in reserves, for $39,079.69 in all. In 2019 it asked for approvals and reserve payments for lease renewals, expansions and contractor repairs, and although the loan was performing, LNR handled those requests; the borrower says LNR was obstructive and forced it to pay costs itself. From May 2020 the borrower paid only principal and interest and directed that its payments be applied that way, but the lender side spread them across principal, interest and reserves, which produced a default. In November 2020 the borrower stopped remitting rents, and the trustee later sued to foreclose. Erie County Supreme Court granted the trustee partial summary judgment on foreclosure and rents, which the borrower did not appeal, and then held a damages hearing. Justice Emilio Colaiacovo's amended order and judgment, entered May 21, 2025, awarded the full $583,938.25 in default-rate interest requested but refused $120,882.59 more in note-rate interest, because the default rate was five points above the note rate and the trustee had not documented its calculation. On fees, the borrower's expert put customary Western New York commercial foreclosure rates at $350 to $450 an hour, while the trustee's witness said LNR paid $650 to $800 for partners and $350 to $575 for associates, and the invoices did not show the rate for each charge. The court found the rates unreasonable and many charges "duplicative and exaggerated," awarded $250,000 of the roughly $588,000 sought, and said the trustee had come "perilously close" to having the entire judgment vacated over its fee request. The Fourth Department affirmed. It acknowledged that unambiguous contracts are enforced as written but noted that a foreclosure invokes the court's equitable powers. It held that the plaintiff bears the burden of proving damages, that the duplicative-interest ruling was supported by a fair interpretation of the evidence, and that contractual fees are enforceable only to the extent reasonable and warranted for services actually rendered. It found no abuse of discretion in the $250,000 award and rejected the trustee's remaining challenges.
live-268: Long Street Associates, LLP owns the building at 31-55 West Long Street in Columbus, which the lease acknowledged is listed on the national register of historic buildings. On December 9, 2019, it leased the unfinished space to the Young Men's Christian Association of Central Ohio. The lease set out a process for building out the premises: the landlord would furnish preliminary plans, the parties would work in good faith toward final plans, and the landlord would then prepare a construction budget. The landlord was to contribute a tenant-improvement allowance of $30 per square foot, about $323,100, and the YMCA agreed to fund up to $200,000 more, amortized over the initial term at five percent interest, and to pay any excess beyond that. The key provision, Section 10.10, gave the tenant a one-time right to terminate if the construction budget showed improvement costs above a fixed threshold of roughly $523,100, exercisable by written notice within seven days of receiving the budget. On July 30, 2020, the YMCA received a budget showing costs of $1,036,697.38, nearly double the threshold. On August 6, 2020, it gave written notice that it was terminating under Section 10.10. The landlord asked it to withdraw the notice and proposed in writing to share the overrun costs, but no written modification was ever signed. The landlord sued in November 2020 in the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas for declaratory judgment, breach of contract and anticipatory breach, and argued on appeal that the tenant had used the clause to escape the lease because of pandemic-era financial strain. The trial court granted the YMCA summary judgment in May 2024, finding that final plans had been reached and that a budget exceeding the threshold had been delivered, which triggered the termination right. After a remand to resolve the YMCA's claim for attorneys' fees under the lease, the parties entered an agreed fee judgment in January 2026, and the landlord appealed again. Writing for the panel, the court rejected each of the landlord's arguments. The landlord said the spreadsheet sent on July 30 was not the lease's construction budget and that final plans had not been agreed, but its own complaint alleged that it sent the budget in accordance with Section 10.10 after the final plans were finalized. The court treated those allegations as judicial admissions and noted the lease draws no line between an initial and a final budget. The landlord next said it had orally offered on August 6 to cover costs above the threshold, so the budget never really exceeded it. The court held that such an offer would be a material change to price terms, and the lease's no-oral-modification clause required any change to be in a signed writing. Finally, the court found that approvals from the Ohio Historic Preservation Office and the National Park Service, which bore on historic tax credits, were not a condition precedent to the final plans. The takeaways for owners are concrete. If a lease gives the tenant an exit when build-out costs exceed a cap, the landlord should control when and how the budget is delivered, label preliminary numbers clearly, and recognize that any budget sent after plans are settled may start the clock. Fixes to a cost overrun need to be papered and signed before the option window closes, not negotiated by phone afterward. Pleadings matter too: describing a document in a complaint as the one the lease requires can foreclose arguing otherwise later. For tenants, the decision confirms that a cleanly drafted cost-overrun termination right, exercised on time and in writing, will hold up.
live-269: A commercial tenant of ESRT Empire State Building LLC sued its landlord in New York County Supreme Court (Index No. 655283/24), asserting constructive eviction and breach of the lease. Justice Lyle E. Frank granted the landlord's motion to dismiss the complaint in an order and judgment entered June 6, 2025, and the tenant appealed. In a short unanimous decision dated October 6, 2026, a four-justice panel affirmed on independent grounds. First, the tenant had expressly waived its constructive eviction rights in the lease, which barred the claim; the court cited its earlier decisions in 558 Seventh Ave. Corp. v E&B Barbers Inc. and Schwartz, Karlan & Gutstein v 271 Venture. Second, even without the waiver, the claim was not adequately pleaded. Quoting the Court of Appeals' standard in Barash v Pennsylvania Terminal Real Estate Corp., the panel said neither the complaint nor the affidavits explained how the tenant was "substantially and materially deprive[d] . . . of the beneficial use and enjoyment of the premises." Third, the breach-of-lease claim was properly dismissed because the tenant did not identify any lease provision that was breached. The court did not reach the parties' remaining arguments.
live-270: The underlying case, filed in New York County Supreme Court under Index No. 657290/19, concerns an HVAC system that Henick-Lane, Inc. installed. According to the decision, the plaintiffs, 5 Beekman Property Owner, LLC and Broadway Construction Group, LLC, allege the system leaked, damaging the owner's property and forcing them to spend money containing the damage. They sued for breach of contract, and Henick-Lane counterclaimed for nonpayment and to foreclose a mechanic's lien. Those claims were not part of this appeal. During settlement negotiations, one of Henick-Lane's insurers, apparently believing the parties had reached a settlement, paid $850,000 to Broadway Construction Group even though a full settlement agreement was not in place. The check said it was a "Settlement Payment for" Henick-Lane. Justice Andrew Borrok ordered the plaintiffs to return the money with interest, later held them in civil contempt for not doing so, and on December 11, 2025 entered judgment against them for $850,000 plus prejudgment interest. The plaintiffs appealed the judgment and the contempt order. A five-justice panel affirmed both. It held that the judgment brought up the earlier return order for review because the dispute over the payment was separate from the HVAC, nonpayment and lien claims still in the case. It held that Henick-Lane had standing, an issue the plaintiffs raised for the first time on appeal, because its insurer paid on its behalf out of a policy Henick-Lane paid for. It rejected the plaintiffs' reliance on the voluntary payment doctrine: the insurer had reserved its position by labeling the check, and because there was no settlement, the payment rested on a mistake. The court also upheld the contempt finding. Although contempt may not be used to enforce a money judgment, no judgment existed when the contempt order issued. The panel rejected Broadway Construction Group's argument that it could not be held in contempt because the return order did not name it, noting that the plaintiffs' corporate representative stated that both plaintiffs received and deposited the check.
