live-273: The premises are Suite A at 33501 Lake Road in Avon Lake, Ohio, a roughly 15,000-square-foot space in a shopping center. Beach Park Railway, LLC used the space to operate a museum it established with state grant money, and in 2019 it signed a non-disturbance and estoppel agreement with the Ohio Facilities Commission and the then-owner protecting the Commission's interest. The tenant originally occupied as a subtenant of TBP Avon Lake, LLC, paying $583 a month. After TBP sold the property and leased it back, Stop 65, LLC acquired the shopping center, evicted TBP in a separate Lorain County case decided in March 2024, and became the museum operator's direct landlord. Inspecting the space after that case ended, the landlord's representative concluded the museum occupied only about a quarter of it. Deposition testimony and photographs showed an individual running a private motorcycle-repair business out of the warehouse area, storing large quantities of parts, and apparently living on site, with the tenant's board member acknowledging the arrangement and payments toward utilities of at least $1,100. On March 22, 2024 the landlord served a contractual 30-day notice of default for unauthorized subleasing and storing items outside the leased area. The tenant responded that it had ended subleases with two entities and cured, but the landlord served a statutory three-day notice to vacate on April 29 and filed a forcible entry and detainer action on May 3, 2024. The tenant counterclaimed on six counts, including retaliatory eviction, failure to repair with rent abatement, tortious interference, breach of quiet enjoyment and breach of the lease's maintenance duties. The municipal court dismissed the counterclaim in July 2024, granted the landlord summary judgment on the unauthorized-sublease breach in April 2025, and issued a writ of restitution, which was stayed on bond pending appeal. A panel of Seventh District judges sitting by assignment affirmed on every assignment of error. On the central question, the court held that the arrangement was a sublease as a matter of law: the occupant had exclusive possession of dedicated space, used it for a business unrelated to the museum and as a residence, and kept it month after month, so the parties' own labels did not matter. The court rejected the tenant's waiver and estoppel arguments. It held that Ohio's statutory 30-day notice to terminate a tenancy does not govern commercial leases, and that the lease's 30-day language attached to the landlord's optional self-help remedy, not to a court eviction. On the counterclaims, it upheld dismissal of the repair and quiet-enjoyment counts, largely because the arguments the tenant pressed on appeal, including those about the non-disturbance agreement's written notice-of-default requirement, had not been preserved in its response to the dismissal motion. Finally, the municipal court did not have to transfer the case to common pleas court merely because the counterclaim demanded more than its $15,000 limit, once the counts offered to justify that demand were dismissed. The opinion is long and fact-specific, but its holdings travel well. Anti-subletting clauses in shopping-center and industrial leases often collide with informal uses by a tenant's affiliates, volunteers or friends, and the court's focus on exclusive, dedicated and ongoing occupancy gives both sides a workable line between a license and a sublease. Landlords enforcing use or subletting covenants should document actual occupancy with inspections and photographs, follow the lease's cure procedure first, and then use the statutory eviction notice. Where public grant money or a lender sits behind the tenancy, landlords and tenants alike should read any non-disturbance agreement for notice and cure conditions, because here the agreement's notice requirement was central to the fight over the tenant's repair claim. Tenants defending an eviction should also expect a court to look past a large counterclaim demand when deciding whether a municipal court with a $15,000 limit keeps the case.
live-274: The owners of a 98,000-square-foot industrial building at 2000 Folsom Street in San Francisco's Mission District sued tenant Physical Intelligence in San Francisco Superior Court, The San Francisco Standard reported on October 6, 2026, describing the suit as filed the previous week. The landlords allege the robotics startup has stayed on since its lease ran out in September, and they want the space back plus holdover damages of more than $13,000 a day. The building, a former food manufacturing site, had been vacant until the recent AI robotics boom, according to The Standard. According to the lease attached to the complaint, as described by The Standard, Physical Intelligence signed a lease in January for about 29,000 square feet on the ground floor at $60,000 a month, running from February to May with an option to continue month to month. The space was used to develop and test robots and for related office work. In May, the landlord sent a termination notice setting a June move-out date. Instead of leaving, Physical Intelligence agreed in June to an amendment that raised the rent to $160,000 a month for a larger footprint through September and eliminated the month-to-month option. In that amendment the company said it intended to relocate and wanted to time its exit to the delivery of new space; The Standard previously reported that it has an agreement to lease 60,000 square feet at 808 Brannan St. The complaint also alleges Physical Intelligence expanded into areas outside the lease without written consent and made improvements without permission. The Standard reported that the landlord agreed to waive that violation but is seeking the company's immediate departure. The landlords say a new tenant wants to move in as early as the week of the article, and The Standard reported that sources confirmed the tenant is Anthropic. Physical Intelligence had not responded to the complaint, according to court records cited by The Standard. Anthropic, Physical Intelligence and the landlords' attorney did not respond to The Standard's requests for comment. The allegations have not been tested in court.
live-275: The property is the Oakmont 410 industrial warehouse at 542 SE Loop 410 Access Road on San Antonio's East Side. The San Antonio Report, in a story republished by Texas Public Radio, reported that ICE acquired the nearly 640,000-square-foot building in January 2026 and plans to convert it into a detention and processing facility that could hold up to 1,500 people. The San Antonio Current put the purchase price at $66.1 million and reported in late August that ICE had picked GardaWorld Federal Services to renovate the warehouse; the San Antonio Report put that contract at $17.3 million. The city filed its complaint on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in the Western District of Texas. The CourtListener docket lists it as a review of agency action under NEPA, with an environmental-matters nature of suit. The defendants are DHS, ICE, and the DHS Secretary and an ICE official in their official capacities. City Attorney Andy Segovia said the required review covers not only air and water quality but also effects on the surrounding community, and that he expects a preliminary environmental assessment to find significant impacts, which could trigger a fuller study taking months. The complaint asks the court to restrain and enjoin further work on the conversion. City officials said they had sent five letters to DHS and ICE since February seeking details on environmental reviews, permits and public input. Federal officials answered once, in June, promising coordination, community feedback and engineering and design reports, which the city says it never received. The week before the suit, the City Council directed city departments and local utilities to assess the facility's effects on water, wastewater, electricity and emergency services. DHS and ICE did not respond to the San Antonio Report's request for comment. Council members Marc Whyte and Misty Spears opposed the suit; Whyte called it "political theater" and estimated it could cost the city $500,000 or more. On Oct. 16, the court ordered the city to file any request for a restraining order or preliminary injunction separately from its complaint, as local rules require. On Oct. 22, Judge Pulliam granted the city's unopposed motion to vacate that order, held the request for injunctive relief in abeyance and directed the parties to file an advisory by Nov. 30, 2026. Government counsel appeared for the defendants on Oct. 21.
live-276: Silver Fox 606 LLC, the developer of a data center project in Indiantown, Florida, has filed a complaint and verified petition for a writ of prohibition against the Village of Indiantown, its village council and its planning, zoning and appeals board, CBS12 reported on October 12, 2026. The suit, which also names local residents, alleges that village officials are illegally derailing the $25 million project. According to CBS12, Silver Fox bought the more than 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 after zoning verifications confirmed that computer and data processing facilities were an as-of-right use in the Heavy Industrial district. The suit alleges that after the 2026 municipal elections, the newly seated council tried to stall or ban data center development despite the village's earlier efforts to recruit such projects. CBS12, describing the suit, said the village manager and the longtime village attorney were ousted at a September 1 meeting. WQCS reported that at that meeting the council voted 4-1 to hold off on a proposed moratorium until an interim village attorney gave a legal opinion and voted 3-2 to fire the village manager, and that the village attorney had resigned on August 18. Silver Fox alleges the council violated Florida's Sunshine Law in making the personnel changes. According to CBS12, the village's community and economic development director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17, and a resident then filed an administrative appeal seeking to overturn the approvals. Silver Fox argues the appeals board lacks jurisdiction because state law makes a recorded plat unassailable without the landowner's consent. It seeks emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction against any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews, and declarations affirming its vested development rights. CBS12 reported on October 23 that a Martin County circuit judge had issued an injunction earlier in the month blocking a planned zoning appeals hearing while the case proceeds. At an October 22 meeting, the council scheduled a first reading of a temporary data center moratorium that would exclude Project Silver Fox and two other sites, and council members called for lawsuits over the developments to be dropped as the village seeks to negotiate with developers. No response from the village to the suit's allegations has been reported.
live-277: AZ 175th Street LLC, owner of a mixed-use building in Jamaica, Queens, filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition on October 10, 2026 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of New York, Case No. 1-26-44763. According to a filing alert from the bankruptcy tracker Bondoro, the company reports $14 million in assets and $12.6 million in liabilities and indicates funds will be available for unsecured creditors. By October 20, the docket showed the petition, a notice of prior filings, a deficient-filing notice, a meeting-of-creditors notice and one notice of appearance. This is the company's second Chapter 11 case. The first, No. 1-25-42550, was filed May 23, 2025, and a week later the debtor refiled the petition's first pages to designate itself a single-asset real estate business. Creditor UC 175th Street Apartments Holder, LLC appeared in early June and moved to dismiss the case on June 18, 2025, supported by declarations and an affirmation from the property's receiver. After adjournments and a September 12, 2025 hearing, the court entered an order on October 9, 2025 dismissing the case and barring the debtor from refiling. The case was closed April 16, 2026. The public docket descriptions available without charge do not state the length of the refiling bar or whether the dismissal was by consent, and the new case does not yet show a motion by a secured creditor.
live-278: Merchants Bank of Indiana has sued in Cook County Circuit Court to foreclose on three South Side Chicago apartment buildings owned by GRV Jackson Park LLC, The Real Deal reported on October 10, 2026. The buildings, in the South Shore and Jackson Park areas, are at 6750-52 South Merrill Avenue (also known as 2116-20 East 68th Street), 6920-30 South Oglesby Avenue and 6952-58 South Paxton Avenue. The article says the complaint was filed earlier in October but does not give the date. The complaint says the bank lent the borrower $6.4 million through two loan facilities in June 2024 and that the monthly mortgage payments stopped in March 2025. It also names two individual investors who, the bank says, signed unconditional guaranties when the loans were made, and asks the court to hold them liable for any deficiency. The complaint describes sewage backups, standing water and fire damage at the buildings. According to the article, the city won a court order in April 2025 requiring the Paxton Avenue building to be evacuated and secured, and the bank paid for new boilers through protective advances. An attorney for one of the guarantors told The Real Deal that his client resigned as manager of GRV Jackson Park before the March 2025 defaults and the alleged code violations, and that the other guarantor's company, Ruby Development Group LLC, took over. The bank's position, according to the suit, is that both men signed their guaranties at closing regardless of later changes in management. The other guarantor and the bank did not respond to requests for comment. The two investors are also suing each other in a separate case over their shared portfolio. The Real Deal also reported that the bank disclosed $124.1 million in 2025 charge-offs, about 70% of it from five borrower relationships tied to suspected mortgage fraud; it is not known whether this borrower group was one of them.
live-279: Pacific Collective, LLC, a real estate developer, learned in 2018 that ExxonMobil Oil Corporation was selling a parcel at 3800 Sepulveda Boulevard in Culver City that sat inside the city's zone for retail cannabis dispensaries. Pacific signed an option with ExxonMobil in September 2018 and, on September 26, 2018, signed a lease with TGS CC Ventures, LLC, a subsidiary of national cannabis operator Jushi, Inc. Jushi signed a guaranty of the tenant's obligations the next day. Pacific was to buy the land, build a 5,000 square foot building at a cost of no more than $1.75 million, and rent it to TGS for 15 years at a starting rent of $20 per square foot, while TGS pursued a city cannabis license. The lease was made contingent on Pacific acquiring fee title under a purchase agreement with ExxonMobil that had not yet been drafted, and it gave no deadline for closing. Pacific let the option lapse and obtained extensions, signed a $4.2 million purchase agreement only in November 2019, missed the deadline for its $70,000 earnest money deposit, and by early 2020 still had no financing in place. TGS, which had been selected by the city to move forward in the licensing process, would not file its next city submission naming Pacific as owner while Pacific did not own the property. After a failed renegotiation, TGS rescinded the lease on February 28, 2020, and in December 2020 bought the property from ExxonMobil itself. Pacific sued TGS for breach of the lease and Jushi for breach of the guaranty in October 2022, alleging damages above $20 million. A retired judge sitting as a referee under the lease's dispute resolution clause tried the case over five days in January 2024 and found that Pacific never had the funds or loan commitments to close, had been stalling, and was in material breach of a lease that made time of the essence. The trial court entered judgment for the defendants on May 28, 2024. On appeal, the Second District accepted that the lease's reference to acquiring title under the purchase agreement could be read to tie Pacific's deadline to the ExxonMobil contract, but refused to let that reading give Pacific unlimited control over its own performance. Applying Civil Code section 1657 and the implied covenant of good faith, the panel held that Pacific had to close within a reasonable time. It found ample support for the referee's conclusion that Pacific's delay was unreasonable, pointing to the option terms that contemplated a 2019 closing and to testimony that the delay was a deliberate cost-saving choice. The court also rejected Pacific's argument that its duty to buy the land was excused until TGS obtained its cannabis license. Nothing in the lease made the purchase conditional on licensing, while a separate clause expressly deferred construction until permits issued, which the panel read as showing the parties knew how to write such a condition when they wanted one. The court called the risk of buying land before licensing the deal Pacific struck. The judgment for TGS and Jushi was affirmed and they were awarded appellate costs. The opinion is not certified for publication. For developers, the practical point is to put a firm acquisition deadline, financing contingency or licensing condition in writing in any lease signed before closing on the land, rather than relying on a pending purchase contract. Tenants and guarantors, for their part, can use the reasonable-time rule to exit a deal when a landlord's delay goes to the heart of the bargain, provided they document repeated requests to perform, as TGS did here.
live-280: According to the decision, Ordinary Faces LLC leased space from Bohemian Brethren Presbyterian Church to operate a preschool. To run the school it needed a letter of no objection from the city Department of Buildings. The Department denied the initial application because there was no functional fire alarm system, and the Fire Department did not sign off on an alarm until July 26, 2016, nearly two years after the lease was signed. Department of Buildings violations related to a defunct dumbwaiter shaft, issued against parts of the building outside the leased premises, also stood in the way of a permanent letter. The preschool and its founder sued the church in New York County Supreme Court (Index No. 654614/17). After a jury trial before Justice Joel M. Cohen, judgment was entered on August 20, 2025 awarding the plaintiffs $1,216,177.36. The church appealed the judgment and several rulings, including the denial of its motion to set aside the verdict and of its motion to strike the jury demand. The First Department found the evidence sufficient. It held that the church breached section 18(a) of the lease, which required it to cooperate in obtaining approvals for the school, by failing to file the paperwork needed to clear the violations; the church's treasurer testified that it never had its elevator company file that paperwork. The church also breached a lease rider requiring the parties to act "expeditiously and diligently" on the fire alarm. Because the violations were issued against areas outside the leased premises, the court said curing them was the church's obligation. The panel rejected the church's argument that a 50 percent rent abatement from January through August 2015 was the tenant's sole remedy, because the rider did not say so. It upheld the $734,353 lost-profits award, which the plaintiffs said approximates two and a half years of projected profits, noting that the figures were based on data from a preschool that had operated in the same space for nearly 40 years, which the founder testified the church provided, and that the church offered no contrary evidence. It held that section 19 of the lease, limiting the tenant to the landlord's interest in the building, allowed recovery from the proceeds of the church's 2019 sale. It also upheld the finding that the church waived the lease's jury waiver by raising it four months after the note of issue, and declined to order a new trial over brief, unsolicited testimony about the founder's personal history, to which the church did not object at trial.
live-281: Recycled Properties, LLC operates a construction and demolition debris landfill and borrow pit in Chesapeake, Virginia, operations the court described as legally nonconforming. In May 2024 it submitted a site plan to the city's Department of Development and Permits for a warehouse and an office building on the property. In August 2024 the city disapproved the plan on three grounds: the buildings would expand the nonconforming use, contrary to a provision of the Chesapeake zoning ordinance; approval would wait until the owner provided more information about how the buildings would be used; and a conditional use permit for the nonconforming operations was required first. The city had also cited notices of past zoning violations, a ground it later withdrew. The owner appealed to the Chesapeake Circuit Court under the Virginia statutes that let an applicant challenge a site plan disapproval as not based on the applicable ordinance or as arbitrary or capricious, and attached the city's denial letter to its complaint. It argued that the ordinance did not require it to prove the buildings were not an expansion, to provide "adequate information," or to obtain a conditional use permit, and it sought damages under a state statute on unconstitutional conditions. The city demurred. Circuit Judge David J. Whitted sustained the demurrer, holding the owner had not adequately pleaded its appeal on the requirement to submit more information, and noted the owner "may file a new site plan application." In an unpublished memorandum opinion by Judge Kevin M. Duffan, for a panel that also included Judges Beales and White, the Court of Appeals affirmed. It relied on the denial letter the owner had attached, which cited an ordinance provision barring additional buildings or structures that support a lawfully nonconforming use and the city's authority to review site plans for conformity with the zoning ordinance, and it noted Virginia Supreme Court precedent allowing localities to preclude the expansion of nonconforming uses. Because nothing in the complaint factually disputed that the buildings would alter or expand the nonconforming use, or that more information was needed, the court treated the owner's contrary assertions as legal conclusions that need not be accepted on demurrer. The court also rejected the owner's argument that the circuit court had decided the case on a summary judgment standard rather than the demurrer standard, finding the circuit court had ruled on the adequacy of the pleading. It did not reach the owner's argument that the denial was unconstitutional, because that argument was not included in an assignment of error or argued in the opening brief.
live-282: In December 2023 the City of Bradford, Pennsylvania filed a declaration of taking to condemn 374 square feet of an alley running through the rear of a property owned by DewBoi Properties, LLC, as part of a project to build a new bus station. DewBoi filed preliminary objections, and the parties' lawyers negotiated a settlement over several months in 2024. On October 3, 2024, DewBoi's counsel emailed that DewBoi agreed to the city's offer of $30,000 and the removal of both telephone poles from the alley, relocated 'from DewBoi's property to the City's property' at the city's expense. The city's draft agreement of sale, sent October 15, instead said the poles would be moved out of the alley to DewBoi's property. DewBoi's counsel revised a related joint stipulation to drop the express reference to DewBoi's property but left the agreement of sale language unchanged, and the city accepted the revisions. The city signed in December 2024, the parties told the court they had settled, and DewBoi's counsel received the city's $30,000 check on January 6, 2025. The deal unraveled when the city sent over the local electric utility's easement, which showed one pole moving to another spot on DewBoi's lot. DewBoi objected that the proposed locations would further cut into parking for its tenants and their customers. After the city began building the bus station and put up a temporary fence across the condemned strip, affecting access to DewBoi's parking lot, DewBoi sought a preliminary injunction in May 2025, arguing the city did not own the land. The city responded with a petition to enforce the settlement. After two days of hearings, the McKean County Court of Common Pleas granted the city's petition and denied the injunction on August 25, 2025. On appeal, DewBoi argued there was no meeting of the minds on where the poles would go and, at most, a mutual mistake. In a non-precedential memorandum opinion by Judge Lori A. Dumas, the Commonwealth Court disagreed. It held that the settlement documents, read together, clearly provided for relocating both poles from the alley to other places on DewBoi's property. It also deferred to the trial court's findings, based on months of correspondence, the city attorney's testimony, the joint report of settlement and DewBoi's request for the $30,000 check, that the owner had approved the deal and later had second thoughts about vehicle access. Without clear, precise and convincing proof of a shared mistaken assumption, the mutual mistake defense failed. The case is small in dollars, but the issue is common in partial takings for transit, road or utility projects: site details such as pole, sign, curb-cut and parking locations can matter as much as the price. Here the court held that the signed documents controlled, and that the owner could not undo the settlement through a mutual-mistake defense without clear, precise and convincing proof.
live-283: ApplianceSmart, Inc. ran a store in the big-box space of a Columbus, Ohio shopping center owned by Trustees Main/270, LLC from 2008 until 2022. The lease began with a predecessor, Appliance Recycling Centers of America, which became the guarantor in 2017 when ApplianceSmart took over as tenant and the term was extended to June 30, 2025. That guarantor was reincorporated as JanOne, Inc. and remained guarantor after JanOne sold ApplianceSmart to Live Ventures, Inc. in 2019. According to the Sixth Circuit's opinion, the tenant defaulted three times. A 2019 rent default ended in a settlement of a state-court suit. A second default during ApplianceSmart's 2021 bankruptcy was resolved with a lease modification under which Live Ventures agreed to pay more than $185,000 in back rent and the landlord gained a right to terminate on 30 days' notice. After a third payment default in February 2022, the landlord used a lease clause letting it retake possession and change the locks without ending the lease, leaving the tenant liable for rent and reletting costs, and sued ApplianceSmart and JanOne in the Southern District of Ohio in April 2022. The defendants did not dispute the breach; their defense was mitigation. JanOne proposed an affiliated recycling business that would assume the lease and keep trading as ApplianceSmart, and Live Ventures offered one of its portfolio companies, a flooring retailer. The landlord asked the first candidate to prepay all arrears and post a nonrefundable six-month deposit, which JanOne declined, and sent the second a standard questionnaire that went unanswered. The landlord's leasing agent kept marketing the space, and AutoZone signed a lease in September 2024; because of zoning and permitting contingencies, it did not begin paying rent until after the ApplianceSmart term would have ended. District Judge Algenon L. Marbley awarded $155,267.15 in undisputed rent on summary judgment and, after a bench trial on mitigation, entered final judgment on October 3, 2025 awarding $1,064,674.64 more in rent and charges and $126,637.52 in broker fees, plus interest. In an October 7, 2026 opinion by Judge John B. Nalbandian, not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding that Ohio law does not require a landlord to mitigate by dealing with "demonstrably unreliable parties." It rejected the defendants' analogy to employment-discrimination cases and found their argument about a rejected purchase offer likely forfeited. The panel first raised the complaint's failure to plead the parties' citizenship and accepted post-argument letter briefs as amendments confirming diversity jurisdiction.
live-284: The dispute concerns a 117-bed assisted-living facility built on land in Conroe, Texas. The property-owning company, Conroe WM LLC, financed construction with a loan from Greystone Funding Company LLC, insured by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development under its Section 232 program for residential care facilities. HUD required Greystone to collect three escrows: working capital, minor movable equipment and an initial operating deficit. HREF Senior Worthington LLC, which once operated under a MidHudson name, came into the deal in May 2019 to fund them. HREF put $4.5 million into WM Conroe Property Holdings LLC, the holding company that manages the property owner. About $3.24 million covered the HUD escrows. The other $1.27 million funded the first 25 months of HREF's monthly return. HREF took special membership interests rather than common equity or management rights. In exchange, it bargained for the right to become the holding company's sole manager immediately if it was not paid. The redemption date was later extended to August 2024, and the monthly payment was raised to $40,000. According to the Chancery opinion, payments stopped after February 2024. HREF declared its step-in right in November 2024 and sued in the Court of Chancery that month. One count sought a summary declaration under 6 Del. C. Section 18-110 that HREF was now the holding company's sole manager. That count was tried on a paper record in August 2025. The defendants were the property owner and WM Property Holdings LLC, the sponsor-side manager. They argued that the HUD documents and the property owner's operating agreement barred any change in management without HUD's prior written approval. They also argued that HREF's step-in addendum was illegal and that HUD had to be part of the case. In a January 12, 2026 memorandum opinion, Vice Chancellor Morgan T. Zurn rejected each argument. The court held that the HUD approval provisions bound the property-owning borrower, not the holding company above it. It also held that the HREF addendum was not illegal and that the parties before the court were enough to resolve the control dispute. The court ruled that HREF was entitled to become the holding company's sole manager immediately. It held HREF's fee request in abeyance while the remaining claims proceed. The defendants appealed. After briefing and oral argument, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed by order on October 8, 2026, on the basis of and for the reasons in the Court of Chancery's opinion. The panel was Chief Justice Seitz and Justices Traynor and Griffiths. When the Court of Chancery ruled in January, five other claims remained pending there. For investors in HUD-financed senior housing, the ruling shows step-in rights placed at a holding company outside the HUD-regulated borrower being enforced, because the court read the HUD approval provisions as binding the borrower rather than the holding company. Sponsors in similar structures should not expect approval rules written for the borrower to block an upstream investor's contractual takeover once its triggers are met.
live-285: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, through its lawyers at an environmental-law nonprofit, sued in the Seventh Judicial Circuit on July 6, 2026 over how Spartanburg County was permitting a data center campus by Valara Holdings, which the Spartanburg Herald-Journal, in a story republished by South Carolina Lawyers Weekly, describes as a subsidiary of NorthMark Cloud and Compute. The project on South Pine Street, at the site of the former Kohler plant, is reported as a $2.8 billion investment. The group's lawyers, announcing the suit, described about 500,000 square feet of new buildings, a power yard, internal roads and a 450-megawatt gas-fired power plant. The group argued that the county's Unified Land Management Ordinance required the project to be reviewed as a 'major' land development, which goes to the Planning Commission with public notice and comment, rather than as a 'minor' development reviewed by staff. It asked for a declaration that Valara must obtain a major development permit and for an injunction stopping the county from processing the minor application. FOX Carolina reported that the first permit, to redevelop the Kohler building, was approved in August 2025, and that a second application, for four new buildings, the power yard and cooling systems, is still pending. County officials have said the classification depends on the ordinance's specific language rather than a project's size alone, according to the Herald-Journal. Judge Cole dismissed the case on October 6 without deciding whether the classification was correct. According to FOX Carolina, he found the group's concerns about noise, dust, traffic, health and transparency too general to show the special damage South Carolina law requires of neighbors, and he said the group should have appealed to the county Board of Zoning Appeals within 10 days before going to court. He called the challenge to the second permit premature because the county has not acted on it. The dismissal also ended the group's request to pause construction, which had been heard on September 17. A senior attorney for the group told FOX Carolina the ruling conflicts with controlling South Carolina Supreme Court precedent and that residents could not have used the zoning-appeal route because they were told at the time that the project was not a data center; she said the group's lawyers expected to file a notice of appeal within days. The same lawyers are also pursuing a case, now before the South Carolina Court of Appeals, over whether Valara needed Public Service Commission approval, and has asked state regulators to reopen public comment on the project's air permit, issued September 18, over formaldehyde emissions from its planned gas turbines. Valara representatives have said the companies followed all state and local permitting requirements, and a county council member called the suit 'frivolous,' the Herald-Journal reported. FOX Carolina also reported that the county's one-year pause on new data center applications, adopted in June, does not reach Valara's project.
live-286: Hetley Associates owns Hetley Plaza, a strip shopping center in Lemoyne Borough, Cumberland County, zoned Commercial General. It also owns three residential lots around the corner in the borough's Urban Residential District; one of the houses is rented. According to the opinion, the plaza is a prior nonconforming use with fewer parking spaces than the district requires. Its businesses mostly serve few customers, but one space, formerly occupied by a restaurant, is vacant. The owner argued that changing conditions around the plaza had worsened its parking problem. In January 2025 the owner asked the borough Zoning Hearing Board for a use variance to demolish the three houses and build a parking lot. After a hearing, the Board denied the request on March 27, 2025, finding among other things that the owner's decision to rent to a restaurant had aggravated the parking problem. The Court of Common Pleas of Cumberland County affirmed on September 4, 2025, after argument on August 11. It found that the residential lots could continue to be used as rentals, which are in demand, and that the claimed hardship concerned the plaza, not the lots that were the subject of the request. On appeal the owner challenged the Board's findings on neighborhood character, self-created hardship, practicality and minimum variance. In a memorandum opinion by Judge Christine Fizzano Cannon filed October 9, 2026, the Commonwealth Court affirmed on a single ground. Applying the borough ordinance, Section 910.2(a) of the Municipalities Planning Code, and its decision in Bawa Muhaiyaddeen Fellowship v. Philadelphia Zoning Board of Adjustment, it held that the owner was claiming a hardship to its separate commercial plaza, while the residential lots remain usable and valuable for residential purposes. The owner cited no authority allowing a variance on one property based on hardship to another, so the court did not reach the other factors. In footnotes, the court noted that the plaza and the residential lots remain separate parcels despite common ownership, that nothing showed an attempt to consolidate them, and that it expressed no opinion on a reverse subdivision. It also rejected the owner's argument that the minimum-variance requirement does not apply to use variances. The opinion is designated as not reported.
live-287: San Francisco Care Center, L.P. borrowed up to $23,108,000 in 2002 from Pacific Commonwealth Mortgage Company to build a senior health care facility in San Francisco. It began operating the property as an assisted-living facility for elderly and memory-care residents in 2004. The loan was assigned to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in May 2006, and HUD sold it to Lenox Mortgage IX LLC that December. The bankruptcy court later called the loan documents "terribly outdated and nothing like what is routinely seen today." The borrower first defaulted around 2006 or 2007. After Lenox recorded a notice of default in January 2008, the borrower paid the $252,470.56 cure amount, which included no attorneys' fees. It then sued Lenox in state court to force the release of more construction funds, and later dismissed that suit voluntarily. Years later, legal costs from a suit brought by the City of San Francisco over building code violations, which the operator won in 2023, combined with the pandemic to strain its finances. It stopped making loan payments in early 2024. Lenox recorded a notice of default in September 2024 and set a foreclosure sale for January 14, 2025. The operator filed Chapter 11 that same day. Lenox filed a proof of claim for $19,189,226.25. In May 2025 the bankruptcy court approved a section 363 sale of the property for $27,750,000 in cash. Under the sale order, any challenged part of a payoff demand was held in escrow. Lenox's demand was $19,822,204.53, plus per diem interest, $1,910,657.89 in unpaid interest and $419,266.94 in attorneys' fees. Lenox broke the fees down as $187,324.54 for the first default, $139,035.94 for the state-court suit, $56,073.32 for the second default and $87,162 for the bankruptcy and payoff litigation. Judge Dennis Montali disallowed all of the fees. In a December 1, 2025 order he also granted the debtor its own fees and costs under California Civil Code section 1717. The case was converted to Chapter 7 in April 2026. The panel read the note, deed of trust and security agreement closely. The note allowed only fees that a court adjudged reasonable in an action on the note, and no court ever did that. The deed of trust covered actions affecting Lenox's security, but the construction-funds suit did not threaten the lien. The nonjudicial notices of default were also not court proceedings. The security agreement allowed fees only out of foreclosure-sale proceeds, and the property was sold through the bankruptcy court rather than at foreclosure. The panel ruled the other way on the bankruptcy-related fees. Lenox had appeared in the case to protect its lien, through the cash-collateral order, its proof of claim and its objections to the sale order. The panel also held that the payoff litigation could not be an action on the contract for the borrower's section 1717 fee claim and yet not an action for Lenox's own fee recovery. It reversed on those fees and sent the case back for a reasonableness determination. It also vacated the borrower's fee award so the bankruptcy court can decide whether the borrower is still the prevailing party. The decision is a nonprecedential memorandum. For lenders holding seasoned or agency-originated loans, it shows that narrow fee clauses tied to court awards or foreclosure proceeds may not reach legal costs accrued over years if the collateral is sold in bankruptcy, and that contesting a payoff can bring a reciprocal fee claim under section 1717. The amount of Lenox's bankruptcy-related fees, and who prevailed, remain for the bankruptcy court on remand.
live-288: Enterprise Bank and Trust held the first deed of trust on ten Laguna Beach, California parcels. Each parcel was owned by its own single-asset real estate entity, including Laguna Festival Center, LLC, Laguna Art District Complex, LLC, 891 Laguna Canyon Road, LLC, 694 NCH Apartments, LLC and Duplex at Sleepy Hollow, LLC. The properties had a collective book value of about $95 million, and Enterprise was owed roughly $80 million. Each parcel carried at least three deeds of trust. The owners had stopped paying property taxes and regular loan payments. Enterprise sent a default notice in November 2024 and recorded notices of default in February 2025. The defaults came against the backdrop of a long-running dispute between two investors over control of the ownership entities. Within three weeks of the default notices, the owners and twelve affiliates filed voluntary Chapter 11 cases in Delaware, jointly administered under MOM CA Investco LLC. Enterprise obtained unopposed stay relief on July 15, 2025, and the Delaware cases were dismissed in August 2025. Enterprise then sued in California state court, which appointed a receiver over the properties on October 7, 2025. Enterprise also noticed nonjudicial foreclosure sales for 3:00 p.m. on October 15, 2025. On the afternoon of the sales, between 2:28 and 3:02 p.m., involuntary Chapter 11 petitions were filed against all ten owners in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California. The petitioning creditors included Vierergruppe Management, Inc., which the panel described as connected to one of the investors. Neither Enterprise nor the foreclosure trustee knew. The sales ran from 3:13 to 3:52 p.m. About twenty unrelated parties attended, but only one outside bid was placed, on the 694 NCH property. That sale was later canceled and the money returned. Enterprise took the other nine properties by credit bid. The owners opposed stay relief by offering a $102 million purchase agreement with Special Assets Laguna, LLC; the panel noted it was signed for both the sellers and the buyer by the same person, an officer of Vierergruppe. Bankruptcy Judge Scott C. Clarkson found the involuntary cases were filed in bad faith. At a December 12, 2025 hearing he granted Enterprise prospective and in rem relief and retroactively annulled the stay as to the nine properties without outside bids, which validated those sales; the orders were entered December 15, 2025. He also ordered the petitioning creditors to post a $1 million bond. They did not, and the ten cases were dismissed on March 18, 2026. The owners dropped their own appeals in June 2026, which left only the appeal of a prospective bidder. That bidder said he held back because he had heard of the filings, and argued that the petitions chilled the bidding; the panel noted he reached the sale site only after the property he most wanted had been sold. The panel first held that the appeal was not moot and that the bidder had standing, because he had changed his conduct in reliance on the stay. On the merits, it held that the equities analysis under the Fjeldsted factors properly looked at the debtors' bad faith, the lender's lack of notice, its earlier stay relief and how quickly it moved, and not only at the bidder's position. It noted that the bidder had not alerted the trustee or placed a bid. It also found nothing inconsistent in treating the rescinded 694 NCH sale differently, because that property is the subject of a separate appeal. The decision is a nonprecedential memorandum. It shows how the panel weighed the equities of a last-minute involuntary filing: the debtors' bad faith, the lender's lack of notice and prior stay relief, and its prompt motion all favored annulment, while a bidder who knew of the filings and stayed silent had little room to claim harm.
live-289: Braemar Hotels & Resorts Inc. (NYSE: BHR), a Dallas-based REIT focused on luxury hotels and resorts, settled a dispute with its largest stockholder, Al Shams Investments Limited, a Bermuda company. The Cooperation and Settlement Agreement is dated October 6, 2026; Ashford Hospitality Trust, Inc. and Ashford Inc. also signed, and Al Shams's beneficial owner signed for limited purposes. Braemar filed the agreement with a Form 8-K on October 8, 2026, and a company press release that day announced it alongside a portfolio update that included the previously announced $372 million sale of the Four Seasons Resort Scottsdale. The agreement's recitals describe what was resolved. Al Shams had nominated a slate of directors for the 2026 annual meeting. It had asserted or threatened direct claims against the company group, including defamation and libel claims, claims under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and claims similar to those brought by another investor and Morning View Hotels BH1, LLC. It had also asserted or threatened derivative claims alleging fiduciary breaches by the board and management, and was pursuing a verified petition under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 202 to depose two former Braemar directors before filing suit. The company group denies wrongdoing, and no party admits liability. Braemar agreed to pay $25 million for the settlement and releases plus $15 million to reimburse Al Shams's expenses, $40 million in all, payable as $20 million on signing and $10 million each four and eight months later. Each installment is conditioned on Al Shams's continued compliance. Disputes over a claimed breach go to expedited JAMS arbitration in Dallas, and a final finding of material breach requires Al Shams to return everything paid. If cash is short, Braemar may pay up to $4 million of the later installments in common stock, and the board must grant an exception to the 9.8 percent ownership limit if needed. Al Shams withdrew its nominations, agreed to dismiss the Rule 202 petition with prejudice, and accepted a 10-year standstill barring proxy contests, share purchases and litigation or pre-suit discovery against the companies and their current and former directors and officers, except to enforce the agreement. It must vote with the board's recommendations and may consult with Braemar's search firm on candidates for one board seat, with the board retaining sole discretion. Both sides exchanged releases and agreed not to disparage each other. In the 8-K, Braemar said it expects its own contribution to be $4 million to $6 million after insurance proceeds and Ashford's share; under a separate Allocation Agreement, Braemar and Ashford each bear 50 percent of the payments net of insurance. Braemar cautioned that it may not recover the insurance proceeds and said its contribution would likely be less than the cost of the litigation it avoided. The press release said the 2026 annual meeting will be held December 21, 2026. In a later 8-K filed November 10, 2026, Braemar reported that its advisory agreement with Ashford terminated that day as part of its move to self-management.
live-290: Schell Road, LLC bought 80 acres on Schell Road in Grant Township in 2022, planning to develop and operate a gravel mine. It submitted a special use permit application on September 20, 2022, with site plans from a civil engineer; it was the first mining application the township had received since 2003. Township officials, advised by counsel, questioned whether the ordinance's mining rules, unchanged since 1998, accounted for a 2011 amendment to state law. The company submitted supplemental information in December 2022 and January 2023 to address deficiencies, and officials told it they intended to delay consideration until the ordinance was amended. After an exchange of letters in which the company's counsel accused the township of delaying review to defeat the application, Schell Road filed a complaint on February 17, 2023, seeking a writ of mandamus to compel a public hearing. Following a planning commission recommendation, the township adopted amendments to the ordinance on March 23, 2023, effective March 30. Schell Road amended its complaint to allege the amendments were enacted in bad faith to stop its mine and exceeded the township's authority under MCL 125.3205, and added due process, injunctive and declaratory claims. The trial court granted the township summary disposition, finding the application incomplete, finding no bad faith, and holding the amended ordinance complied with the statute. A panel of Judges Korobkin, Rick and Maldonado affirmed on all three issues. On mandamus, it held the trial court could decide completeness on the documentary record at summary disposition, and agreed the application was incomplete: among other gaps, the reclamation plan lacked required information on phasing and timing, and the record did not show the plan had been submitted to the county extension office and soil and water conservation district as the ordinance required. On bad faith, it agreed the record did not support the claim: the township had not received a mining application since 2003, acted on counsel's advice, told the company in December 2022 that amendments were under way, and adopted amendments that apply to any mining application. The court said the application was "a catalyst" for the amendments but that this did not establish bad faith. On validity, the court rejected the company's arguments that MCL 125.3205 sets only a standard for courts on appeal and that the amended ordinance's requirements on market need and on property-value effects along the haul route go beyond the statute, finding those requirements track the statute's need and "very serious consequences" factors. The opinion is unpublished.
live-291: According to the opinion, C&B Development, LLC is the equitable owner, under an August 2022 purchase agreement, of a 75.5-acre tract in Maxatawny Township, Berks County, now improved with a restaurant, a mobile home park and an airport. The tract lies in three zoning districts, Commercial (C-1), Light Industrial (L-I) and Agricultural Preservation (AP-1), and has frontage only on Kutztown Road. The developer plans to demolish the existing uses and build a commercial building and a 709,000-square-foot warehouse on the L-I portion, which can be reached only by a new private road, Road A, through the commercial district. An ordinance amendment effective October 13, 2022 made warehouses a conditional use in the L-I district and added Section 593(c), which requires warehouse buildings and "all related impervious surfaces" to be at least 500 feet from a building occupied by an existing residential, institutional or educational use. On August 31, 2023 the zoning officer determined that Road A was an impervious surface serving the warehouse that could not meet the setback, and that the developer needed a variance before its conditional use hearing could proceed. The developer appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board and alternatively sought a dimensional variance. After hearings ending in January 2024, the Board on January 15, 2024 upheld the zoning officer and denied the variance, finding the property could be used for many permitted uses without the 500-foot buffer and that Road A would bring hundreds of tractor trailers onto Kutztown Road in a largely residential area used by Kutztown University students. The Berks County Court of Common Pleas affirmed on July 14, 2025. In a memorandum opinion by Judge Patricia A. McCullough filed October 14, 2026, the Commonwealth Court affirmed. The zoning officer's absence from the hearings was no ground for reversal, because the Board interprets the ordinance itself and the developer withdrew its plan to subpoena him. The conditional use provision and the setback did not conflict, so the Municipalities Planning Code's rule resolving doubtful language in the owner's favor did not apply. And because the developer admitted the L-I land could be used for other purposes, its hardship was self-imposed rather than a function of the property. The court noted that the developer had not brought a formal challenge to the ordinance's validity, and it declined to consider material from the developer's separate, pending inverse condemnation suit against the township. The opinion is designated as not reported.
live-292: 865 East 49th Street Associates LLC, a commercial landlord, sued its tenant Valdo Auto Sales Corp. and others in Miami-Dade County Circuit Court (Lower Tribunal No. 22-17871-CA-01). The trial court, Judge Valerie R. Manno Schurr presiding, entered summary judgment orders on liability and damages in the landlord's favor. Liability was resolved by an order titled "Agreed Summary Final Judgment as to Liability," which covered all of the landlord's claims, including fraud and unjust enrichment. The only money awarded, however, was $76,199.37 in past-due rent for breach of the commercial lease. The landlord appealed, arguing that once liability was established on the fraud and unjust enrichment counts, the trial court could not award zero dollars on them. The tenant did not appear in the appeal. A panel of Judges Fernandez, Gordo and Rebull decided the appeal, and Judge Gordo wrote the opinion affirming the trial court. The court started from the rule against double recovery. A plaintiff who wins a contract award must show that its fraud or unjust enrichment damages are separate and distinct from that award, and not just the same loss counted again. Fraud requires actual damages as an essential element, and a liability finding alone does not establish them. Unjust enrichment requires competent, quantified evidence of the value of the benefit conferred. The panel cited Florida cases holding that a plaintiff can win liability and still recover nothing. Procedure also decided the appeal. The trial court resolved liability, damages and rehearing only after full in-court hearings, but the landlord did not supply a transcript of any of them or an approved statement of the evidence. Because the liability judgment was an agreed order, nothing in the record showed what the parties had agreed to. In particular, the record did not show whether the landlord kept or gave up any claim to separate damages. The panel would not assume that the agreed judgment decided more than the liability it recites. It agreed with the trial court that the landlord had failed to raise a genuine issue of material fact as to any compensable, non-duplicative damages, and affirmed. The opinion is not final until any timely rehearing motion is resolved. There are several lessons for commercial landlords and their lawyers. First, fraud and unjust enrichment counts in a rent case need their own damages proof, with a dollar figure tied to a loss the lease award does not already cover. Second, an agreed liability judgment should say expressly whether damages on each claim are reserved for later decision. Third, if a summary judgment or damages hearing may be appealed, have a court reporter there; as the court noted, the lack of a transcript is usually fatal to an appellant.
live-293: Valley Post is a four-building dining development off Dunnavant Valley Road in Chelsea, Alabama, in Shelby County south of Birmingham. A Birmingham developer built it, and its only operator was a Pihakis Restaurant Group affiliate. It housed four concepts: Hero Diner, Luca & Lucy, Little Donkey and Rodney Scott BBQ. According to court documents described by AL.com, the development opened in December 2025, and no rent was paid from that month on. In April 2026 the Pihakis Restaurant Group began closing restaurants, and all four Valley Post restaurants shut. That month the landlord side filed liens on several properties leased to the group and its affiliates. WBRC reported that the amended Valley Post lien, filed April 27, claimed $7,166,296.20 plus attorney fees and other expenses for rent due under the leases. In June, the landlord entity, Dunnavant Valley Dining LLC, sued in Shelby County Circuit Court. It alleged that PRG Valley Post had defaulted on a long-term lease of the four buildings, with charges totaling about $7.35 million. The tenant never answered, and the court entered a default judgment for $7.19 million in unpaid rent, attorney fees and court costs, as AL.com reported on October 7, 2026. According to that report, the court certified the judgment as final, which makes it immediately enforceable, and post-judgment interest accrues until it is paid. Published reporting does not say how the judgment will be collected, whether the leases carried guaranties, or how the award was calculated against the roughly $7.35 million originally claimed. Waldo's Chicken and Beer opened a Valley Post location on September 29, and Saw's BBQ is expected to open there later this fall.
live-294: The Massachusetts Appeals Court on October 14, 2026 reversed a Land Court judgment that had declared CRG Acquisition, LLC's proposed warehouse and distribution facility in Holliston a use permitted as of right, and directed entry of a declaration that the warehouse requires a special permit in the town's industrial district. Justice Toone wrote for the panel of Justices Sacks, Singh and Toone. According to the opinion, CRG is the buyer under a pending agreement to purchase 72 acres in Holliston's industrial district from New Hopping Brook Realty Trust. In 2019 it sought site plan approval for an approximately 800,000-square-foot warehouse and distribution facility with 423 trailer truck spaces, 170 loading docks and 129 passenger vehicle spaces. The planning board approved the site plan in March 2020 with 31 conditions, noting the building inspector's concern that the use might need a special permit as a general industrial use. In June 2020 CRG applied for a special permit while maintaining none was required, and for approval of a modified site plan with fewer trailer spaces and loading docks. After eleven public hearings, the board denied both in July 2021, citing traffic, noise and effects on the town's historical and agricultural character and on surrounding neighborhoods. CRG and the trust sued in the Land Court on August 27, 2021, appealing the denials under G. L. c. 40A, § 17, and seeking a declaration under G. L. c. 240, § 14A that the warehouse is allowed by right under bylaw § III.G.1, which covers a "[w]holesale office or showroom, including warehouse facilities." A Land Court judge granted summary judgment to CRG on the declaratory claim; the judgment dismissed the special-permit appeal as moot and sent the modified site plan back to the board. Under the judgment's terms, if the town's appeal succeeded, the plaintiffs would not further pursue the project. The Appeals Court agreed with CRG that neither the planning board nor the town was owed deference, because the board never decided, and had no authority to decide, whether a special permit was required. On the merits it sided with the town. It read "including warehouse facilities" as describing warehouse space that is part of a wholesale office or showroom, not a standalone warehouse, and held that a warehouse used for storage and distribution falls under § III.G.3, which requires a special permit for general industrial uses, including storage, processing and packaging, occupying more than 15,000 square feet. It also rejected CRG's reliance on the board's 1999 approval of a different site plan.
live-295: All American was the framing, drywall, insulation and acoustical ceiling tile subcontractor on a five-story hotel project. After the original general contractor was terminated, GSD was hired as the replacement general contractor. The subcontract let GSD terminate for convenience, in which case All American could recover payment for work performed through termination plus demobilization costs, but nothing for work not performed. A separate clause required ten percent of each partial payment to be held back until ninety days after final completion of the project. When GSD took over, All American had completed about 93.9% of its work and was owed a $71,582.98 retainage; the rest of its work was waiting on other trades. The project then developed significant mold from water intrusion, and All American refused to finish until the mold was properly remediated for its workers' safety. GSD said it had done enough by removing some drywall and doing limited mold testing; All American said that was insufficient because GSD never hired an industrial hygienist or prepared a formal remediation plan. GSD terminated All American and never paid the retainage. All American sued in Broward County circuit court for the retainage, and its owner testified at trial that it was not seeking the $45,300 for unperformed work. The trial court, Judge John B. Bowman, found GSD breached by not paying for work performed and by not properly remediating the mold, and awarded $116,882.98: the retainage plus $45,300. In an opinion by Judge Spencer D. Levine, joined by Judges Klingensmith and Lott, the Fourth District held the subcontract's plain language supported the retainage award: the project was completed in 2023, the ninety-day period had long expired, and the subcontract had no termination-for-cause clause or other provision letting GSD keep the retainage after a termination. The court noted its analysis "could be different" if the contract had a for-cause provision. Having affirmed on that ground, it did not decide whether GSD also breached by failing to remediate the mold. It reversed the $45,300 because the complaint sought only the retainage, All American conceded the point, and the subcontract barred payment for work not performed. The opinion is not final until any timely rehearing motion is resolved.
live-297: On October 14, 2026, the Appellate Division, Second Department, affirmed an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Justice Cassandra A. Johnson), that denied CG & J Realty, LLC's motion to vacate a lien bond and to dismiss CFS Enterprises, Inc.'s cause of action to foreclose a mechanic's lien against it. The panel was Justices Francesca E. Connolly, Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, Barry E. Warhit and James P. McCormack. According to the decision, CFS Enterprises filed a notice of mechanic's lien on November 7, 2022 against real property in Queens owned by CG & J Realty, and sued to foreclose the lien in February 2023. In April 2023, CG & J Realty posted a bond under Lien Law §19 to discharge the lien. In July 2023, Century Construction Group Corp. filed a bond under Lien Law §37 and moved to discharge all liens and claims against the property. In an October 10, 2023 order, the trial court discharged all liens and claims against the property and said the Section 37 bond would supersede all prior bonds. CG & J Realty then moved, by order to show cause, under Lien Law §59 to vacate and cancel its Section 19 bond and to dismiss the foreclosure claim against it. The trial court denied the motion on October 24, 2024. On appeal, the Second Department noted that mechanic's liens are purely statutory and that strict compliance is required. Section 59 requires that notice be served on the lienor personally or left at the lienor's last known place of residence with a person of suitable age. The court found that CG & J Realty had only filed the order to show cause on NYSCEF, so its motion was properly denied. The court declined CFS Enterprises' request for the attorneys' fees and expenses of the appeal under New York's frivolous-conduct rule, finding CFS had not shown that CG & J Realty's appeal was frivolous. The order was affirmed with costs.
live-298: The building on the property operated as a bowling alley until 2019. Zecorra signed a purchase agreement in June 2022, contracted with Mann Construction in September 2022 to convert the building for a proposed Dollar General store, and closed in October 2022 for a total acquisition cost of $450,000: a $200,000 contract sales price plus $250,000 in other consideration, which the owner's appraiser attributed to personal property, fixtures and furniture. The property had been listed at $525,000 in June 2021. In December 2022 Zecorra leased it to Dolgencorp, LLC (Dollar General), agreeing to complete construction by April 1, 2023, and Dollar General took possession in May 2023. Zecorra challenged the township's 2023 assessment, which turned on value as of December 31, 2022. Its appraiser valued the property at $180,000 after a renovation allowance of about $57,000. The township's appraiser valued it at $570,000, calling the $200,000 price a significant outlier and deducting $525,000 from a stabilized income value for renovation costs and lost rent over a four-month holding period. After a three-day hearing, the tribunal on May 27, 2025, gave the owner's deduction no weight, found the owner's photographs of the property's condition inconsistent and incomplete, and made its own determination: $529,000 by sales comparison and $521,000 by income capitalization after adopting the township's deduction, reconciled to $525,000. Judges Borrello, Bazzi and Lievense affirmed in an unpublished per curiam opinion. They held the tribunal's adoption of the township's deduction was supported by substantial evidence, because that figure was a market-based calculation of what an investor would pay on tax day rather than a measure of actual construction costs, and evidence showed some work had been done in 2022. They also held the tribunal properly valued the property for its undisputed highest and best use, a repurposed commercial use, rather than as a vacant bowling alley, and was not required to accept the sale price, noting the $525,000 value matched the property's 2021 listing price.
live-299: Orchard BJK and Pocono Mountains Industries own commercially and industrially zoned properties in Coolbaugh Township, Monroe County. In April 2023 the township's Board of Supervisors approved their subdivision of one tract into a 35.5-acre Lot 1 and a 73.16-acre Lot 2 and conditionally approved a land development plan for an approximately 333,000-square-foot warehouse on Lot 1 under the ordinances then in effect. On August 2, 2023, the Board amended the township's Stormwater Management and Earth Disturbance Ordinance, increasing the minimum inner wetland buffer from 50 to 150 feet and the minimum buffer between buildings and wetlands from 100 to 150 feet. The amendments left in place a provision allowing the Board, on application, to modify or waive stormwater requirements development by development. On April 29, 2024, the developers filed a preliminary land development plan for an approximately 186,000-square-foot warehouse on Lot 2 and a petition asking the Board to apply the pre-amendment buffers. On May 3, 2024, with both still pending, they sued the Board in the Monroe County Court of Common Pleas, alleging the amendments violated their constitutional right to enjoy their property and were invalid special legislation, and seeking a declaration that the amendments were void. They alleged the amendments effectively prevented warehouses on Lot 2, reduced the value of their other properties, and were designed to restrict industrial development because of local opposition to warehouses. The Board filed preliminary objections, and on June 27, 2025, the court dismissed the complaint as unripe. Citizens for Pennsylvania's Future, the Tobyhanna Creek/Tunkhannock Creek Watershed Association and the Tobyhanna Conservation Association are also named as appellees. In an unreported memorandum opinion by Judge Lori A. Dumas, joined by Judge Christine Fizzano Cannon and Senior Judge Bonnie Brigance Leadbetter, the Commonwealth Court affirmed. It rejected the developers' argument that the trial court raised ripeness on its own, pointing to the Board's preliminary objections, which argued there was no actual controversy until the Board ruled on the waiver request. Applying the lenient ripeness standard for declaratory judgment actions, the court still held the suit premature: whether the buffers would block development of Lot 2 or other properties "remains purely theoretical" while the developers may still obtain relief through the waiver process they had invoked four days before suing.
live-300: Waterworks, which makes and supplies high-end bathroom fixtures, sued 514 West 24th Owner LLC and its surety in New York County Supreme Court for breach of contract, lien foreclosure and account stated over bathroom and cabinet materials delivered for the owner's redevelopment of a building in Chelsea. Under purchase orders and change orders, the owner agreed to pay $2,577,166.99. Both sides agree the owner paid $1,608,827.37 for goods delivered and accepted, and Waterworks filed a mechanic's lien for $968,339.62, the balance it says is due. Justice Joel M. Cohen granted Waterworks summary judgment on the contract and lien claims in an order entered June 12, 2024, dismissed the account stated claim as duplicative, and on December 5, 2024, entered judgment for $1,396,058.74, based on the unpaid balance of the full contract price plus pre-judgment interest, costs and disbursements. On appeal, the owner argued it was not bound by $390,605.51 in change orders approved by the project's original construction manager, Sunrise Construction, LLC, because their agreement barred Sunrise from entering change orders without the owner's prior written approval. The panel of Justices Webber, Friedman, Kapnick and Pitt-Burke unanimously rejected that argument, holding that the owner's acceptance of the materials without objection was an implied ratification. The owner also argued there were factual disputes over how much was delivered. The court held Waterworks' invoices established delivery of $2,340,098 in materials, since the owner identified no invoiced item it did not receive. But Waterworks offered its proof that the remaining $237,069 was delivered only in an affidavit from its accounts receivable manager filed with its reply papers, which the court disregarded because the owner had no chance to respond. Because the judgment rested on the full contract price, the court vacated it and remitted the case for further proceedings on damages, and dismissed the separate appeal from the June 2024 order as subsumed.
live-301: The parents of a 17-year-old high school senior who was shot and killed in the Mall of Louisiana food court on April 23, 2026 filed a wrongful-death and negligence suit on Oct. 7 in East Baton Rouge Parish's 19th Judicial District Court, Acadiana News First reported. The suit names Mall of Louisiana LLC, Brookfield Properties Retail Inc. and Marksman Security LLC, described as the mall's owner, its operator/manager and its security contractor, along with the person accused of firing the gun. Four people who were sitting with the teen joined as plaintiffs: two who suffered gunshot wounds and two who allege severe emotional distress. According to the suit, a confrontation broke out in the food court and multiple shots were fired. The accused shooter, who was 17 at the time, has been indicted as an adult on one count of second-degree murder, six counts of attempted second-degree murder and one count of illegal use of a weapon during a crime of violence, and has pleaded not guilty. The plaintiffs allege the defendants failed to take reasonable steps to protect patrons despite a history of violence at the property, citing a 2013 food court disturbance that led to the mall's evacuation and closure and a 2022 shooting near the mall that killed two people. They allege failures in security staffing, monitoring of the food court, response and de-escalation, threat assessment, surveillance and enforcement of the mall's firearms ban. "There were zero security officers in the food court on April 23, 2026," the suit alleges. The family seeks damages for the teen's pain and suffering before death and for their own losses, including grief, loss of companionship and funeral expenses; the other plaintiffs seek damages for physical injuries or emotional trauma. The suit does not state a dollar amount but says damages exceed the threshold for a jury trial. The article did not include a response from the defendants.
live-302: The Supreme Court of Alabama on October 16, 2026, affirmed a Montgomery County circuit court's decision to strike as untimely the response that Montgomery Civic Ballet, Inc., doing business as Montgomery Ballet Studios, and two individual plaintiffs filed to their landlord's motion for partial summary judgment. On the landlord's cross-appeal, the court affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded, holding that the trial court could not certify the partial summary judgment as final under Rule 54(b) while also declaring the entire case dismissed. Justice Will Sellers wrote the opinion, and four justices concurred. According to the opinion, Commercial Properties, Inc. leased two suites in a shopping center it owns and manages to the Ballet under leases signed in May 2008 and January 2012. The leases contained tenant indemnification, default and attorney-fee provisions. In December 2020 the Ballet vacated, citing the landlord's alleged failure to eliminate mold, and in January 2021 the Ballet and two individuals sued the landlord, alleging the individuals were injured by mold exposure and the Ballet's property, including costumes, was damaged. The landlord counterclaimed for unpaid rent and for defense and indemnity on the individuals' claims, and the Ballet did not respond to its written demand for a defense. In February 2023 the landlord moved for partial summary judgment on the claims involving the Ballet, seeking a declaration that the Ballet owes $65,827.50 in unpaid rent and owes defense and indemnity on the individuals' claims, plus judgment on the Ballet's own claims. A hearing was not set until March 2025; the landlord attributes the delay to the original judge's injuries and retirement, not to the parties. The plaintiffs filed their response on Friday, April 18, 2025, for a hearing on Monday, April 21. The trial court struck it as untimely, later refused to accept it when it was resubmitted, and on December 22, 2025, entered partial summary judgment for the landlord. The Supreme Court agreed the response was late. Rule 56(c)(2) requires opposition to be served two days before the hearing, and Rule 6(a), as then in effect, excluded the weekend from that count, so the response was due Thursday, April 17. The court found the plaintiffs had notice of the hearing and the motion to strike, said it would not fault the trial court if their counsel did not attend, and noted they never sought a continuance under Rule 56(f) or more time under Rule 6(b). The plaintiffs did not challenge the merits of the summary judgment in their opening brief, and the court declined to consider merits arguments raised for the first time in reply. On February 3, 2026, the trial court had certified the partial summary judgment as final under Rule 54(b) and stated that "this case is dismissed." The Supreme Court called that order "legally inconsistent": the individual plaintiffs' claims against the landlord were still pending, as was the determination of damages owed to the landlord. It affirmed the certification, reversed the order to the extent it dismissed the entire case, and remanded for further proceedings.
live-303: 68V BTR Holdings, LLC applied to Fairhope's Planning Commission to develop two townhome apartment complexes, Skyline Village and Gables on Lawrence. According to meeting minutes, the commission denied Gables for adverse drainage effects, unmet greenspace requirements, inconsistency with the comprehensive plan and traffic problems, and denied Skyline for drainage, traffic and health, safety and general welfare concerns. 68V sued in federal court in the Southern District of Alabama in 2022. After that court entered summary judgment against 68V on its federal claims and declined to hear its state-law claims, 68V refiled in Baldwin Circuit Court, seeking damages for negligence, invalidation of the denials as arbitrary and capricious, and damages for a deprivation of property without substantive due process under the Alabama Constitution. The city and commission moved for summary judgment on all three claims, citing municipal immunity, volunteer immunity and substantive immunity. The circuit court denied the motion, and they petitioned the Supreme Court for mandamus on the negligence claim only. Writing the main opinion, Justice Parker reasoned that the claim rested on respondeat superior, so the city and commission could not be liable if their agents were immune. The nine unpaid commissioners were protected by the Volunteer Service Act for negligence, and to the extent 68V alleged bad faith, the opinion said Alabama's municipal-immunity statute also shields agents' bad-faith acts. The planning director, city attorney and mayor, whom 68V faulted for their advice and responses, were protected by substantive immunity because acting on development applications is a public-policy function; the opinion distinguished a 2013 plurality decision that allowed a tort claim on what it called unique facts. The main opinion called its holding narrow, saying it does not leave planning commissions free to act arbitrarily, does not address 68V's pending claims and does not foreclose a mandamus petition, a remedy 68V chose not to pursue earlier. Justices Wise, Sellers and Cook joined it. Chief Justice Stewart, joined by Justice McCool, and Justices Shaw and Bryan concurred in the result. Justice Mendheim, also concurring in the result, wrote that the negligence claim fails under the municipal-immunity statute alone and that the main opinion's use of substantive immunity deserved more caution, noting that the federal court had found the substantive-immunity arguments lacking when it ruled on a motion to dismiss in 2023.
