live-310: A panel of Texas's First Court of Appeals in Houston, in an October 16, 2026 memorandum opinion by Justice Clint Morgan, affirmed a Harris County judgment against a restaurant operator and its owner, who had sued 2020 Harwin 59 Shopping Centers, Ltd., Harwin Exchange Center, Inc. and Harwin Exchange's president for breach of contract, fraud, Deceptive Trade Practices Act violations and quantum meruit over repairs and a refused sublease. According to the opinion, the five-year lease for a restaurant space on Richmond Avenue in Houston was signed on October 1, 2019, on a Texas Association of Realtors form, with Harwin Exchange as landlord. It made the landlord responsible for roof repairs after prompt written notice from the tenant, and the tenant responsible for grounds, parking, plumbing, drainage and HVAC, including an HVAC service contract. The tenant accepted the space "as-is," and subletting required the landlord's written consent. The appellants alleged they were not told the lease had been assigned to 2020 Harwin in January 2021, that they spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on repairs and improvements the landlord would not reimburse, and that Harwin Exchange's president promised to approve a sublease and a sale of the business. They signed an estoppel certificate stating the landlord was not in default as a condition of seeking that consent, but consent was refused, and a materialmen's lien was later placed on the property. The court upheld each ground for summary judgment. The lease assigned electrical, plumbing and air-conditioning repairs to the tenant, and the appellants did not address those terms. There was no evidence of a written request for roof repairs, the lease imposed no duty to reimburse, and the as-is clause defeated any claim that the roof had to be fixed before move-in. The proposed sublease ran longer than a year, so an oral agreement to consent to it was unenforceable under the statute of frauds. Quantum meruit was unavailable because the lease covered the same repairs. The DTPA claim failed because base rent of $8,700 a month over the 60-month term totaled $522,000, above the statute's $500,000 exemption for nonresidential transactions, and the appellants did not challenge the dismissal of their fraud claim for failure to replead after special exceptions. The court also affirmed the fee awards of $23,580 for the trial court and $15,000 for appeal. The appellees had requested $31,574.87 for the trial court; the court said the lower award indicated the billing records adequately separated recoverable fees, and the appellants had not preserved their complaint that a jury should have decided fees.
live-311: The Appellate Division, First Department on October 1, 2026 unanimously affirmed an October 2024 order of Supreme Court, New York County (Alexander M. It was undisputed the tenant did not meet those last two conditions. The court held the two clauses create "ambiguity and irreconcilable conflict" and rejected the landlord's argument that the good guy clause overrides the surrender clause. Citing the Court of Appeals' 2025 decision in 1995 CAM LLC v. West Side Advisors, LLC, which involved similar facts, and applying the rule that ambiguity is construed against the drafter, the court noted it was undisputed that the landlord's counsel drafted the lease and guaranties and held the guarantors' liability terminated on September 30, 2020.
live-312: Shadowbox Studios and an affiliated real estate company, Henrico 183, sued DeKalb County in DeKalb County Superior Court on Aug. 5, 2026, Decaturish reported in a story published by WABE. live-313: Sommers Development Group has a contract with Rockwell Automation, Inc., which owns property in Mayfield Heights that Sommers plans to redevelop as a townhome community. At Sommers' request, the city council on May 27, 2026, adopted an ordinance rezoning the property from the "Headquarters or Executive Offices Park Districts" classification to "Planned Unit Development Districts" and a resolution approving a density variance. Sommers also sought approval of a preliminary site plan. On July 24, a committee opposed to the project filed an initiative petition proposing an ordinance to return the property to its prior zoning. The council held a hearing on August 18 without voting and on September 1 voted 4-3 to reject the petition. The committee filed a supplemental petition on September 2, the board of elections found 691 valid signatures, enough to qualify, and on September 9 the council adopted an emergency resolution certifying the initiative for the November 3 ballot. Sommers filed a protest the next day, the board denied it after a September 21 hearing, and Sommers filed this original action four days later. In a per curiam opinion joined by all seven justices, the court first rejected the board's and the committee's laches defense, holding Sommers could not have presumed the initiative would reach the ballot until the board confirmed sufficient signatures on September 4 and acted promptly after that. It then rejected each of Sommers' four arguments. The petition was a valid initiative, not an untimely referendum in disguise: Ohio law has long allowed voters to repeal council legislation by initiative, and under the charter an initiative, unlike a timely referendum, does not suspend the ordinance in the meantime. The initiative is a zoning measure and therefore legislative, not administrative, and any question about its effect on Sommers' existing approvals was premature. Sommers did not show the petition was not submitted to the clerk of council or that the clerk failed to determine its sufficiency. On timing, the council certified the initiative 55 days before the election, within the charter's timeline for supplemental petitions but after the 90-day deadline in R.C. 3501.02(F)(1). Noting that no case had resolved such a conflict, the court held the board did not abuse its discretion or clearly disregard the law in placing the measure on the ballot, citing the statute's wording and precedent on municipal home rule over elections. The ruling left the initiative on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
live-314: California's Second Appellate District, Division Seven, on October 19, 2026 affirmed a Los Angeles County Superior Court judgment confirming an arbitration award for Tucker Investment Group, LLC (TIG) and its managing member in a lease dispute brought by restaurant tenant The Waffle, LLC. Justice Feuer wrote the unpublished opinion, joined by Presiding Justice Martinez and Justice Segal. According to the opinion, TIG held a 10-year master lease on a commercial property in Westwood and on March 30, 2017, signed a 10-year lease with The Waffle, which wanted to open a second restaurant there. Under an addendum and construction work letter, TIG agreed to provide a four-inch grease waste line connected to a 3,000-gallon grease interceptor. The lease set no deadline for that work. Its cure provision said the landlord was not in breach unless it failed to perform within a reasonable time, at least 30 days after written notice, or, for work needing longer, failed to start within 30 days and diligently pursue it. Installing the interceptor would have required excavating a slope behind the premises, and from late 2017 into early 2018 the parties discussed a smaller Schier grease trap instead. The Waffle sent a notice of breach on March 19, 2018, and on April 6 rejected the Schier as final; TIG's managing member replied that he was going back to engineers about the 3,000-gallon unit and was interviewing shoring engineers. The Waffle sued on May 2, 2018, for fraud and negligent misrepresentation against the Tucker defendants and TIG's project manager and his firm, Coastline Construction Management, Inc., and for rescission, breach of contract and declaratory relief against TIG. After a six-day bench trial in November 2021, the trial court found TIG did not breach the lease because installation was not a 30-day cure and TIG had started within 30 days. In a 2022 jury trial on the misrepresentation claims, the jury found for the Coastline defendants on negligent misrepresentation and deadlocked on the rest, and the court declared a mistrial. The parties then stipulated to binding arbitration of the remaining claims, waived any appeal except on the grounds in Code of Civil Procedure section 1286.2, and agreed the arbitrator could use the evidence from both trial phases. Coastline settled with The Waffle for $5,000 in January 2024. In a 43-page final award in March 2024, the arbitrator found the fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims not proven and awarded the Tucker defendants about $2.2 million in fees and costs. The trial court confirmed the award, and judgment was entered on July 31, 2024. The Court of Appeal held the arbitrator did not exceed his powers by referring to the phase I findings: the stipulation allowed use of that evidence, and the award rested on 63 findings of his own. It held the award was reasoned because it set out the arbitrator's reasoning on the central issues, even though it did not address The Waffle's argument that partial performance does not defeat a fraud claim. And it held The Waffle's objection to fees for work connected to the settled Coastline defendants was a claim of legal error, which courts cannot review after a binding arbitration.

live-316: The Ohio Supreme Court on October 20, 2026 denied a writ of mandamus sought by data-center developer Bristolville 25 Developer, L.L.C. and BHGH Properties, L.L.C. against the Village of Lordstown and its planning-and-zoning administrator. In a per curiam opinion joined by all seven justices, State ex rel. Bristolville 25 Developer, L.L.C. v. Lordstown, 2026-Ohio-4073, the court held that the village's temporary moratorium on data-center permits and applications means it has no clear legal duty to continue reviewing Bristolville's site plan. According to the opinion, Bristolville develops large-scale data centers and in February 2025 agreed to buy industrially zoned land in Lordstown from BHGH Properties. The Vindicator reported that the site plan covers 98.68 acres in Lordstown and 34.38 acres in neighboring Jackson Township, and The Vindicator and The Business Journal both reported the project at $3.6 billion. On October 20, 2025, Bristolville took the first step in the village's site-plan-review process by delivering a project outline and site plan. The next day the zoning administrator said the office could not proceed until the village council acted on a proposed data-center ban, and on November 3, 2025, the council passed Ordinance No. 57-2025 as an emergency measure, barring data centers in the village. The village solicitor then wrote that the village was not refusing to review the submission and that its engineer had begun reviewing it, but that the project would likely be prohibited by the new ordinance. Bristolville and BHGH then sued. The court dismissed the claim against the solicitor and granted an alternative writ against the village and the administrator. Before the ban took effect, the council repealed it and unanimously adopted a moratorium of up to 180 days on issuing data-center permits and on receiving or processing applications, which suspended any duty to conduct site-plan review. The review halted on January 5, 2026, and the council also declined to approve the village engineer's work authorization. On June 15, 2026, the council extended the moratorium another 180 days, through the end of 2026. The court first rejected the village's arguments that the case was a disguised declaratory-judgment action, that it was moot because the ban was repealed, and that the village was already doing the review. On the merits, it held that Gibson v. Oberlin gives a property owner a vested right to the law in effect when it applies for a permit only if it has met all legislative requirements for that permit. Under Lordstown's code, site-plan approval must come before a zoning-permit application, and Bristolville had not applied for a permit. The court distinguished State ex rel. Fairmount Ctr. Co. v. Arnold on the same basis and declined to create a duty on policy grounds, calling that a legislative function. It denied the writ without reaching whether an administrative appeal was an adequate remedy.
live-317: New York's Appellate Division, First Department ruled on October 20, 2026 that New York City's "guaranty law," Administrative Code § 22-1005, does not violate the Contracts Clause of the U.S. Constitution. The law makes certain personal guaranties of commercial leases unenforceable against individual guarantors for defaults between March 7, 2020 and June 30, 2021. Justice Llinét M. Rosado wrote for the majority in 513 West 26th Realty LLC v. George Billis Galleries, Inc.; Justice David Friedman dissented. According to the opinion, landlord 513 West 26th Realty LLC alleges that tenant George Billis Galleries, Inc., which operates an art exhibition space, breached its lease, and that the tenant's individual guarantor breached his guaranty, after the tenant stopped paying rent during the pandemic. The City Council introduced the guaranty law on April 22, 2020 as part of a small-business relief package and passed it on May 13, 2020; the mayor signed it on May 26, 2020, and it was later extended twice. Supreme Court, New York County first dismissed the claims against the guarantor under the law. The First Department reversed in 2023 and sent the case back so the record could be developed on the law's constitutionality, in light of Melendez v. City of New York, a federal district court decision that found the law unconstitutional and was later vacated by the Second Circuit in Bochner v. City of New York for lack of standing. The City intervened. On remand, in an order entered on or about December 31, 2024, Supreme Court declared the law unconstitutional, reinstated the claims against the guarantor and denied the guarantor's and the City's motions to dismiss. The First Department reversed. Applying the three-part Contracts Clause test from Energy Reserves Group, Inc. v. Kansas Power & Light Co., the majority relied on the presumption that statutes are constitutional and on the deference owed to the City Council's judgment, which it called particularly appropriate given the declared state emergency when the law passed. It concluded the landlord had not carried its burden, noting that relief applied only to individual guarantors of businesses hit by the governor's executive orders, only for the 16-month period, and that the debt remained enforceable against the tenant. The majority said it made "no judgment as to the wisdom of the guaranty law." The court also held that its 2023 order barred reviving the landlord's claims for amounts due outside the guaranty law's period. It vacated the declaration of unconstitutionality and granted the guarantor's and the City's motions to dismiss.
live-318: The Grandview Heights Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Neighborhood Alliance filed a complaint on October 14, 2026 in the 15th Judicial Circuit, alleging that Palm Beach County violated Florida's Government in the Sunshine Law when it approved financing for a planned convention center hotel, WPTV reported. live-319: New York's Appellate Division, Second Department ruled on October 21, 2026 that sublessor VK Dental Group, Inc. was not entitled to summary judgment on its claims for unpaid sublease rent, reversing a Supreme Court, Kings County judgment of $1,004,426.20 against Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC and the other sublessees. live-320: The Michigan Court of Appeals on October 21, 2026 affirmed a Wayne Circuit Court judgment of $411,131.50 for Padilla Investments, LLC, entered on an arbitration award in its lease dispute with Trucks Rx, Inc., Jana Trucking Line, Inc. and their owners. According to the opinion, Padilla Investments owns a Detroit property previously used as a hardware store. In February 2022 the two companies signed a three-year lease to use it to sell new vehicle tires, and their owners personally guaranteed it. The tenants agreed to comply with all laws and ordinances at their own expense and accepted the property "as is." The city issued correction orders to the landlord in April and June 2022, the June order requiring the use to stop because no permit had been issued. The tenants stopped paying rent in July 2022. The Court of Appeals held the arbitrator did not exceed his authority or make an error of law evident on the face of the award. It rejected the appellants' impossibility and impracticability argument, noting the tenants were in the better position to know what their business required; rejected their mutual-mistake argument because the need for a sprinkler system did not go to the whole substance of the agreement; and held that, as in Lenawee County Board of Health v. Messerly, the as-is clause meant the tenants took the risk of the property's condition. The court addressed the arguments even though most had not been preserved.
live-321: A Cook County judge has ordered Chicago real estate investor Sean Conlon to pay $11,508,950 plus legal fees to Alecko Lending over a defaulted loan on the long-vacant former Rainforest Cafe building at 605 N. Clark St. in River North, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. Circuit Judge Jerry Esrig ruled for the lender on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Crain's Chicago Business, which reported the ruling the same day, put the amount at $10 million in its headline. The Sun-Times said attorneys for both sides did not immediately respond to requests for comment. According to the Sun-Times, Alecko made Conlon a short-term $8.3 million bridge loan in January 2024 that was due January 30, 2025, and later extended the deadline to May 2025. After Conlon missed that date, the lender gave him a chance to pay $99,204.83 by July 10, which he did not pay. Alecko's breach-of-contract complaint, filed in October 2025, said it was owed $9.2 million including interest and forbearance fees. Alecko, led by founder Alexander Pissios, also filed a foreclosure suit in November 2025 against the Conlon-led entity that owns the building, seeking foreclosure, a receiver and a deficiency judgment, The Real Deal reported at the time. That case is still pending, according to the Sun-Times. Conlon told The Real Deal then that the suit was premature, that he had been paying penalty interest since June and that he planned to repay the full debt from a refinancing. CBS Chicago, citing Crain's, reported that he described the dispute as being over a single late payment. The 22,000-square-foot building has been empty since the Rainforest Cafe closed in August 2020. The Sun-Times, citing property records, said Conlon bought the site in 2015 for more than $13 million; The Real Deal reported a $13.7 million purchase in 2013. A planned cannabis dispensary in the space fell through: the Sun-Times said the plans were dropped after lawsuits sought to block it, and The Real Deal reported that the would-be tenant backed out amid neighborhood opposition and after it emerged that the site was too close to other dispensaries to comply with state law.
live-322: California's Second Appellate District, Division One, on October 22, 2026 reversed in full a Los Angeles County Superior Court judgment of $12,245,108.42 against HPC Vineburn, LLC and Meruelo Maddux Properties-1919 Vineburn Street, LLC, the current and prior owners of 1919 Vineburn Avenue in Los Angeles. Justice Bendix wrote the unpublished opinion in Joseph F. Farivar Investment Group, Inc. v. HPC Vineburn, LLC, joined by Presiding Justice Rothschild and Justice Weingart. The plaintiffs are Joseph F. Farivar Investment Group, Inc., which owns the adjacent downgradient property at 4335 Valley Boulevard, and its tenant, Bordan Shoe Company, Inc. According to the opinion, before 1989 the Nardon Manufacturing Company, a metal fabricator, operated at the Vineburn property and discharged waste including 1,4-dioxane. The plaintiffs do not allege that the defendants themselves put the chemicals into the groundwater; they alleged Meruelo Maddux owned the site from about 2005 to 2013 and HPC Vineburn since 2013. In 2018 the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board directed HPC Vineburn to assess possible sources, and a May 7, 2020 report by its consultant, Hazard Management Consulting, concluded the Vineburn property had contributed to the 1,4-dioxane groundwater problem at the Farivar property. HPC Vineburn then proposed a cleanup and said it had money set aside for it. A 2023 board order called for further investigation. Relying heavily on that report, the plaintiffs won summary adjudication in September 2024. Their experts put the present value of a 20-year cleanup of the Farivar property at $11,779,000 and loss of use at $192,887. HPC Vineburn's expert estimated cleanup of the combined contamination at $5 million and said some of it originated on the Farivar property. After the plaintiffs dismissed their remaining claims, the court entered judgment on November 7, 2024 for $12,245,108.42, including prejudgment interest, and declared the defendants responsible for the contamination. Meruelo Maddux had not opposed the motion. The Court of Appeal held that a landowner owes a duty to act reasonably toward adjacent property, but that there were triable issues on whether the defendants breached it, and the statutes the plaintiffs cited did not create a presumption of negligence. Damages for continuing nuisance and continuing trespass are limited to injury suffered before the suit, and the plaintiffs sought prospective, 20-year damages. The court also held the trial court erred by partially adjudicating the declaratory relief claim. It reversed the judgment, which also reverses the prejudgment interest award, and said it expressed no opinion on the merits at trial.
live-323: Ohio's Eighth District Court of Appeals released a new decision on October 22, 2026 in Crocker Park, L.L.C. v. Westlake, 2026-Ohio-4138, after granting reconsideration and vacating its July 30, 2026 decision in the same appeal. Presiding Judge Eileen T. Gallagher wrote both opinions, with Judges Emanuella D. Groves and Mary J. Boyle concurring. The judgment is the same, affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded, but the new opinion narrows the ruling against Crocker Park on its right of first refusal. According to the opinion, Crocker Park is a mixed-use development on Crocker Road in Westlake with retail stores, restaurants, offices, apartments and green space, governed by a Declaration of Covenants, Conditions, Restrictions and Easements recorded in 2003 that names Crocker Park, L.L.C. as declarant. Under a 2014 development agreement, Crocker Park conveyed about two acres to the city at no cost, and the city built Market Square, which opened in 2015. The city took the land subject to the Declaration, and the agreement gave Crocker Park a right of first refusal to buy the property "at the same price offered by such third party." Crocker Park Management, L.L.C. ran Market Square under an operation and maintenance agreement until the city ended it in December 2023. Disputes followed over the city's share of common expenses, a $22,367.37 lien that CP Commercial Delaware, L.L.C. placed on Market Square, and the city's planned sale to E&C Sports Group, L.L.C. The city set deadlines for Crocker Park to exercise its right, and Crocker Park sued in October 2024. In November 2024 it offered $2.6 million, E&C's price, on conditions that the property be exempt from property tax and that the price be eligible for reimbursement from the "Crocker Park Phase 3 waterfall." The city rejected the offer. In January 2025 Crocker Park agreed to forbear, and E&C bought Market Square for $2.6 million. The trial court ruled for Crocker Park on the city's counterclaims and declared that Crocker Park had not waived its right of first refusal on any offers. The appeals court affirmed the rulings against the city's slander-of-title and abuse-of-process claims, finding no evidence of malice or an improper purpose and a legitimate basis for the lien. On the right of first refusal, it said whether Crocker Park acted within a reasonable time was a fact question, but held that its conditional offer was a counteroffer, so it waived the right as to E&C's offer. The July decision had stopped there and sustained the city's assignment of error in full. The reconsidered opinion adds that the agreement "expressly confers the right of first refusal to CP 'any time' following an offer from 'any unrelated third party,'" so Crocker Park did not waive it as to future offers.
live-324: Twitter signed a 10-year lease in 2020 with Colorado landlord Lot 2 SBO, LLC for a 64,557-square-foot building in Boulder that was still under construction, Courthouse News reported. BizWest has identified the building as being at 3401 Bluff St. in the S'Park development and Lot 2 SBO as a holding company affiliated with S'Park co-owner The John Buck Co. Under the lease, monthly base rent was $199,866.88 once the build-out was complete, and the landlord offered a tenant-improvement allowance of $90 per square foot to get Twitter to sign. Twitter spent $40 million over two years turning the shell into a flagship office but never used it, according to Courthouse News. After Elon Musk bought Twitter in October 2022 and renamed it X, the parties disputed whether the improvement allowance had to be applied as a credit against rent. The landlord said it was waiting on draw documents confirming that no contractors were owed before paying out the credit, and it evicted the tenant for nonpayment. X Corp. countersued, alleging the landlord breached the lease by failing to apply the credit; BizWest reported that X filed that suit (Case No. 2023CV30461) in June 2023 seeking about $5.8 million in allowance money. After a five-day bench trial in March 2025, Boulder County District Court Judge Nancy Salomone found in May 2025 that Lot 2 SBO had properly evicted X and ordered the company to pay $8.2 million in past-due rent and expenses. On October 22, 2026, the Court of Appeals reversed in a 22-page opinion by Judge Karl Schock, joined by Judges Katharine Lum and Craig Welling. The panel held that once the improvement project crossed the lease's threshold and X gave written notice, the credit applied automatically to the next rent payments, whether or not the landlord had received the draw documents. Schock wrote that the court's job was to enforce the bargain the parties made, not to decide which side got the better deal. The panel did not enter judgment for X. It sent the case back to the trial court to reconsider in light of the opinion. X's appellate counsel declined to comment, and counsel for Lot 2 SBO did not respond by press time, Courthouse News reported.
live-325: In December 2023, the Law Offices of Jason W. Estavillo, P.C. signed a 66-month lease for 7,755 square feet in Suite 1280 at 555 12th Street in downtown Oakland, owned by USPA City Center, LLC. Rent started at $30,333.33 a month and went up each March. According to the opinion, the tenant's security-deposit check bounced, and by June 2024 it owed $107,618 in unpaid rent. The landlord filed an unlawful detainer action that month. The parties settled: the tenant would pay an extra $15,000 a month on top of rent, and if it failed, the landlord could have judgment entered for possession, unpaid rent, fees and future rent through the end of the lease. The tenant missed the settlement payments, and the landlord asked for judgment in April 2025. At a July 2025 evidentiary hearing, a Cushman & Wakefield broker qualified as an expert. He testified that Class A vacancy in downtown Oakland was 35 to 36 percent and that about 200,000 square feet of tenant demand faced roughly 4,000,000 square feet of available space. The building's property manager, Harvest Properties, testified that occupancy had fallen to about 55 percent and that Matson Navigation, the largest tenant, was leaving a year before its lease ended. The evidence also showed the suite could not practically be split up because of code, exit and kitchen issues. The tenant called no witnesses. On August 28, 2025, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Chad A. Stegeman awarded $350,677.82 in back rent, holdover and other damages. Instead of the four years the landlord asked for, he awarded three years of future rent, reduced to present value: $1,219,015.63. He found the landlord could not mitigate while the tenant was still in the space, and he discounted the outer end of the expert's estimate. Post-judgment, the tenant got a stay and remained in the premises while paying rent. Writing for the First District, Justice Richman held that substantial evidence supported the award. The court found the expert's opinion grounded in market data, not speculation, so it passed the Sargon reliability standard. It also held that the stipulation was not an unlawful liquidated-damages penalty: it did not increase damages beyond what the lease and Civil Code section 1951.2 provide, and the tenant offered no evidence that the clause was unreasonable when signed. The court declined to consider a double-recovery argument first raised in the reply brief, which was based on rent the tenant paid during the stay, and left any offset claim for enforcement proceedings. The opinion was first filed as unpublished on September 21, 2026, and was certified for publication on October 19, 2026. It now binds California trial courts on these issues. For commercial landlords, the case is a guide to proving future rent after a tenant defaults: expert broker testimony, comparable time-on-market data for similar suites, building-level occupancy trends, and evidence of physical features that make the space hard to re-let. For tenants, it shows the cost of answering a detailed mitigation case with argument alone. It also shows that a settlement stipulating to future rent will be enforced when it matches what the lease and statute already allow.
live-326: Port Washington's ordinance was proposed in fall 2025 by opponents of the $15 billion AI data center campus being developed there by Vantage Data Centers, Oracle and OpenAI, as the project's $458 million in local tax incentives moved through approval, according to the Wisconsin Law Journal. The citizen group Great Lakes Neighbors United gathered the signatures needed to put the measure on the ballot, and voters approved it on April 7, 2026 with about 66 percent support, WUWM reported. It requires a referendum for future tax incremental districts with project costs or base value above $10 million and does not affect the TID already approved for the Vantage project. Before the vote, the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce, Associated General Contractors of Greater Milwaukee, Building Advantage, the Commercial Association of Realtors Wisconsin, the Commercial Real Estate Development Association of Wisconsin, the Wisconsin Realtors Association and Sid's Sealants LLC sued the city in Ozaukee County Circuit Court on January 29, 2026. They argued the ordinance would slow development, conflict with state laws on how TIF incentives are approved, and was too vague. City officials said they largely agreed with the groups but had to advance the ordinance under Wisconsin's direct legislation law, which dates to 1910. Great Lakes Neighbors United intervened to defend it, and in February Judge Gerol denied a preliminary injunction and let the vote proceed, calling it "protected speech." In an oral ruling on October 19 that lasted over an hour, Gerol found that the groups had not identified a specific development, financing plan or proposed TID that the referendum requirement would harm, so their claims rested on speculation. He also addressed the merits, concluding that a referendum supplements rather than conflicts with the state's TID procedure and that the ordinance, though awkwardly drafted, is understandable. He relied in part on the Wisconsin Supreme Court's 2003 decision in Mount Horeb Community Alert v. Village Board of Mount Horeb. In a statement to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, an MMAC spokesperson said the group was disappointed and confident that "further examination in higher courts is warranted." Great Lakes Neighbors United called the ruling "a win for every voter in Port Washington." On September 16, the same judge dismissed the group's separate suit challenging the Vantage campus's tax incentives.
live-327: Denver-based Vantage Data Centers is developing the roughly $15 billion Lighthouse campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin, with Oracle and OpenAI, according to WPR. The campus would include four data centers on roughly 670 acres. Its first phase would draw about 1.3 gigawatts of power, with potential growth to 3.5 gigawatts. In July 2026, an environmental law nonprofit sued the DNR in Ozaukee County Circuit Court on behalf of the Sierra Club, challenging the agency's decision to issue permits for the project without an environmental impact statement. WPR reported that the groups had obtained emails showing the agency first told Vantage officials that an impact statement would be required, and that company officials were "reviewing (and panicking) internally" about it. The settlement, reached October 16 and signed by the DNR, the Sierra Club and Vantage, ends the case without an impact statement for Lighthouse. The parties agreed that the permits remain valid and that no further environmental review of those approvals is required. The Sierra Club will withdraw its petition for a contested case hearing, and the DNR will provide records the groups had requested. By January 31, 2028, the DNR must analyze the direct, indirect and cumulative effects of planned AI data center build-out and related infrastructure on agriculture, air and water quality, climate, energy, the economy, cultural resources and other areas. The agency will take public comment, hold one or more public hearings and summarize effects on energy bills. Vantage will pay for the analysis, the DNR will keep sole control of it, and the agency keeps full authority to decide whether future projects comply with state law. The deal does not halt permitting while the review runs. A Vantage spokesperson said the company "supports a thoughtful, fact-based discussion about responsible data center development." Counsel for the Sierra Club said the statewide study would provide "a holistic, comprehensive look" at environmental impacts. WPR reported that data centers have become an issue in the governor's race.
live-328: Exit 4A is a new I-93 interchange serving Derry and Londonderry that, according to a New Hampshire Attorney General's office release republished by InDepthNH, the New Hampshire Department of Transportation, the two towns and the Federal Highway Administration have pursued for about 40 years. NHDOT acquired land for the project by eminent domain from 101 Franklin Derry, LLC and S&L Elm Street Holdings, LLC, two companies the release says are run by a local developer. The companies challenged the takings in State v. 101 Franklin Derry, LLC, et al., arguing that the project mainly benefits Woodmont Commons, a private development in Londonderry, to the detriment of the companies and the Town of Derry. The state argued that the interchange addresses long-standing traffic problems and that any benefit to a private development is incidental. After a four-day trial, jurors were asked whether NHDOT had shown, more likely than not, that the acquisition serves a qualifying public use, that it is reasonably necessary and reasonable in scope, and that the project will produce a net public benefit when weighed against business displacement, lost tax revenue and harm to the community. After about an hour of deliberation, the jury unanimously answered yes to all three, and the judge said an order consistent with the verdict will issue. The release does not name the court or judge, give a compensation figure, or say whether the companies will appeal.
live-329: In September 2023, Sound Development Group LLC proposed a commercial and residential project in Oak Harbor on land next to Hal Ramaley Memorial Park: a one-story brewpub with single-story residential units. The city rejected that plan and encouraged a proposal with more urban density for downtown. The developer came back with a four-story Home2 Suites by Hilton with 107 rooms and meeting space. Its parking lot would extend onto part of the park. At the time, the city code required voters to approve any sale of developed park property. According to the opinion, city planning staff gave the developer several options: hold an election, drop the fourth floor, cut the pool and other amenities to free up parking, or amend the code. The developer pursued the amendment. At an August 13, 2024 public hearing, the city council passed Ordinance 1999 by a six-to-one vote. It allows park property to be sold or traded without a vote if the council approves a development agreement and finds that the exchange meets set land-area and market-value tests, or that the private party's park improvements are worth at least 150 percent of the land conveyed. The city's planner told the council the change was prompted by the hotel proposal. Whidbey Environmental Action Network sued on August 30, 2024. It argued the city violated SEPA by passing the ordinance without first reviewing its environmental impacts. The trial court granted summary judgment to the city on May 1, 2025, ruling that the ordinance was not an action covered by SEPA and was categorically exempt in any event, and dismissed the suit with prejudice. Division One reversed in an unpublished opinion. Writing for the panel, Acting Chief Judge Bowman held that Ordinance 1999 is a nonproject action under WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(i). Its conditions tie the transfer of park land to a specific purpose, development, and so they control the use or modification of the environment, much as a zoning ordinance does. The court rejected the city's position that review could wait until a sale or development was actually proposed. It noted that a concrete proposal already existed, with site plans, floor plans, landscaping plans and renderings showing the parking lot, and that accommodating the project was the city's motivation for the ordinance. The court also held that the procedural-action exemption in WAC 197-11-800(19) does not apply, because the ordinance contains substantive standards. The case goes back to the trial court for further proceedings.
live-330: Valcourt Building Services of Georgia, L.C. had a contract with the owner of a commercial building to provide exterior maintenance, including pressure washing the rooftop cooling-tower fans. BSC Realty Services, LLC managed the building. Valcourt subcontracted the fan cleaning to a maintenance company owned by the worker who was later hurt. In the contract, Valcourt agreed to defend and indemnify both the owner and BSC against injury claims arising from its work or its subcontractors' work. The only exception was liability arising from the sole negligence of the owner or manager. On October 7, 2021, the worker checked in with the building's engineers, who worked for a BSC affiliate. They confirmed that power to the first fan was off, and he cleaned it. After they confirmed power was off to a second fan, he climbed a ladder, held a blade with one hand and began washing. He heard a click, the fan began to turn, and he fell and was seriously injured. The engineers could shut fans down either through the building automation system or at a locked rooftop electrical room, and there were no written procedures for doing so at the time. Only the electrical room allowed a federal lockout/tagout procedure. The worker's expert testified that cutting power through the automation system alone did not properly de-energize the fan. The worker sued several defendants, including BSC. BSC filed a third-party claim against Valcourt for breach of contract and indemnification. The trial court granted summary judgment to Valcourt, accepting its argument that any liability arose from the sole negligence of the owner or manager, through the engineers' failure to keep power to the fan cut off. Valcourt also argued that BSC's appeal was untimely. The appeals court disagreed: no civil case disposition form had been filed, so no final judgment was entered under OCGA 9-11-58(b), the order remained interlocutory, and the trial court could vacate and re-enter it. On the merits, Presiding Judge McFadden's opinion for the Fourth Division found no direct evidence of whether the fan had power when the worker fell. The automation logs had not been kept. The circumstantial evidence pointed both ways. The click suggested power was restored, but other evidence showed the fan makes little or no noise when re-energized, water pressure from a power washer alone can turn the blades, and a co-worker saw the blades slowing after the fall. A jury could reasonably find that water, not electricity, moved the fan. Because of that dispute, Valcourt could not show as a matter of law that the sole-negligence exception applied, so the summary judgment was reversed. The court did not reach BSC's separate argument about Valcourt's training of the worker.
live-333: Industrial Park Center LLC, which does business as Mainspring Capital Group, sued Great Northern Insurance Co. after the insurer refused to pay for structural damage to Mainspring's commercial building in Arizona, Business Insurance reported. The tenant, Star Fisheries, had used water and salt in its operations for decades, gradually damaging the building's stairs, walls and foundation. Great Northern, a Chubb unit, denied the roughly $2.7 million claim, arguing the damage was too foreseeable to be insurable. The suit was filed in Maricopa County Superior Court and removed by Great Northern to federal court in July 2022, according to the federal docket. In July 2024, U.S. District Judge Michael T. Liburdi granted summary judgment to Great Northern, applying the Ninth Circuit's reasonable-foreseeability test from Ingenco Holdings v. Ace American Insurance Co. and concluding the loss was "reasonably foreseeable and almost certain to occur," as the Ninth Circuit later summarized; the court also awarded Great Northern attorney's fees. Mainspring appealed, and in December 2025 the Ninth Circuit certified the question of what fortuity means under Arizona law to the Arizona Supreme Court. In a Sept. 1, 2026 opinion by Justice Clint Bolick, the Arizona Supreme Court rejected the Ingenco test and held that a loss is non-fortuitous only when the insured knew, at the time coverage attached, that the loss-causing event had already occurred, was in progress, or was certain to occur. The court called this "a subjective standard." Business Insurance noted that the ruling did not decide who wins the case. On Oct. 16, 2026, a Ninth Circuit panel of Judges Graber, Tallman and Bade, in an unpublished memorandum, vacated the summary judgment for Great Northern on the breach of contract and bad-faith claims, the denial of Mainspring's own summary judgment motion and the fee award, and remanded. The panel said the district court should decide in the first instance whether the wear-and-tear and settling exclusions, which Great Northern cited in denying the claim, bar coverage.
live-334: Cook County Judge Edward Robles has entered a foreclosure judgment against AmTrust RE over Illinois Center, the two-tower office complex at 111 East Wacker Drive and 233 North Michigan Avenue in Chicago's East Loop, and set a sheriff's auction for Nov. 12, 2026, The Real Deal reported on October 19, citing Crain's Chicago Business. The 2.1 million-square-foot complex secures $260 million in commercial mortgage-backed securities debt. Special servicer LNR Partners, acting for the bondholders, is positioned to bid at the auction and take title. According to Crain's, the CMBS debt balance had grown to $285.7 million as of June 2026, while a March appraisal valued the complex at $66.5 million. AmTrust bought the property for $376 million in 2015. The Real Deal reported that AmTrust did not oppose the lender's motion for summary judgment this summer, after its workout talks with LNR failed. Leasing at the towers fell after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services left 170,000 square feet at 233 North Michigan in 2023. By mid-2026 that tower was 17% leased and 111 East Wacker was 52% leased, according to the report. AmTrust had drawn up plans in 2023 to renovate the conference center and add a rooftop deck. The Real Deal described the auction as AmTrust's third major office loss in downtown Chicago in two years: it lost 30 North LaSalle Street to foreclosure in 2023 and handed 33 West Monroe Street to its lender earlier in 2026.
live-335: Four Goochland County property owners filed suit in Goochland Circuit Court on December 4, 2025, against the county, its Board of Supervisors and its Planning Commission, seeking to void the Technology Overlay District (TOD) that supervisors approved in November 2025, Virginia Lawyers Weekly reported; one supervisor cast the lone vote against it. According to Richmond BizSense, the overlay spans roughly 4,400 acres along Route 288, about 3,500 of them in the West Creek Business Park, and allows uses such as pharmaceutical plants, biomedical research and data centers by right; in the 900-acre western portion, data centers need a conditional use permit. The suit alleges that before the vote, county officials did not properly identify the properties that would be affected and adopted a measure that differed from what appeared in published notices, Virginia Lawyers Weekly reported. It asks that the ordinance be vacated and that the county pay the plaintiffs' legal fees. In February 2026, supervisors approved $250,000 for the county's defense by outside counsel. In May, Judge Timothy Sanner ordered the county to pare down the roughly 8,500 pages of documents it had filed in response to the suit. At the three-hour hearing on October 20, 2026, on the county's demurrer, the plaintiffs dropped four more claims; the county said that left three of the nine original claims. Counsel for the county disputed that the residents had shown particularized harm from the overlay, while the plaintiffs' opposition brief said they are nearby property owners facing lower property values, noise, pollution and traffic, BizSense reported. Judge Sanner took the motion under advisement without setting a timeline. Before the hearing, the county said it was confident the suit would be dismissed, the Daily Signal reported, and County Administrator Jeremy Raley told WTVR that the overlay added buffers, setbacks and noise limits to protect residents.
live-336: Michelmann Steel Construction Company, an Illinois corporation, owns a lot on 24th Street in Quincy, Illinois, that it has leased for billboard advertising since a 1956 agreement with Quincy Outdoor Advertising Co. Leases from 1968 on used a preprinted form with a one-year original term and automatic year-to-year renewals for up to five years unless a party gave 30 days' written notice. The lease at issue, signed May 1, 1987 with Outdoor Graphics, Inc., leased "the existing structures" on the lot for $400 a year with 10% annual increases, and said structures the tenant placed there would remain its property, removable up to a reasonable time after the lease ended. Link Media Midwest, LLC, which admitted it was Outdoor Graphics' assignee, had the billboard structures dismantled and removed on April 19, 2019. Michelmann sued in Adams County circuit court for conversion, tortious interference with prospective business relationships and breach of contract for unpaid rent. After a bench trial on documentary evidence only, Judge Scott Douglas Larson ruled on December 18, 2024 that Michelmann had not proved it owned the billboards, but awarded it $19,907.97 in past-due rent. Link Media appealed the rent award and Michelmann cross-appealed. Justice Peter C. Cavanagh delivered the judgment, with Justices DeArmond and Grischow concurring. Reviewing the record de novo, the court held that the structures, fixtures that had stood on Michelmann's land for over half a century, were presumed to be Michelmann's, that Link Media did not rebut the presumption, and that removing them was a conversion. Michelmann's damages evidence went to the $68,931.17 cost of building replacement billboards and a claimed 10% loss in value from a required setback. It cited no authority for that measure, and with no proof of fair market value it was entitled only to nominal damages. Its tortious-interference claim was forfeited for lack of a reasoned argument. On rent, the court held that Michelmann had elected to treat Link Media as a holdover tenant, creating a new tenancy on the 1987 lease's terms, including its automatic renewals, and that no written termination notice was proven. Link Media argued its liability ended when it removed the structures in April 2019; the court found it owed rent through April 2024 and held its request for equitable relief forfeited for lack of supporting authority. The case was remanded with directions to enter judgment for Michelmann on conversion and award nominal damages.
live-337: According to Alexandria's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, its subsidiary ARE-East River Science Park, LLC holds an option, granted in 2006, to add a parcel adjacent to and north of the Alexandria Center for Life Science in New York City to its existing ground lease, which would allow an additional life-science building. Its investment in pre-construction costs for the parcel was $185.9 million as of September 30, 2026. On August 6, 2024, the subsidiary sued New York City Health + Hospitals Corporation and the New York City Economic Development Corporation in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York over the ground lease and option. It amended its complaint on January 24, 2025 to assert fraudulent inducement, breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and a claim for a declaration that the option remains valid. On March 27, 2026 the court dismissed the fraud and implied-covenant claims; Alexandria says it intends to appeal, and the declaratory claim remains pending. On April 10, 2026 the agencies answered and counterclaimed, seeking among other things a declaration that the option expired, entitlement to a $5.0 million security deposit, and damages of at least $3.8 million. Separately, on April 20, 2026 the EDC delivered a notice alleging that the subsidiary had defaulted on obligations to provide sublease, tax and financial information for the existing towers on the campus, with daily charges of $1,000, rising to $2,000, if not cured within 30 days. Alexandria disputes the allegations. On May 12, 2026 the subsidiary sued in the Commercial Division of New York State Supreme Court for a Yellowstone injunction, a preliminary injunction and a temporary restraining order to toll the cure period and bar a notice of termination. The subsidiary appealed, and on September 10, 2026 the Appellate Division, First Department denied interim relief pending the appeal, which remains pending. On July 2, 2026 the subsidiary amended its state complaint to add claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant, tortious interference and unfair competition, alleging the agencies misused confidential subtenant information and diverted a subtenant to a competing City-sponsored project. The agencies moved to dismiss on August 6, 2026, and oral argument is scheduled for January 15, 2027, according to the filing.
live-338: Thor Equities, LLC, joined by Urbana Owner LLC, Urbana Owner I LLC, Urbana Owner II LLC and Highland55 Investments LLC, filed a civil rights complaint under 42 U.S.C. 1983 on June 19, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio against the City of Urbana, the Urbana City Council and the city's Building and Zoning Appeals Board, according to the federal docket. The case, No. 3:26-cv-00196, is assigned to U.S. District Judge Michael J. Newman. According to DatacenterDynamics, Thor says it worked with city officials for more than a year, assembled about 230 acres and submitted a complete site plan in February 2026 for a $1 billion, 460,000-square-foot data center that would use closed-loop cooling, and that it spent $19.6 million of its own funds on preliminary work. The city passed a 12-month "emergency moratorium" in March and in June rezoned Thor's land as unsuitable for data centers. live-341: Renaissance Midtown West LLC sued its former tenant, Lividini & Company, LLC, and the tenant's principal in New York County Supreme Court in November 2024, seeking rent for the balance of the lease term, enforcement of a guaranty and an order piercing the corporate veil. According to the decision, the tenant's counsel gave notice in August 2020 that the tenant was vacating, the tenant returned the keys without objection, and the landlord later signed a lease with a new tenant; the landlord acknowledged there was no further communication between the parties until it sued. Justice Lyle E. Frank granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the amended complaint in an order entered July 24, 2025. A First Department panel of Justices Webber, Kapnick, Shulman, Pitt-Burke and Hagler unanimously affirmed on October 27, 2026. Paragraph 17(1) of the lease is a conditional limitation that lets the landlord end the lease for defaults other than nonpayment, including if the premises become "vacant or deserted," by serving a five-day notice to cure and then a three-day notice of cancellation. Citing Holy Properties v. Cole Products, the court held that the tenant's vacatur triggered its right to that notice before reentry and reletting. It rejected the landlord's argument that it meant only to collect rent, not to terminate, because taking back the keys and reletting the space were at odds with a continuing landlord-tenant relationship. The court also held that lease paragraph 17(2) and rider paragraph 66, which the landlord invoked for unpaid amounts, apply only while the tenant remains in possession. It distinguished 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v. Hyatt Leader Ltd., where the landlord had told the tenant that accepting the surrender was without prejudice to a claim for unpaid rent; no such allegation was made here. The guaranty claim failed under General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(2) because the standard-form guaranty attached to the lease was blank and unexecuted, and the landlord alleged no facts warranting leave to replead. On veil piercing, the court, citing Cortlandt Street Recovery Corp. v. Bonderman, said the doctrine is not a separate cause of action, and a bare allegation that the principal did not keep a bank account separate from the tenant's did not show domination and control used to commit a wrong against the landlord.
live-342: GRE Downtowner LLC operates Addison on Fourth, a low-income apartment complex near downtown Seattle. According to the opinion, the company bought the property in 2012 for $12.5 million and invested another $26.5 million to qualify it for the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, with bond financing from the Washington State Housing and Finance Commission. The complex has 254 studio and one-bedroom apartments for residents earning 60 percent of the area median income, along with 46 artist studios and four commercial spaces, and HUD sets its maximum rents. The company alleges that ordinances and a resolution adopted by the Seattle City Council starting in 2018 made the property impossible to run sustainably: the Fair Chance Housing Ordinance, the 2019 Roommate Ordinance, the 2020 Winter Eviction Ban, a COVID-19 eviction moratorium in effect from March 2020 to February 2022, a 2021 ordinance extending the notice period for rent increases from 60 to 180 days, and the 2021 Economic Displacement Relocation Assistance ordinance. As the court summarized the complaint, the share of maximum rental income collected fell from about 90 to 94 percent in 2015 through 2018 to 44.1 percent in 2023, and the property lost $683,353 in 2020, $980,043 in 2021, $1.8 million in 2022 and $2.7 million in 2023. GRE Downtowner alleges the complex is now functionally valueless on an income-approach appraisal. GRE Downtowner sued in King County Superior Court on October 22, 2024, alleging partial and per se regulatory takings under article I, section 16 of the Washington Constitution. The trial court granted the City's motion to dismiss under CR 12(b)(6) in February 2025, and a Washington Supreme Court commissioner later denied the City's motion to transfer the appeal to that court. Division One reversed. Applying Washington's CR 12(b)(6) standard, which is more lenient than the federal one, the court held the complaint pleaded enough on each of the three Penn Central factors to support a partial takings claim. It rejected the City's arguments that the losses flowed from the tax-credit restrictions and that an owner in a highly regulated field cannot have reasonable investment-backed expectations. Rejecting the City's call for a three-year limit, it adopted the six-year period in RCW 4.16.040(3) for partial regulatory takings claims, so that claim was timely. It also held that the Roommate Ordinance, by giving occupancy rights to uninvited third parties who are not tenants, supports a per se takings claim under Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid, over the City's argument that a landlord-tenant regulation cannot effect a per se taking.
live-344: Boston-based developer Copper Mill has sued POB Capital of Chicago and Pactolus Private Wealth Management of Virginia, alleging they committed fraud during negotiations to partner on a 754-unit project at 75 Morrissey Boulevard in Dorchester, Bisnow reported on October 19, 2026. live-345: On October 19, 2026, 111 West 57th Investment LLC, on its own behalf and derivatively for 111 West 57th Partners LLC and 111 West 57th Mezz 1 LLC, filed a summons with notice in New York Supreme Court, New York County, against ACREFI Mortgage LLC and Apollo Commercial Real Estate Finance, Inc. live-346: Fannie Mae filed suit on October 22, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia against SYS Augusta LLC, which Mortgage Professional America describes as a company set up solely to own Falcon Crest Apartments at 1700 Valley Park Court in Augusta. live-347: More than three decades ago, Hidden Valley Corporation bought two neighboring properties in Miami. It leased one to BellSouth Mobility and later gave BellSouth and its successors an easement to use part of the other for telecommunications. The easement agreement's "Remedies for Breach" section entitles the prevailing party in a suit to enforce it to reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Both properties later changed hands; when this dispute arose, RJ's International Trading, LLC (RJI) owned the burdened parcel, and Crown Castle South, LLC subleased the neighboring property from BellSouth and held the easement rights. In 2020, Crown Castle excavated parts of RJI's land beyond the easement and installed underground fiber-optic cable. RJI sued in federal court. The district court granted RJI partial summary judgment on trespass and breach of the easement, and after a six-day trial a jury awarded $1 for the breach and $40,000 for trespass; Crown Castle did not appeal. The district court then denied RJI's motion for attorney's fees under the easement, agreeing with Crown Castle that the provision did not touch and concern the land. On RJI's appeal, the Eleventh Circuit rejected RJI's argument that it was a party to the agreement and certified the covenant question to the Florida Supreme Court. Justice Jamie Grosshans wrote for the court. A covenant runs with the land only if the original parties intended to bind successors, successors had notice, and the covenant touches and concerns the land; the court decided the case on the third element. Tracing the doctrine from Spencer's Case (1583) through Florida decisions, it held that courts should ask whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is used, occupied or enjoyed. The fee provision does not restrict how RJI's land can be used or who can use it, and it applies only after a dispute is resolved, serving "solely to allocate litigation costs between the parties," the court wrote. It distinguished Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp., which held that a deed's arbitration clause ran with the land, and noted that most courts outside Florida to address fee provisions agree. Chief Justice Couriel and Justices Labarga, Muñiz and Francis concurred. Justices Barrios and Tanenbaum concurred in result only: Justice Barrios would require a direct effect on the physical use of the property and called Hayslip an outlier, and Justice Tanenbaum wrote that a prevailing-party fee provision can never be a real covenant.
live-348: Cobleskill Enterprise, LLP owned a hotel and restaurant complex in the Town of Cobleskill, Schoharie County, with a bowling alley, banquet room, kitchen and pool. After a fire there in December 2018, it sought coverage under its commercial property policy. Seneca Insurance Company Inc. denied the claim on several grounds, including misrepresentations in the application and the claim and breach of the policy's protective safeguards endorsement, or PSE, and sued for fraud and declarations that the policy was void and that it owed no coverage. Cobleskill Enterprise counterclaimed and brought a third-party action against Links Insurance Services, LLC, the retail broker that placed the policy. Seneca later added fraud and negligent-misrepresentation claims against Links, alleging Links filed the claim knowing a third party had cancelled the policy before the fire. In an order entered March 4, 2025, Supreme Court (Justice James Ferreira) denied Links' motion to dismiss and Seneca's cross-motion for summary judgment on the PSE, finding Seneca's own submissions raised fact issues. Seneca's evidence included an October 2018 Village of Cobleskill citation for inadequate carbon monoxide detectors and testimony from a technician with the fire-equipment firm hired about a month later. He testified that there were no smoke detectors in the pool area, bowling alley, basement or dining room ceiling, only heat detectors in the banquet room and kitchen, and a few nonfunctional "dummy detectors." He also said the reporting panel for the restaurant, kitchen, banquet room and bowling alley could not communicate with the main panel, so a fire in those areas would not set off the building's alarms. Writing for the panel, Justice Stan L. Pritzker held that Seneca established breach and materiality as a matter of law. Giving "operational" its ordinary meaning, detectors that might light up but would not sound an alarm were in effect nonoperational, and some areas had none at all; the bowling alley, a public space, was clearly a common area. The lack of operational detectors in a public space was material to the risk of fire loss, and the property suffered fire and smoke losses, including in areas without them. Cobleskill Enterprise offered no substantive opposition. The court also dismissed Seneca's claims against Links. The fraud claim rested on concealment and required a fiduciary duty that an arm's-length broker relationship did not supply, and Seneca's reliance was not reasonable because, as a sophisticated insurer, it could have checked whether the policy was in force. The owner's third-party claims against Links were dismissed because they were limited to denials based on cancellation or application misrepresentations, not the PSE breach on which coverage was denied.
live-349: In October 2024, the City of South Bend, acting at the direction of its mayor, filed a complaint to condemn real property owned by Argos 316, LLC in a redevelopment project area established by the South Bend Redevelopment Commission. Portage Township of St. Joseph County had already contracted to buy the property and completed the purchase shortly after the City filed. The Township and 350 Columbia Street, LLC, which held easements on the property, intervened and objected that the action was not authorized by the South Bend Common Council, as Indiana Code section 36-7-14-20(a) contemplates. The Marshall Circuit Court, Judge Janette E. Surrisi presiding, overruled the objection, concluding that Council authorization is one way, not the only way, for the City to condemn property in a redevelopment project area. The Court of Appeals reversed in an opinion by Judge Nancy H. Vaidik, joined by Judge May. The City argued that the statute only sets a procedure for when the legislative body chooses to act and leaves other officials' broad condemnation power under Indiana Code section 36-1-4-5(a) intact; the objectors argued it confines the power to the legislative body. Finding both readings reasonable on the text alone, the court looked to the surrounding chapter, which sets out how a redevelopment commission is created, how a project area is designated with plan commission and legislative body approval, and how the commission must first try to negotiate purchases. Read as a whole, the redevelopment scheme "makes clear that the power lies with the unit's legislative body," the court wrote. Because the Common Council never authorized the action, the court held the trial court erred in overruling the objection, and it did not reach the objectors' other arguments. Chief Judge Tavitas concurred in the result, noting that neither party had argued the statute was ambiguous.
live-350: In December 2004, The Weitz Company, LLC, general contractor on a multi-building retirement community in Shelby County, Tennessee, and Commercial Painting Company, Inc. entered into a drywall subcontract for $3,222,400, later raised by change orders to $3,315,189. Weitz paid 12 of Commercial Painting's 17 pay applications and refused the other five, saying they were untimely and contained improper change order requests. Commercial Painting sued Weitz and its sureties, Federal Insurance Company and St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company, in Shelby County Chancery Court in August 2006, and Weitz counterclaimed for delay and defective work. Commercial Painting later added fraud and misrepresentation claims, alleging Weitz concealed a six-month extension it had negotiated with the project owner, which carried a bonus of $8,597 a day for up to 45 days of early completion, and then compressed the schedule, supplemented the drywall work and charged Commercial Painting for it. In October 2018, a jury found for Commercial Painting on breach of contract, unjust enrichment, intentional misrepresentation and the payment bond, and the award totaled $8,359,863.83: $1,272,952.46 in compensatory damages, $2,083,362.16 in prejudgment interest, $1,103,549 in attorney's fees and $3.9 million in punitive damages. The trial court upheld the punitive award, finding that Weitz knew before signing that the project was about eight months behind, planned to compress the schedule and supplement the drywall work without telling Commercial Painting, and misrepresented the extension it later obtained. In 2022 the Court of Appeals reversed the punitive award under the economic loss doctrine. The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed that ruling in 2023 and, after a further appeal, directed the Court of Appeals in June 2025 to decide whether Commercial Painting had contractually waived punitive damages on its misrepresentation claim. Judge Jeffrey Usman, joined by Judges J. Steven Stafford and Carma Dennis McGee, held that it had not. Section 11.6 of the subcontract bars anticipatory profit and indirect, special or consequential damages and waives "any other measure of damages" beyond those the subcontract provides, but it does not specifically waive damages for fraud or misrepresentation and appears to address contract remedies rather than tort. Under either the traditional view, reflected in Tennessee cases holding that "fraud vitiates all that it touches," or an approach that enforces only clear and specific waivers, the court concluded the clause does not bar the punitive award. It treated the jury's misrepresentation finding as the law of the case and held Weitz's ratification argument waived.
live-351: PMC Property Group, Inc. filed a new federal lawsuit against Apogee Enterprises, Inc. on Oct. 27, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, USGlass magazine reported. Three affiliated property entities joined as plaintiffs, according to the CourtListener docket (No. 0:26-cv-04642). The complaint alleges that Apogee controlled its subsidiaries, Wausau Group and Viracon, and directed their responses to complaints about spontaneous glass breakage at Franklin Tower, Riverwalk Tower I and Riverwalk Tower II in Philadelphia. It follows an August ruling by a Pennsylvania federal judge that dismissed several claims in PMC's earlier suit, including the claims against Apogee for lack of personal jurisdiction. PMC alleges that Wausau supplied defective window systems and that Viracon made at least some of the insulating glass units used in them. It claims nickel sulfide inclusions in the glass caused windows to break spontaneously at all three properties, and that the inclusions could not have been found at delivery or installation because they cannot be seen with the naked eye. PMC says breakage has increased since 2024, leading to inspections, violations, penalties and costs for inspecting, cleaning and replacing glass. The Minnesota complaint has three counts: unjust enrichment and two requests for declarations that Wausau and Viracon are alter egos of Apogee. PMC asks the court to pierce the corporate veil so that judgments against the subsidiaries can be enforced against Apogee. As evidence of control, it cites a November 2019 email exchange in which Wausau employees indicated that Apogee dictated contract language on glass treatment, an October 2020 exchange in which a Wausau employee allegedly sought Apogee's approval for a warranty credit involving Viracon, and a January 2021 request by an Apogee procurement director to speed deliveries because the orders mattered to fourth-quarter results. PMC also says its warranty requests were forwarded to Apogee personnel. PMC seeks actual, incidental and consequential damages, interest, attorneys' fees and the alter-ego declarations. The complaint does not state a total damages figure, but PMC says it paid Wausau about $50 million for the window systems at the three properties. USGlass did not report a response from Apogee.
live-352: Accord, LLC acquired a parcel in the Hamlet of Accord, Town of Rochester, Ulster County, that is the site of a historic granary and seed mill complex, and asked the Town Board to rezone it into an Economic Enterprise Overlay (EEO) district and approve its conceptual development plan. After a SEQRA review ended in a negative declaration, the Town Board adopted Local Law No. 10 of 2023, granting the rezoning and approving a plan to convert the buildings into a restaurant, a bike shop, an artist gallery, a coworking space, worker housing and an inn. It agreed the project needed 63 parking spaces: 57 on site, 25 of them for the restaurant, and six off site. During site plan review, Accord's architect told the Planning Board in May 2024 that the artist gallery would be dropped, the coworking space reduced by 421 square feet and the six off-site spaces eliminated. On July 8, 2024, the Planning Board granted conditional site plan approval, finding the modified project in substantial conformance with the conceptual plan and adopting the Town Board's on-site parking finding. In August 2024, two individuals with property near the site filed an Article 78 petition, arguing among other things that the restaurant needed 78 spaces under the code's one-space-per-50-square-feet standard applied to its listed 3,914.65 square feet. Accord's engineer responded that he had used an alternative one-space-per-three-seats calculation, presented to the Town Board, because the code does not say whether gross or net floor area applies. Supreme Court, Ulster County (Justice David Gandin) dismissed the petition in a judgment entered April 11, 2025. Writing for a unanimous panel, Justice Christine M. Clark held the approval was not arbitrary or capricious. The EEO rules allow approval of a site plan in "substantial conformance" with the conceptual plan, and the changes here reduced the project's scope without adding a new use or changing on-site parking. The petitioners never asked the Planning Board to seek a code interpretation from the zoning board or code enforcement officer, and in any event the Planning Board did not interpret the code: the Town Board had accepted Accord's parking calculation in Local Law 10, and in EEO districts the code's parking standards are guidelines rather than strict requirements. The court also upheld dropping the six off-site spaces, which tracked the removal of the gallery and the smaller coworking space, and rejected an argument about an "unconditioned event space" because the Planning Board expressly declined to approve events as a use.
live-353: The Kentucky Court of Appeals on October 30, 2026 affirmed summary judgment against Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP in its reverse condemnation suit against Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Louisville and Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, holding the claim was not ripe. In an opinion by Judge Lisa Payne Jones, joined by Judges Combs and Easton, the court found that Lampton never sought the variance the Sewer District's Floodplain Board may grant, so there was no final decision on how the property could be used. In the early 1990s, the owners of a roughly four-acre Ohio River tract received the Sewer District's approval for a two-phase condominium plan. Phase One was built on about two acres; on the remaining two acres, the Tract, only an electrical equipment building and utility lines were installed. In 1997, in response to catastrophic flooding, Metro Government enacted floodplain ordinances that bar most new construction in the conveyance zone, which includes the Tract. The ordinances allow construction already begun to continue and let landowners seek a variance from the Floodplain Board, and the record shows the Board has granted variances to other landowners. Lampton bought the Tract for $800,000 in 1998, after the ordinances took effect. Around 2019 it marketed the Tract as commercially developable, and at a later meeting the Sewer District's counsel told Lampton the ordinances prevented development. Lampton neither sought a variance nor tried to start Phase Two and instead sued in Jefferson Circuit Court in May 2020, alleging it had lost all economically beneficial use. In July 2025, Judge Jessica E. Green granted summary judgment to the defendants, finding Lampton had not exhausted administrative remedies and had not filed on time. The Court of Appeals affirmed on a different ground, ripeness. Relying on U.S. Supreme Court decisions including Palazzolo v. Rhode Island, MacDonald, Sommer & Frates v. Yolo County, Suitum v. Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and Pakdel v. City and County of San Francisco, and on the Kentucky Supreme Court's 2002 decision in Spanish Cove Sanitation, Inc. v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, it held there was no final decision on the Tract's permitted uses. It rejected Lampton's futility argument: counsel's opinion did not bind the Board, the record showed variances granted to others, and the Sewer District's designated representative testified that no similar variance had been requested. The court noted the trial court's statement that Lampton may bring a future takings claim once it is ripe.
live-354: The District of Columbia's Office of the Attorney General announced on September 14, 2026 that JBG Associates, L.L.C. (JBG Smith) and Mid-America Apartments, L.P. (MAA) had agreed to separate consent judgments resolving the District's antitrust claims against them. JBG Smith will pay $8.1 million and MAA $1.2 million, a combined $9.3 million that the OAG said covers civil penalties, money for affected residents and legal fees. The case, District of Columbia v. RealPage, Inc., No. 2023-CAB-006762, is before Judge Shana Frost Matini in D.C. Superior Court. The District alleges that RealPage's revenue-management software uses non-public pricing data from owners and managers to recommend rents, and that JBG Smith, MAA and 12 other defendant landlords shared sensitive data and delegated rent-setting to RealPage. According to the OAG, JBG Smith used the software for multiple District properties and MAA for one; the OAG said JBG Smith owns more than 4,500 units in the District and MAA owns 269. Under the consent orders, the companies may not use revenue-management software that relies on other companies' non-public data, promote such software to other owners, or share non-public information with other landlords; the restrictions run for 10 years for JBG and eight years for MAA. If the District believes either company is not complying, it may appoint an independent monitor at the company's expense. JBG's order states that it is not an admission of liability, and MAA's order states that MAA denies liability. The OAG had earlier announced settlements in the same case with W.C. Smith and, in June 2026, with Avenue5 Residential and Bell Partners for $1.4 million combined. In their joint quarterly report for the period ended September 30, 2026, Mid-America Apartment Communities, Inc. and Mid-America Apartments, L.P. disclosed the consent judgment, said the payment was reflected in their accrual for loss contingencies, and said they do not believe the commitments will require material changes to current operations. They also reported that they continue to defend a separate suit filed in July 2025 by Kentucky's Attorney General against RealPage and several of that state's largest landlords.
live-355: The Appellate Division of the Superior Court of New Jersey on October 30, 2026, affirmed a Law Division order dismissing with prejudice a neighboring owner's challenge to approvals for the renovation of the Gottlieb Building, a two-story building erected in 1906 at 641 Arnold Avenue in Point Pleasant Beach's downtown commercial district. The borough's Zoning Board of Adjustment had unanimously approved a restaurant and spa on the first floor and a seven-room hotel on the second. Plaintiff 637 Arnold, LLC owns the adjoining property and shares a lot line with it. This was the building's second approval. Its prior owners applied in 2020 and in 2021 obtained variance relief for a first-floor marketplace and a second-floor hotel, a use not otherwise permitted in the zone; 637 Arnold opposed that application and lost a prerogative writs challenge to it. The prior owners never started the work and in 2023 sold the property to Arnold Shores, LLC, whose managing member is Hollston Hills, LLC; those two companies and Hollston Realty Group, LLC acted jointly on the new application.
