live-359: The Thirteenth Court of Appeals of Texas affirmed summary judgment on October 29, 2026 for Brixmor GA Apollo II TX LP in a suit by dental-practice tenant Veena Dental PA, holding that Veena's claims over the size of its leased space were barred by limitations. Justice Ysmael D. Fonseca wrote the memorandum opinion for a panel with Chief Justice Tijerina and Justice Cron. According to the opinion, Veena leased space at 1548 Wildcat Drive in Portland, Texas, from Brixmor on March 23, 2013, intending to rebuild it as a dental office. The 343rd District Court of San Patricio County granted Brixmor summary judgment on September 30, 2025 and denied reconsideration in November 2025. The appeals court held that the contract claim, which it said is better described as fraudulent inducement, accrued when Veena signed the lease, and that Veena waived the discovery rule for its contract and fraud claims by never pleading it. Even under the discovery-based accrual that applies to fraud and DTPA claims regardless of pleading, the court found the discrepancy was not inherently undiscoverable: Veena could have measured the space during its buildout, and its 2013 plans stated the true square footage. All claims were therefore untimely. Because limitations decided the appeal, the court did not address Brixmor's other grounds, including the lease's release of the landlord upon a transfer.
live-360: The former Mission Mall site in Mission, Kansas, a 17-acre tract known as Mission Gateway that has sat empty for about 20 years, is headed to a sheriff's sale. live-361: Lenders backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have taken apartment properties tied to Chaim Bialostozky, a real estate investor based in Lakewood, New Jersey, to foreclosure court in Illinois, Connecticut and Oklahoma. live-362: NFI Apartment Management's policy with Third Coast Insurance Company, issued March 15, 2020, covered several NFI properties, including an apartment complex in San Antonio, and barred suits not brought within two years and one day after the cause of action accrued. After a May 2020 hailstorm, NFI submitted a claim. On July 21, 2020, Third Coast wrote that it was unable to pay because the covered loss, estimated at $37,058.29, did not exceed the $359,856.60 deductible, and invited any new information. NFI submitted an engineer's report, the parties jointly reinspected in March 2021, and on July 28, 2021, Third Coast said it would close the file because its consultant's revised estimate, $61,839.72, was still well below the deductible. In February 2022 NFI's counsel sent a pre-suit notice demanding that Third Coast reverse its denial and pay about $1 million. Third Coast reopened the claim only to respond, and its counsel wrote that the insurer stood by its measure of the loss, offered to discuss a reinspection, and reserved its rights. Discussions did not resolve the dispute. NFI sued in Texas state court on July 23, 2024, for breach of contract and violations of the Texas Insurance Code and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Third Coast removed the case to the Western District of Texas, which granted it summary judgment on limitations and denied as moot NFI's motion to compel discovery of Third Coast's internal claim records. A panel of Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Richman and Ramirez affirmed in an unpublished per curiam opinion. Relying on Texas precedent that a denial needs no "magic words," it held the July 2020 letter unambiguously denied the claim and that a below-deductible determination is still a denial of coverage. Even if that letter were ambiguous, the court said, the claims accrued no later than July 28, 2021, when Third Coast closed the file. Third Coast's later reinspection and correspondence did not withdraw the denial, so there was no waiver or estoppel. The court also rejected NFI's challenge on the discovery motion, noting NFI did not argue that the withheld material, logged as privileged, was discoverable.
live-363: In 2018, Sinmier, LLC loaned Vintro Hotels and Resorts seven million dollars to buy the Maui Sands Resort and Waterpark on Lake Erie in Sandusky, Ohio, recording a mortgage on September 7, 2018. Vintro, which was required to insure the property, worked through broker Bankers Insurance (now Bearing Insurance Group, LLC). Policies from Berkley and Everest Indemnity Insurance Company were cancelled when the closing was delayed, and Everest's reissued policy, effective October 19, 2018, listed Sinmier only as an additional insured under the general liability coverage, not as a mortgagee. That winter, a frozen pipe burst and flooded the resort, two rooftop HVAC units froze and caught fire, and other wind and cold losses followed. Vintro filed a claim with Everest on January 26, 2019; Everest advanced $350,000 and settled for an additional $775,000 in June 2019. After Vintro defaulted, Sinmier sued it in March 2019 for breach of contract, fraud and intentional misrepresentation and sought foreclosure. In an October 2019 settlement, Vintro conveyed the resort to Sinmier by a deed in lieu of foreclosure, "considered payment in full" of Vintro's obligations under the note or mortgage, and Vintro and its owner agreed to pay Sinmier $627,375 within nine months, secured by a consent judgment. Sinmier then sued Bankers, Everest and EverSports & Entertainment Insurance, Inc. in the Northern District of Ohio, as a third-party beneficiary and, against Bankers, also for negligence, misrepresentation and fraud. Judge James R. Knepp II granted summary judgment to all defendants. Writing for a panel with Judges Gibbons and Davis, Judge Jeffrey S. Sutton held that a mortgagee's insurable interest extends only to the amount of the debt and ends when the debt does, citing Ohio cases going back to the 1840s and decisions from other states. By fully releasing Vintro's mortgage debt, Sinmier ended that interest, and all of its claims depended on it. The panel rejected Sinmier's argument that the deed's no-merger language conflicted with the settlement, finding it forfeited and, in any event, consistent with the release. It held that the settlement's reservation of how insurance proceeds would be divided did not preserve the debt, that the $627,375 obligation was secured by the consent judgment rather than the mortgage, and that the policy clause protecting a mortgagee that has started foreclosure did not apply because the deed ended the action. Sinmier's claims that Bankers negligently failed to tell it about a cancellation or to secure mortgagee coverage were forfeited, and the second also failed on the merits.
live-364: In January 2023, Bartow County approved conceptual site plans from Norhaven Partners, LLC for a 97-unit townhome community, the Overlook on Pettit, on residentially zoned land, and by October 2023 it had fully approved the development plans and a land disturbance permit. Rice Commercial Investments, Inc. and its owner own adjacent property to the east, zoned heavy industrial and used for mulch processing, wood shredding and rock crushing. On July 2, 2024, Rice applied for a conditional use permit to add a recovered-materials processing and solid-waste handling facility for construction and demolition materials. No townhomes had been built, but 46 of the 97 planned units would be within 1,000 feet of the proposed waste handling area. Section 9.5.6 of the county zoning ordinance bars a waste handling area within 1,000 feet of any residential dwelling "so used at the time of the application." The Bartow County Planning Commission recommended approval with conditions in August 2024. After a September 4, 2024 hearing at which Norhaven's representatives and members of the public opposed the application, the Bartow County Commissioner approved it, with a condition that a 1,000-foot separation from residential homes be maintained. Norhaven and Peeples Owner LLC petitioned for review on October 3, 2024, arguing the approval violated section 9.5.6 because the ordinance reads "used" to include "intended, arranged, or designed to be used." The trial court remanded for written findings; the commissioner found the waste handling area was at least 1,000 feet from any residential dwelling in use at the time of the application, and on January 5, 2026 the trial court denied the petition. Presiding Judge Sara L. Doyle wrote for the court, with Judge Davis concurring and Judge Whitaker concurring in the judgment only. The court agreed with Norhaven that the trial court wrongly limited its review to the hearing transcript, but found no harm: read with the ordinance's definitions of "dwelling" and "structure," a residential dwelling means a building or structure, not an undeveloped lot planned for homes. The remand was proper, the commissioner followed its instructions, and undisputed testimony, including from Norhaven's own representative, showed no dwellings had been built. Rice's motion to dismiss the appeal was denied as moot.
live-365: PowerHouse Hillwood's plans for a $20 billion data center campus on about 800 acres in Joliet, Illinois, are on hold and may be at risk because of a dispute with Commonwealth Edison over a financial guarantee, The Real Deal reported on November 2, 2026, citing Crain's. live-366: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. has asked the court to grant summary judgment in its foreclosure on Rochester Tech Park, the Rochester Business Journal reported on October 22, 2026. live-368: A Botetourt County resident has asked the Botetourt County Circuit Court to invalidate the county's economic development performance agreement for Google's data center campus in Troutville, Cardinal News reported. live-369: A Maricopa County Superior Court judge has ruled that the City of Phoenix must prove its data-center zoning ordinance is necessary to guard public health or face a lawsuit seeking more than $54 million, KJZZ reported on Oct. 28, 2026. The ruling, issued earlier in October, narrows but does not end the suit brought by West Buckeye Road L.P. (WBR), a Texas developer, and sets a full evidentiary hearing for Nov. 17. According to KJZZ, WBR says it bought industrial land in Phoenix in 2021 and spent millions preparing it for a data center. In 2025, Phoenix adopted a zoning ordinance requiring special permits to build data centers within city limits. WBR says the rules impair its right to use the property as intended and would force it to buy state-of-the-art cooling equipment and soundproofing panels, resulting in "millions in unexpected costs." It seeks more than $54 million in lost property value under Proposition 207, the Private Property Rights Protection Act approved by Arizona voters in 2006, which requires governments to compensate owners when a new land-use law reduces property values but exempts rules meant to protect public health, such as fire and building codes or waste management. The judge rejected WBR's second claim, ruling that nothing in the city ordinance allows a developer to sue Phoenix for compensation, but kept the Proposition 207 claim alive. Full dismissal depends on whether Phoenix can show at the Nov. 17 hearing that the ordinance is necessary to guard public health. Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego, in a post on X, hailed the decision as a partial victory for the city. KJZZ did not report a statement from WBR.
live-370: The New Jersey Tax Court ruled on October 30, 2026 that its July 31, 2025 judgment reducing the American Dream Mall properties' cumulative assessment to $1,653,960,000 is binding on the Borough of East Rutherford for tax year 2026. The borough had increased the assessment to $1,899,992,100 for 2026, and owner and developer Ameream LLC moved to apply New Jersey's Freeze Act, N.J.S.A. 54:51A-8, which makes a final Tax Court judgment binding for the assessment year and the two years that follow, subject to exceptions. The borough and US Bank and Trust Company, the trustee for the bondholders whose bonds financed the development and are repaid mostly from PILOT funds, argued the mall's payment-in-lieu-of-taxes status barred the Freeze Act. Judge Michael J. Gilmore disagreed. He noted that this PILOT sets payments at 90% of the conventional taxes that would be due on the assessments, and that the agreement requires the borough to assess the property as if conventionally taxed and preserves the developer's right to contest assessments. The statute, he wrote, turns on the conclusiveness of a Tax Court judgment, not on whether the owner is a conventional taxpayer. The court found no exception applied. US Bank offered testimony and news articles about reopened storefronts, tenant improvements, an improving economy and declining capitalization rates, but "[n]one of this was quantified," and general market changes or higher occupancy do not defeat the Act. The court also held that the borough's yearly reassessment program, which changed values district-wide by less than 6% from 2025 to 2026 according to the borough's own evidence, was not the kind of complete reassessment that ends a freeze, because the exception exists to prevent a frozen judgment from being left out of step after a true district-wide reset.
live-371: Clipper Realty Inc., which owns residential and commercial buildings in New York City, disclosed in its Form 10-Q filed November 4, 2026 that the lender on its 250 Livingston Street building in Downtown Brooklyn is suing to foreclose. Clipper describes the property as a 12-story office and residential building. City of New York agencies that occupied all 342,496 rentable square feet of its commercial space vacated as of August 23, 2025; their lease generally provided for rent of $15.4 million a year. The $125 million mortgage loan, made by Citi Real Estate Funding Inc. in May 2019 and now held by Wells Fargo Bank, National Association as trustee for GS Mortgage Securities Trust 2019-GC40, is guaranteed in part by Clipper and its operating partnership. According to the 10-Q, the servicer's counsel first asserted a default in March 2025 over the handling of the property's cash-management account. live-372: The Hartford Business Journal reported on May 1, 2026 that JZ Investments, Inc., a Connecticut investment company, had sued a former business partner and several Greenwich real estate entities over the loss of its ownership stake in a proposed 262-unit housing development at 497-501 Middle Turnpike in Mansfield, near UConn's main campus. live-373: On November 5, 2026, the Tenth District Court of Appeals of Ohio reversed a Franklin County Court of Common Pleas judgment in an eminent domain case brought by the City of Columbus, holding that the trial court was wrong to bar a mortgage lender, Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP, from claiming an interest in the property. Judge Dingus wrote the decision, and Judges Edelstein and Leland concurred. In August 2021 the city petitioned to appropriate a fee simple interest and a temporary easement on a 0.082-acre parcel, and a temporary construction easement on a 0.016-acre parcel, for the Hudson Street Sidewalks Project. It named nine parties with possible interests, including the fee owner, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales, LLC, and Wiltshire as a mortgagee of record. By April 2022 only Wiltshire, Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales and the Franklin County Treasurer remained. Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales pointed out that Wiltshire had filed a foreclosure on the same mortgage in August 2017, which the court dismissed in March 2018 for failure to prosecute after Wiltshire did not obtain service. In July 2023 the trial court ruled that res judicata barred Wiltshire's claim and that Wiltshire lacked standing. Wiltshire's first appeal was dismissed in 2024 for lack of a final, appealable order, although the appellate court noted that the issue was not really one of standing, since the city itself had named Wiltshire as a respondent. In May 2025 the trial court approved the city's settlement with Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales over Wiltshire's objection and vested title in the city upon a $4,014 payment to the owner. It also agreed with the owner that Wiltshire had failed to set forth an interest in the property, citing an apparent assignment of the note underlying the mortgage. On the second appeal, the panel noted that Ohio Civil Rule 41(B)(3) generally treats a dismissal for failure to prosecute as an adjudication on the merits unless the court says otherwise. But under the Ohio Supreme Court's decision in Thomas v. Freeman, when a plaintiff has not obtained service on the defendant, a dismissal under either Civil Rule 41(B)(1) or Civil Rule 4(E) is otherwise than on the merits. Wiltshire had served only the county treasurer in the 2017 case, not the owner, so that dismissal was without prejudice and could not bar its claim. The court said it made no finding on whether Wiltshire holds a valid and enforceable mortgage, and directed that Wiltshire be allowed to assert its claim and argue those issues on remand. It treated Wiltshire's remaining assignments of error as moot.
live-374: Ritz-Carlton Development Co. live-375: Torchlight Loan Services, the special servicer for bondholders who own the JW Marriott Chicago at 208 South LaSalle Street, sued Mike Reschke's Prime Group in Cook County Circuit Court on October 30, 2026, The Real Deal reported. live-377: The Intermediate Court of Appeals of West Virginia, in an opinion by Judge White filed November 6, 2026, affirmed the dismissal of a breach-of-contract and declaratory-judgment suit by Fountain Place, LLC against the City of Logan and the City of Logan Development Authority, and remanded for further proceedings, including the city's counterclaims against Fountain Place, which remain pending. According to the opinion, the city created the Development Authority, and in 1997 the city and the authority signed a development agreement with Monterra, Fountain Place's predecessor, which was developing a shopping center in an unincorporated part of Logan County. In exchange for Monterra not objecting to annexation of the property, the city and authority agreed to remit 57% of the business and occupancy taxes collected from businesses at the center for 20 years, renewable for 10 more. Monterra and its successors were also excused from B&O taxes on construction, rental and leasing at the property, and the opinion says neither has paid any B&O tax related to the mall. Monterra filed for bankruptcy in 1999, the bankruptcy court assigned the agreement to Fountain Place, and Fountain Place finished building the center, which still operates as the Fountain Place shopping center. The authority was no longer active by about 2013, but the city kept paying Fountain Place directly. On June 28, 2016, Fountain Place notified the city that it was renewing the agreement until July 22, 2027. The city paid through May 2021, when it decided it was not legally obligated to continue. Fountain Place sued in the Circuit Court of Logan County on August 9, 2023. On July 18, 2025, the circuit court dismissed the suit, ruling that the agreement created unconstitutional municipal indebtedness under Article X, Section 8 of the state constitution because it was never put to a public vote, that the city was statutorily immune from the dissolved authority's liabilities, and that the city was not estopped from contesting the agreement. The appeals court declined to reach the constitutional question and affirmed on the statutes and estoppel. It held that W. Va. Code § 7-12-8, which says no indebtedness of a development authority is an indebtedness of the municipality, covers the payment obligation, and that § 7-12-13 sends an authority's assets, but not its liabilities, to the city on dissolution. It rejected Fountain Place's argument that the result was a taking without due process, and held that estoppel did not apply because the city acted in a governmental capacity when it annexed the land, used its taxing power and created the authority. The State of West Virginia filed an amicus brief supporting the city and the authority. Fountain Place Realty, LLC and Namdar DG Realty, LLC were also named as respondents and were separately represented.
live-378: For decades General Iron Industries ran a metal scrap recycling business in Chicago's Lincoln Park neighborhood. By July 2018 it had agreed to sell assets to Reserve Management Group, and in a September 2019 term sheet with the city, General Iron and RMG agreed to end the Lincoln Park operations, with RMG stating it intended to transition to a new operation at the Burley site, a 175-acre property where RMG affiliates already ran four recycling facilities. The city agreed to reasonably cooperate on permitting while reserving its authority to enforce its ordinances to protect public health. General III obtained a special use approval from the Zoning Board of Appeals in April 2019, an Illinois EPA construction permit in June 2020 and a city air pollution control permit in September 2020, and built the facility from September 2020 to March 2021 at a cost it puts at about $80 million. General III applied for the city's large recycling facility permit in November 2020. After HUD opened an investigation of a civil rights complaint about the move and U.S. EPA Administrator Michael S. Regan wrote in May 2021 suggesting the city first study cumulative health effects, the department suspended its review and, with U.S. EPA assistance, prepared a health impact assessment that recommended denial. On February 18, 2022, the department denied the permit, relying mainly on that assessment and also on compliance issues at affiliated facilities on the site. After a January 2023 hearing, an administrative law judge vacated the denial on June 1, 2023, finding the assessment beyond the commissioner's authority and the compliance-history rule inconsistent with the code. In August 2024 the circuit court, Judge Allen P. Walker, reversed and reinstated the denial. In an opinion by Justice Pucinski, joined by Justices Hyman and Evans, the First District affirmed. It treated the administrative law judge's decision as the final decision under review but held that the health department, not the hearings department, is owed deference in interpreting the code. It held that the commissioner's code powers to protect public health, conduct studies and cooperate with federal agencies authorized use of the assessment, that the zoning board's approval did not limit the health department's separate review, and that the delegation of authority was constitutional. It also held that the department's rule allowing review of an applicant's compliance history does not conflict with the code provision on prior permit revocations and is not limited to adjudicated violations. The court rejected General III's argument that its spending in reliance on earlier approvals gave it a vested right to the permit, noting that the doctrine has been applied to zoning classifications and that the record showed no pattern of official assurances that this permit would issue. Southeast Side community groups filed an amicus brief supporting the department; business and manufacturing groups filed one supporting General III.
live-379: ZOM Holding Inc. and two affiliates, ZOM Associates and ZH Development I, filed Chapter 11 petitions on October 30, 2026 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Middle District of Florida, where the jointly administered cases are before Judge Grace E. Robson (lead case No. 6:26-bk-08509). The Real Deal reported that the debtors are affiliates of ZOM Living, a Winter Park, Florida-based multifamily and senior housing developer, but that ZOM Holding Inc. does not own any of ZOM Living's apartment properties. According to a declaration by chief restructuring officer Neil Luria, the debtors face an estimated $541 million in unsecured claims, including amounts owed to vendors and guarantees on properties in Miami, Texas, North Carolina and Virginia. According to the declaration, ZT Development terminated the purchase agreement a year later while the owners of the project sites went through bankruptcy, and another ZOM affiliate bought four of the properties out of bankruptcy for $82 million in 2020. live-380: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on November 6, 2026, affirmed the dismissal of a suit by AB Realty, LLC, owner of the Yale Park Apartment Complex in Omaha, Nebraska, over the city's 2018 closure of the property. Judge Jonathan A. Kobes wrote for a panel that included Chief Judge Colloton and Judge Gruender. According to the facts alleged in the complaint and its exhibits, two housing advocates began talking with Yale Park tenants in the summer of 2018, documented conditions and passed complaints to the city, which began planning the closure. Chief Housing Inspector Scott Lane obtained an inspection warrant relying mostly on their information. His application cited suspected health and safety violations in 84 of the complex's 100 units, and the court noted it contained factual errors, including a false statement that an individual plaintiff had refused Lane's request to enter. The city executed the warrant on September 20, 2018, tenants were relocated, and the city ordered that Yale Park could not reopen until the violations were cured. The city later sent notices of about 2,000 violations and prosecuted an individual plaintiff for misdemeanor code violations; a jury convicted on a few counts and acquitted on most. AB Realty and two individuals filed suit in federal court in March 2019 under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983, according to the CourtListener docket, and AB Realty reopened the complex in the spring of 2021 after repairs. The district court dismissed part of the case, stayed the rest until the criminal case ended, and then dismissed the remaining claims. On appeal, AB Realty argued the warrant was invalid under Franks v. Delaware because the application falsely said entry had been refused and that police had been called, that inspections had occurred, that threats were made against tenants and that a gas leak caused an explosion. The panel held that even excluding the disputed information, the application established probable cause under the standard for administrative warrants, citing complaints about 84 of 100 units, holes in the roof, untreated natural gas leaks and an admission that maintenance requests had been handled in a "lackadaisical" way. A Nebraska statute requiring a refusal of consent before an inspection warrant issues did not help, the court said, because a violation of state law alone does not state a Section 1983 claim. The due-process claims failed because the complaint did not identify which protected interests were at stake or who violated them. On takings, the court found no per se taking because AB Realty still owns the property, and no regulatory taking because the plaintiffs did not argue one under the Penn Central test.
live-381: Bethlehem Landfill Company owns and operates a municipal solid waste landfill at 2335 Applebutter Road in Lower Saucon Township, Pennsylvania. To expand it, the company asked the township to rezone 275.7 acres from Rural Agricultural to Light Industrial and to release two 1994 recorded instruments in the township's favor that would bar development on parts of the land. On August 14, 2023, a group of neighboring residents sued the township and the company, arguing the land was subject to Pennsylvania's Donated or Dedicated Property Act and could not be rezoned or released without Orphans' Court approval. On August 30, 2023, the township council voted to release the 1994 instruments in exchange for new conservation easements on about 193 acres, adopted the rezoning ordinance by a 3-2 vote, and approved an amended host community agreement. In December 2023 it conditionally approved the company's preliminary land development plan. After the November 2023 election changed the council's makeup, the township stopped defending the neighbors' suit alongside the company. On April 15, 2024, the township solicitor filed a brief joining the neighbors' position, and two council members said at public meetings that the council had never voted on that change. On May 1, 2024, the council voted 3-2 to ratify the filing, over the company's objections that the motion was not on the agenda and that one council member should recuse herself. The company sued on May 15, 2024, alleging Sunshine Act violations, seeking a declaration that the solicitor's brief was void, seeking to bar the council member from voting on expansion matters, and asserting promissory estoppel based on the township's earlier promise to release the 1994 instruments. The township defendants argued, among other things, that the public ratification vote cured any violation. On May 14, 2025, in an order amended the next day, the trial court dismissed the Sunshine Act and declaratory counts with prejudice as moot because the company had not appealed the ratification vote, dismissed the conflict-of-interest counts without prejudice and with leave to amend, and let the promissory estoppel count go forward against the township defendants. The company did not amend, discontinued the promissory estoppel count, and appealed. In an opinion by Judge Anne E. Covey, for a panel that included Judge Stacy Wallace and Senior Judge Mary Hannah Leavitt, the Commonwealth Court held it lacked jurisdiction. An order sustaining preliminary objections with leave to amend is interlocutory, the court said, and the company had neither filed a praecipe asking the trial court to dismiss its complaint nor sought a determination of finality. The court also rejected the argument that the order was immediately appealable because it denied injunctive and declaratory relief, since the company could still pursue that relief on the counts it was allowed to amend. The court did not reach the merits.
live-382: The Appellate Court of Illinois, First District, ruled on November 9, 2026 that a landlord may assign its right to collect past-due, unpaid rent. Presiding Justice Ellis wrote the opinion, joined by Justices Fitzgerald Smith and Cobbs. The court reversed a Cook County circuit court order that had dismissed the suit "solely on the ground" that the plaintiffs lacked standing, and remanded. According to the complaint, as described in the opinion, Affordable Portables, Inc., doing business as Philips Interiors, leased commercial property on North Clark Street in Chicago in 2002. The property was sold several times during the initial 20-year lease period, and by 2021 it was owned by 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC. The lease required the tenant to pay base rent, utilities and 38% of the property's real estate taxes, and the complaint alleges the tenant failed to pay many of those charges while 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC was the landlord. In 2024 the LLC assigned its right to collect that unpaid rent to two individuals, one of them its managing member, who filed a verified complaint in January 2025. The circuit court relied on the Illinois Supreme Court's 1872 decision in Kennedy v. Kennedy, which held that "rents in arrear are not assignable," and on 1002 E. 87th Street, LLC v. Midway Broadcasting Corp. (2018), which quoted Kennedy. The appellate court agreed that a claim for rent owed to a prior landlord does not run with the property to a new owner; it is a claim held by the landlord to whom the rent was owed. But it concluded that Kennedy is inconsistent with the Supreme Court's more recent decisions in Kleinwort Benson (1998) and Citibank (2017), which treat assignability as the rule and limit exceptions mainly to personal-injury and other personal claims. The court called a lease "a garden-variety, arm's-length business transaction" and found no public-policy reason to bar assignment, and it described Midway Broadcasting's statement as dictum. The tenant also asked the court to dismiss the appeal because only one of the two assignees, who was self-represented, filed a brief; the court declined. It did not rule on the tenant's other grounds for dismissal, including that the complaint did not allege performance of conditions precedent, and sent those back to the circuit court. The decision does not determine whether, or how much, rent is owed.
live-383: Lineage, the cold-storage warehouse REIT, has sued Altus Power, the company that operated a solar array on the roof of its Boyle Heights warehouse in Los Angeles, alleging Altus' negligence caused the fire that burned there for about a week in June 2026, Bisnow reported on September 11, 2026. The suit was filed September 10 in Los Angeles County Superior Court and also names Pearce Services LLC, a CBRE subsidiary that worked on the panels. Lineage's quarterly report filed November 9 says the suit also names Altus subsidiary Los Palos Street Operating LLC. Lineage alleges it asked Altus and Pearce not to re-energize the solar panels until specific safety tests were done, and that both companies did so anyway. "The record is clear: this was a solar fire," Lineage said in a statement. According to Bisnow, Lineage estimates the fire will cost it more than $1 billion in all. Pearce told Bisnow it disputes Lineage's allegations, saying the investigation into the fire's cause, origin and spread is ongoing and "it is premature for anyone to draw conclusions." A spokesperson for Los Palos Street Operating told the Los Angeles Times that Lineage's statement was "riddled with misinformation" and an attempt to deflect blame for its own role, including damage from substances released from the warehouse. Lineage's 10-Q says the June 17 fire destroyed portions of the leased warehouse and all customer inventory, that restoration costs could exceed its insurance claim limit, and that it faces customer claims and suits, plus putative class actions and individual suits by local residents against it and the solar companies. It says it intends to defend those claims and is cooperating with federal, state and local authorities.
live-384: GSL Holdings, LLC, a Michigan real estate developer, owns a roughly six-acre parcel in an industrial complex in Lyon Township. In December 2020 it leased the site to Moba Americas, Inc., a machinery manufacturer for the egg industry, agreeing to use its best reasonable efforts to have a new facility ready for occupancy by October 1, 2021. The parcel had no public sewer access, so GSL needed a septic permit from the Oakland County Health Division. The county had denied a 2018 application for the same property and said it would not issue a permit unless GSL combined the parcel with an adjacent lot. The township preliminarily approved GSL's site plan, which called for an on-site septic field, in January 2021, but its ordinance requires permits from other agencies before construction starts. On March 8, 2021, a GSL representative emailed the township's entire board of trustees about the pace of review. The township's attorney called that inappropriate and later said it risked a violation of Michigan's Open Meetings Act. The same day, GSL signed a hold-harmless agreement so the township would go ahead with building-plan review. GSL applied for the septic permit on March 9, and on March 22 the county again said it would not consider the application until the lots were combined; GSL then applied to combine them. GSL says a township coordinator told it in late March that foundation and shell permits were ready, but it did not pick them up. On April 5 the township said that, at Supervisor Dolan's direction, no building permit would issue until after a utility pre-construction meeting, which required the septic permit. On May 3 the township proposed a second hold-harmless agreement that would have let GSL build without the septic permit if GSL agreed to extend the public sanitary sewer at its own cost should the permit not be obtained. GSL considered the terms atypical and unduly burdensome, and the agreement was never signed. The facility was not ready by October, and GSL and Moba negotiated an end to the lease. GSL sued the township and Dolan in the Eastern District of Michigan. Judge Matthew F. Leitman granted summary judgment to the defendants on all claims except a later First Amendment retaliation claim over the township's denial of a speculative-building designation and a Michigan Freedom of Information Act claim, which the parties settled shortly before trial. The Sixth Circuit panel of Judges White, Thapar and Mathis affirmed. On equal protection, GSL pointed to a neighboring owner that received a building permit around 2017 before it had a septic permit. Assuming that owner was similarly situated, the court held the township's sewage-related reasons were rational and that it was conceivable the earlier permit was a mistake; the township conceded the former coordinator who issued it had breached township policy. Irritation by the township's outside counsel and engineering consultant at GSL's email did not show animus by a final decisionmaker. On procedural due process, the court held that even if permits had issued, GSL did no substantial construction under them, so under Michigan law it had no vested property interest. The substantive due-process claim failed because the township followed its ordinance, and the township rationally denied the speculative-building designation because its tax-abatement guidelines bar applicants with pending suits against it. The First Amendment claim failed because the request not to email the whole board at once was content neutral, narrowly tailored to the township's interest in complying with the Open Meetings Act, and left other channels open.
live-385: According to the trial court's summary quoted in the opinion, SA Living Fund LLC borrowed $3,850,000 in July 2022 for 18 months under a loan secured by mortgaged premises at 827 Spring Garden Street in Philadelphia. Two individuals guaranteed it. The note, the loan agreement and the guaranty each contained confession-of-judgment provisions. First Citizens Community Bank is the successor by merger to Huntingdon Valley Bank, the original lender. In March 2024 the borrower extended the maturity by one month for a $9,625 extension fee and a $750 legal fee. In November 2024 a second modification called for a payment of $103,433.33 to bring the loan current, plus a prepayment of interest for the coming year, and extended maturity to October 2029 unless the bank called the loan sooner. Both modifications contained confession-of-judgment provisions. A January 2025 letter from the bank said the borrower still owed $18,463.33 on the modification payments and $30,010.55 for a principal and interest payment due January 1, 2025, and gave it 15 days to cure. The bank filed a complaint in confession of judgment in March 2025, and the prothonotary entered judgment. The borrower and guarantors petitioned to strike or open the judgment, arguing that the complaint alleged default only in conclusory terms and that the bank's figures were wrong. At the July 9, 2025 hearing the bank agreed its calculations were incorrect, and the trial court denied the petition while directing the bank to file a motion to reassess damages. That motion has been deferred until the appeal is resolved. Writing for a panel with Judges Bowes and Olson, Judge McLaughlin held that the trial court should not have relied on the later-submitted letter and testimony in deciding the motion to strike, because that review is limited to the record when judgment was entered. The error was harmless: the complaint itself averred the default that Pennsylvania Rule of Civil Procedure 2952(a)(6) requires, and the loan documents provided for acceleration on default. On the petition to open, the court noted that the borrower did not claim it was not in default; an error in the amount is not a meritorious defense, and the corrected figure will be set on the motion to reassess damages. The borrower's argument that the bank breached the duty of good faith by pressing it to refinance or sell and by demanding a year of prepaid interest was waived because the petition did not raise it, and the court said it would fail anyway, because an unwillingness to renegotiate is not bad faith, particularly where the bank had agreed to two modifications.
live-386: On November 9, 2026, the Supreme Court denied Rubicon Real Estate Holdings, LLC's petition for certiorari (No. 26-359), which had been filed September 14, 2026; the city waived its right to respond. The order leaves in place a published June 18, 2026 decision of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit (No. 25-1631), written by Judge Readler for a panel with Judges Griffin and Larsen, affirming U.S. District Judge David M. Lawson's grant of summary judgment to the City of Pontiac and its city clerk. According to the Sixth Circuit, Rubicon agreed in March 2019 to buy a derelict 20-acre parcel on Glenwood Avenue, the former Glenwood Plaza, planning a shopping area with a grocery store and facilities for medical marijuana growing and processing. The City Council approved a rezoning and the parties signed a conditional rezoning agreement, but licensing for Rubicon's prospective tenants was held up by the city clerk, who took the position that the project needed a further ordinance change. Rubicon and one prospective tenant obtained declaratory relief in Oakland County Circuit Court on May 21, 2021, and the licenses issued in May and June 2021, but by then the prospective tenants had pulled out, Rubicon's lender refused to disburse funds, and the project collapsed. Rubicon, its managing member and his separate design firm sued the city and the clerk in Oakland County Circuit Court in January 2023, and the defendants removed the case to federal court. Rubicon alleged violations of the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses and an uncompensated taking; the managing member and the design firm alleged the city, through Mayor Tim Greimel, retaliated for the earlier state-court suit by pressing another developer to cancel the design firm's contract. The district court granted summary judgment on all claims. The Sixth Circuit affirmed. It held that Rubicon's due process claims failed because the uses its tenants sought rested on discretionary government approvals; that the delay was not extraordinary enough to be a taking; and that Rubicon offered no evidence of intentional discrimination for its equal protection claim. On the retaliation claim, it held the city could not be liable because the mayor lacked final authority over rezoning decisions. The court wrote that city officials "at worst simply lagged in granting discretionary zoning and licensing approvals."
live-387: Weis Markets, Inc. operates a grocery store under a lease at Bangor Plaza, a 20.3-acre planned development in Washington Township's Commercial District in Northampton County, Pennsylvania. In an application dated June 17, 2022, Weis sought a special exception to add a Gas-N-Go fuel station with six fueling positions at three pumps under a canopy, replacing a previously approved bank use that was vacant. The township's zoning officer had denied a zoning permit for the station on the ground that a special exception was required, and Weis did not appeal that denial. Bluetriton Brands, Inc., which withdraws groundwater from the Greenwaltz Spring as the primary source for its Deer Park brand and holds interests in 15 parcels in the township, including two that directly abut the site, objected. Its geologist testified that water flows from the plaza toward its spring and that the station's oil-water separator would discharge into a stormwater basin that forms part of Greenwalk Creek. Its petroleum-systems expert cited state Department of Environmental Protection records showing storage-tank violation notices at about half of Weis's Gas-N-Go locations in Pennsylvania. Weis's hydrologist testified that the aquifer is confined and not susceptible to contamination from surface spills or tank releases. The zoning hearing board granted the special exception with conditions in February 2023. Common pleas remanded in January 2024, holding the board had to review and approve a site plan. On remand the board approved the site plan in May 2024, but in April 2025 a different common pleas judge reversed, holding the site plan did not meet the ordinance and that the board could not approve it based on future compliance. Weis appealed. The Commonwealth Court rejected Weis's argument that no special exception was needed because a fuel station is permitted by right: because Weis had not appealed the zoning officer's determination within 30 days, that determination was binding. But the court agreed with Weis that the ordinance's provisions on site-plan review for a special-exception use that is also a land development are ambiguous, resolved that doubt in Weis's favor, and held no site plan was required at this time. Because common pleas had not addressed whether Weis met its burden for the special exception or whether the board adequately considered Bluetriton's evidence of harm, the court remanded for common pleas to decide those issues in a new opinion within 60 days.
live-389: On November 10, 2026, the Mississippi Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, affirmed a Hinds County Circuit Court judgment upholding the Hinds County Board of Supervisors' approval of two conditional use permits for Soul City Storage LLC and Soul City Energy LLC (together, Soul City). Soul City plans a solar farm and battery storage facility on about 5,800 acres of undeveloped land stretching from Bolton to an area north of the Natchez Trace. Judge Lassitter St. Pé wrote for a six-judge majority; Judge Westbrooks dissented, joined by three other judges. According to the opinion, Soul City applied to the Hinds County Planning Commission in April 2024. After a community meeting in Raymond attended by more than 100 people, it voluntarily revised its applications, including relocating construction traffic, offering a road use agreement, managing trees and vegetation, and using agricultural fencing and wildlife corridors. At a May 2024 hearing, the Planning Commission voted unanimously to deny both applications after hearing opposition, including from a resident who spoke as a designated spokesperson for opponents. On Soul City's appeal, the Board of Supervisors held a hearing in June 2024, at which the mayor of Raymond asked for a one-year moratorium on solar projects and the county's permit and zoning director said Soul City had followed the zoning guidelines. The Board approved both applications 3-2. The resident appealed to the Hinds County Circuit Court, arguing the Board had not issued the written findings the ordinance requires and that substantial evidence did not support the permits. The circuit court affirmed in April 2025. The Court of Appeals majority held that the ordinance does not prescribe a particular form for the Board's written decision, and that by incorporating Soul City's application, site plan and supplemental materials into its order and minutes, the Board certified the project's compliance. It also found substantial evidence supported the permits, treated Soul City's voluntary conditions as part of what the Board approved, and rejected a judicial estoppel argument. The dissent would have held that the ordinance's mandatory language required a written certification specific to the permit criteria, which the minutes did not provide. It pointed to the project's size, its expected 30-year life, the Planning Commission's unanimous denial and the close Board vote.

live-393: On November 12, 2026, Florida's Fourth District Court of Appeal affirmed in part and reversed in part a final default summary judgment entered for landlord Congress Ave Boynton, LLC against tenant First Care Therapy, LLC and the individual who guaranteed its lease. Judge Alan O. Forst wrote the opinion, joined by Judges Shepherd and Shaw. The tenant had leased commercial premises in Boynton Beach from SNH Medical Office Properties Trust in September 2021; Congress Ave Boynton bought the property in May 2024 and took an assignment of the lease and guaranty. The landlord sued on February 21, 2025, for nonpayment of rent without pleading a sum certain, attaching a lease ledger showing $34,337.91 in unpaid charges. Neither defendant responded, and the clerk entered defaults in March 2025. The landlord then moved for summary judgment on an affidavit of indebtedness from its managing agent totaling $85,782.80: $48,480 in rent, $4,222 in legal fees to draft and negotiate a new lease, a $10,557 reletting commission and $22,523 in tenant improvements for reletting. At a July 2025 hearing the guarantor appeared without a lawyer and no attorney appeared for the tenant. The court heard argument and entered judgment for the full amount requested, plus interest, and found the landlord entitled to attorney's fees. The panel rejected the tenant's and guarantor's arguments that the judgment was void. The circuit court had subject-matter jurisdiction, and any objection to its authority in this particular case was waived. The landlord did not have to attach the written assignment, and by defaulting the defendants admitted the allegation that the lease and guaranty had been assigned to it. A company cannot appear in court without counsel, and the tenant's failure to retain one was not a due-process violation. The damages award was another matter. Following its August 2026 decision in Affinity Health Partners, LLC v. Hayes Locums, LLC, the court held that a clerk's default supports only liquidated damages, and that these damages were unliquidated because the complaint pleaded no sum certain, the ledger showed less than half the award, and the final figure could be reached only by weighing the affidavit. The prejudgment interest and costs were likewise unliquidated. Because the July 2025 hearing was a non-evidentiary summary judgment proceeding rather than a damages trial noticed under Rule 1.440(d), the court reversed the award and remanded for such a trial, leaving the liability ruling in place. The opinion is not final until any timely motion for rehearing is resolved.

live-396: The owners of a building on West Burnside in Portland had for decades leased its large west wall to advertising companies that sold space for signs. In 2009 they leased the wall to Onsite Advertising Services, LLC under a revenue-sharing arrangement, and in 2010 Onsite assigned the lease to OnDisplay Advertising. A 2014 addendum extended the lease to June 30, 2019, with automatic five-year renewal unless either side gave notice. After the state designated that stretch of West Burnside a state highway in 2012, ODOT began requiring a permit for the sign as of June 30, 2015. The owners agreed to give OnDisplay a consent letter for ODOT on the condition that they would own the permit when the lease ended, and the letter stated the permit "shall be in the name of" OnDisplay and the owners. ODOT issued the permit only to OnDisplay. OnDisplay sold its assets, including the lease, to Lamar in a deal that closed June 16, 2015, and ODOT reissued the permit in Lamar's name alone. The owners were not told. The owners gave notice that they would not renew, and in February 2019 Lamar said that if the lease ended it would remove the lighting and cabling and relinquish the permit, which the court said was the owners' first notice that the permit was in Lamar's name. Lamar declined to sell the permit, telling the owners through counsel that doing so would not serve its interest because it would "allow a competing advertising agency to saturate the market even further." On July 18, 2019, despite the owners' written instruction not to surrender it, Lamar used the permit to obtain a relocation credit from ODOT, and no location was available where that credit could be used. ODOT refused to issue a new permit to the owners, whose separate challenges against ODOT were later rejected. The owners sued OnDisplay and Lamar, settled with OnDisplay, and went to trial against Lamar in Multnomah County. The jury found for the owners on the good-faith claim but not on conversion, and the judgment, including costs, was $1,237,191.92. In an opinion by Presiding Judge Darleen Ortega, joined by Judges Joyce and Hellman, the Court of Appeals held two of Lamar's nine assignments of error unreviewable and rejected the rest. It held that, as a matter of law, the parties could have held the expectations the owners claimed, grounded in the lease's limited term and its renewal and termination provisions, including that Lamar would not act to prevent the owners from leasing the wall to others once the lease ended. Whether the parties actually held those expectations and whether Lamar's conduct breached them were questions for the jury. The court also found the future-damages evidence sufficient and no error in the jury instructions.

live-399: On February 8, 2023, Ms. Audrey's Crafting Emporium, LLC signed a 62-month lease for retail space with Ghasem Properties, Inc., and an individual guaranteed it up to $155,124.60. Rent and common-area maintenance totaled $2,585.41 a month starting in the third month. The tenant paid through December 2023 and then stopped. The landlord said it mailed a default notice on January 6, 2024, and a forcible-detainer action was dismissed in April 2024 after the tenant vacated. The landlord sued in Jefferson Circuit Court on April 8, 2024. The tenant and guarantor admitted signing the lease, defaulting and not paying rent from January 2024 on, but denied responsibility for damages. The landlord moved for summary judgment on an affidavit from its president stating that rent for the rest of the term would have totaled $131,855.91 and that a listing agreement had not produced a new tenant. The defendants did not respond, and on September 30, 2024 the court signed the landlord's tendered judgment for $131,855.91 with 8% prejudgment interest from January 1, 2024, 6% post-judgment interest, and fees and costs. The court later denied the defendants' motion to vacate, saying their arguments should have been made before judgment, and entered a supplemental award of $8,299.30 in fees and costs. The Court of Appeals, in an opinion joined by Judges Caldwell and Taylor, held that the defendants could not wait until after judgment to challenge the affidavit, and that their own admissions established liability. It found the interest issue properly raised, however, because the 8% rate first appeared in the landlord's tendered order. With no rate in the lease, the statutory rate for a judgment, including prejudgment interest, is 6% under KRS 360.040. On future rent, the court acknowledged the defendants never raised the point but addressed it to avoid applying the wrong law: under Kentucky precedent, without an acceleration clause, rent that has not yet accrued cannot be awarded in advance. Only nine months of rent had accrued at judgment, while the award covered the remaining 42 months, which the court called a windfall. The landlord may seek supplemental judgments for rent as it comes due if it cannot relet the space before the term ends in March 2028. The court affirmed the 6% post-judgment interest.

live-401: The special servicer on 1440 Broadway, a 745,000-square-foot office building near Times Square, has gone to court to foreclose. live-402: New York Supreme Court Justice Francis Kahn on November 11, 2026 denied summary judgment to 109Co in its $44 million foreclosure against Fortuna Realty's Hotel Hayden, finding that the note and mortgage had not been properly attached to each other, The Real Deal reported. The ruling sends the case to trial. The 122-room hotel is at 127 West 28th Street in Manhattan. Fortuna bought it in 1999 and refinanced it with Morgan Stanley Private Bank in 2018. Morgan Stanley started the foreclosure in April 2025 and, in February 2026, sold the loan for an undisclosed price to 109Co, a firm formed in 2023. Default is not in dispute: according to the report, the owner's principal signed a forbearance agreement admitting it. The dispute is over standing. A foreclosing lender has to show how and when it came to hold the note along with the mortgage, and courts have required the papers to be "so firmly affixed thereto as to become a part thereof." The Real Deal reported that Morgan Stanley filed the note and mortgage separately when it refinanced the hotel, and Justice Kahn found the requirement was not met. The rule protects borrowers from a second party later claiming the same debt and trying to foreclose again. These challenges became common in the foreclosures after the 2007 housing crash, and they usually come up after a loan has changed hands. "No staple, no case," the borrower's attorney told The Real Deal. He said 109Co must now try to prove its standing at trial or go back and fix the attachment problem, which could be hard if it means finding people involved in the 2018 loan, and that he expects more such challenges as banks sell off bad loans. Representatives of 109Co and Fortuna could not immediately be reached. The ruling gives the hotel owner more leverage in any settlement talks.
live-403: Prologis, the San Francisco-based industrial real estate company, has sued the City of Trenton, Ohio, in federal court over a voter-approved limit on data centers. live-404: The dispute traces to a group of founders who built a small portfolio of buildings leased long-term to federal government tenants. In 2016 they formed HC Government Realty Trust, Inc., a Maryland REIT, and its operating partnership, HC Government Realty Holdings, L.P., and signed a management agreement under which their own company, Holmwood Capital Advisors, LLC, would run the REIT for an asset management fee of 1.5% of stockholders' equity, a 1% acquisition fee and a leasing fee. A related entity, Holmwood Capital, LLC, contributed seven single-property entities to the operating partnership in a May 2017 exchange for 1,078,416 partnership units valued at $10,784,161. The management agreement promised the manager a termination fee of three times the fees earned over the prior 24 months if the REIT ended the arrangement without cause, and a November 2017 side letter scaled that fee to how much equity the REIT managed to build: waived below $15 million, halved between $15 million and $35 million, and paid in full above $35 million. In March 2019, over the objection of one founder-director, the REIT's board approved a recapitalization with a new outside investor that included up to $20.5 million of preferred stock, $3 million of common stock and a secured loan of up to $20.5 million. At the same meeting the board voted not to renew the management agreement, which ended March 31, 2020. On that date the REIT told the manager the termination fee was $1,645,453, paid as $1,275,000 in cash and the balance in common stock at $7.17 a share. That figure used the halved, 1.5x multiplier, because the REIT's new finance chief had begun booking a $1.75 million estimate of the termination fee itself as an accrued liability, which pulled reported stockholders' equity just under $35 million. The manager sued in May 2020, and the REIT counterclaimed. Vice Chancellor Bonnie W. David sided with the manager on the central question. The agreement's definition of stockholders' equity excludes non-cash items that have affected equity as reported in the financial statements, and an accrued but unpaid termination fee is such an item, so it had to be added back. The court also read the side letter's reference to the REIT 'building' equity to $35 million as a high-water mark rather than a snapshot on the termination date, so the full 3.0x multiplier applies. The REIT's late arguments that equity had been overstated all along, because dividends were never deducted from retained earnings and because the contributed properties were overvalued by about $3.2 million, were rejected. The court found the REIT waived both points by using the same method in its own March 2020 fee notice, and found the appraisal evidence unpersuasive in any event. The manager did not win everything. The court held that accrued acquisition fees were paid in stock on the termination date and so do not get added to the fee base, and that no acquisition fee is owed on three properties the REIT bought in October 2019 in Fort Lauderdale, Lawrence, Kansas and Oklahoma City, because the manager did no work on those deals. Applying contra proferentem against the founders, who controlled every party when the agreement was written and then marketed the REIT to outside investors, the court held the REIT could choose to pay the termination and acquisition fees in common stock, and that the manager must bear organization and offering expenses above 15% of the $8,871,660 raised, an excess of $723,932. The $408,514 that Holmwood advanced to cover operating shortfalls was not proven to be an interest-bearing demand loan, but the court found it must be repaid on terms the parties are to propose. On the counterclaims, the REIT failed to prove $76,322 in allegedly duplicative property management fees, and its unjust enrichment claim fell with the valuation argument. It did prevail on the contribution agreement. Three of the contributed properties secured a CMBS loan that barred any transfer of direct or indirect interests without lender consent. Holmwood transferred the economic interest in those properties without telling the lender, the servicer issued a notice of default in November 2022, and the REIT spent $517,463.35 obtaining a consent and loan modification in March 2023. The court held that Holmwood's representation that the deal would not cause a default under any contract was false, and awarded that amount as damages. The practical lessons are plain. A termination fee tied to an equity measure should say whether the accrual of the fee itself counts, and whether thresholds are tested once or continuously; here silence on timing cost the REIT half the multiplier. A company that pays under one calculation method will struggle to attack that method years later. Sponsors who sit on both sides of a management agreement should expect ambiguities to be read against them once outside investors are in the capital stack. And a cost-allocation clause for obtaining lender consents before closing does not protect a contributor who never sought consent at all. The final dollar amount of the fee remains open until the parties submit a revised calculation.
live-405: The landlord, HCJV 115 & 135 Hoyt Avenue Owner, LLC, leased a commercial unit in Mamaroneck to Project Veritas in 2020 for five years, from November 1, 2020 through October 31, 2025. Rent was due on the first of each month, payments more than 10 days late drew additional interest, and section 20 of the lease required any modification to be in writing and signed by the party against whom it would be enforced. According to the decision, in December 2023 the tenant told the landlord it would need to terminate the lease that month and would be vacating. The landlord sent a lease termination agreement, which the tenant never signed or returned. The landlord sued in January 2024 for breach of the lease, and the tenant answered in March 2024 with affirmative defenses including estoppel. Supreme Court, Westchester County (Justice William J. Giacomo) granted the landlord summary judgment on December 20, 2024 and, after an inquest on damages, entered judgment on March 6, 2025 in the principal sum of $114,098.96. The Second Department affirmed, with costs. Under General Obligations Law section 15-301(1), a contract that requires written modifications cannot be changed orally, unless part performance is "unequivocally referable" to the oral change. The tenant pointed to a "termination payment" covering rent due to date, forfeiture of its security deposit, and leaving behind its "desks, chairs and other office equipment." The court held that the rent payment and deposit forfeiture were what the lease itself provided for, and that leaving the furniture, which the tenant said without substantiation was worth thousands of dollars, was not unequivocally referable to a termination deal. The tenant therefore raised no triable issue on part performance or estoppel. The court did not reach the parties' remaining arguments.
live-406: H&R Block Eastern Enterprises, Inc. had leased space at the Hallwood Plaza shopping center in Flint, Michigan since 1998, under a lease signed with the predecessor of the current owner, Hallwood Plaza LLC. Just after midnight on August 8, 2023, an intoxicated driver with no known connection to the tenant drove into the center, struck the H&R Block unit and started a fire that left the space unusable. In November 2023 the landlord moved the tenant into temporary space elsewhere in the center. Each side then waited for the other to repair the original unit. According to the opinion, the landlord billed full rent on both the fire-damaged unit and the temporary space while the stalemate continued, and warned that nonpayment of either would be a default. H&R Block sued on July 30, 2024, alleging breach of the lease and seeking a declaration that the landlord's refusal to rebuild amounted to constructive eviction. In October 2024, after roughly a year of paying rent on two spaces, it moved to a new permanent location. Hallwood Plaza counterclaimed, alleging that the tenant failed to maintain the sprinkler system, failed to make repairs, failed to indemnify the landlord and failed to carry required insurance. It sought repair costs, lost rent and legal fees. Both sides moved for partial summary judgment. The central question was which lease provision controls after a fire. The landlord relied on the general repair sections, under which it maintains the foundation, roof, exterior walls and common areas while the tenant maintains the interior. The tenant relied on Section 13, titled "Fire or Other Casualty." That section gives the landlord a choice after serious fire damage: terminate the lease, or keep it in force with a fair and proportionate rent abatement. If the lease continues, the section says the landlord shall rebuild the premises to the condition in which they were originally delivered, after which the tenant restores its own property and reopens. Applying the Michigan rule that a specific contract provision controls over a general one, and that section headings help identify the applicable provision, the court held that Section 13 governs and is unambiguous. The court also pointed to a sentence in the tenant-repair clause making the tenant responsible for fire-damaged HVAC equipment "notwithstanding Article 13," which would be unnecessary if the tenant already bore all interior fire repairs. On rent, the court read the lease to give the landlord three paths after a fire: terminate, continue with abated rent, or continue while providing temporary space that is treated as if it were the leased premises. None of those paths, the court said, allowed full rent on both the untenantable unit and the temporary space. The court also declined to grant the landlord summary judgment on constructive eviction, noting that the temporary space had become effectively permanent because the landlord refused to restore the original unit. Photographs in the record showed the unit in much the same condition in April 2026 as shortly after the fire. The landlord's counterclaims fared worse. The sprinkler claim failed for lack of evidence; the landlord's own representative testified that he had no records or facts indicating the system was not maintained or did not work. The repair counterclaim failed because the tenant's limited restoration duties were conditioned on the landlord rebuilding first. The indemnification counterclaim failed because the clause addresses third-party claims and because the landlord had limited its counterclaims in discovery to the sprinkler and insurance theories. The insurance counterclaim failed because the record showed the tenant carried the required general liability policy naming the landlord as an additional insured. With those four claims resolved, the court dismissed the landlord's remaining declaratory counterclaim as presenting no live controversy. The landlord's only win was the dismissal of the tenant's request for legal fees, since no statute or lease provision authorized them. For owners and tenants of multi-tenant retail property, the practical points are concrete. A casualty clause that says the landlord shall rebuild will be enforced as written even where everyday repair clauses put the interior on the tenant. A landlord that elects to continue a lease after a fire should decide promptly whether it is abating rent or providing temporary space, and should not charge for both. A landlord that wants the tenant to clear fixtures and debris before rebuilding should give the notice the lease calls for. And positions taken in discovery about the scope of a counterclaim can foreclose broader theories at summary judgment. The tenant's breach-of-contract and declaratory claims remain pending.
live-407: A second lawsuit over the Project Delta data center site was filed in Stokes County Superior Court on November 12, 2026, according to an announcement by the plaintiffs' lawyers; the complaint posted on their case page carries file number 26CV0000976-840. The plaintiffs are four organizations, the National Hairston Clan, CleanAIRE NC, the Dan River Basin Association and 7 Directions of Service, joined by 16 county residents, some of whom own land next to the site. They challenge the Stokes County Board of Commissioners' 3-2 vote on September 14, 2026, to rezone about 1,850 acres of farmland and forest along the Dan River near Walnut Cove for a data center campus, which the plaintiffs' lawyers call speculative and one of the largest AI data center campuses in the country. Public radio station WFDD identifies the developer as Engineered Land Solutions. This is the second rezoning of the same land and the second suit. Commissioners first approved a rezoning in January 2026, by the same 3-2 margin, WFDD reported. The same lawyers sued on March 12, 2026, challenging the decision's process, and in April the county voided that rezoning. In August the parties filed a joint motion for a consent judgment and the court formally voided the January rezoning. Engineered Land Solutions then reapplied, and the plaintiffs say the commissioners approved the new request against the county Planning Board's recommendation and heavy public opposition. The new complaint, as described by the plaintiffs' counsel, shifts from process to the substance of the county's decision. The plaintiffs allege the supporting analysis was rushed and deficient and appears to have been generated by AI without independent verification. They say the approval came during a drought, without a confirmed water source, without limits on on-site power generation and without a complete survey of graves and archaeological sites on the land, which they say include Saura village sites and a mapped cemetery of about 65 graves. For its part, the developer revised its proposal several times after January, in part to add stricter standards on noise, energy generation and water use, which its CEO said responded to community concerns, WFDD reported in September. Timing matters. The plaintiffs' counsel says the commissioners are set to vote on November 23 on a 15-year development agreement for Project Delta. According to the lawsuit as described by counsel, that agreement would lock in the rezoning's shortcomings, exempt the property from any future data center moratorium and commit the county to help defend the developer's interests against challenges from residents. The plaintiffs ask the court to declare the rezoning void and to block the county from relying on or implementing it. No hearing date or assigned judge has been reported, and the allegations have not been tested. A second approval after a procedural defect is now being tested on the strength of its record, and a development agreement signed while the rezoning is challenged protects only as much as the rezoning itself.
live-408: The case arises from the long-running effort to rebuild the Hill Top House Hotel in Harpers Ferry. According to the opinion, SWaN Hill Top House, LLC bought the century-old, derelict hotel in 2007 intending to reconstruct it as a luxury hotel. The project languished for more than a decade, and when SWaN began moving forward in 2019, friction developed with town residents. SWaN has said it intends to spend more than $138 million on the redevelopment. Harpers Ferry had 269 residents in the 2020 Census. In 2020 the Legislature adopted the Tourism Development District Act, W. Va. Code § 5B-1-9. It lets the state's commerce and economic development officials approve a district around a qualifying tourism project. Inside a district, the project is not subject to municipal zoning, historic preservation, noise, viewshed, lighting or land use rules, municipal regulation of alcohol sales, municipal building permitting and code enforcement, municipal licensing, or municipal taxes and fees except as the statute provides, and the town may not adopt rules that impede the project. The respondents oversee building code and land use matters instead. The project must be in a municipality of 2,000 people or fewer and have projected costs of at least $25 million, and no more than five districts may be approved statewide. The Hill Top House project is the only applicant and the only district approved since 2020. In January 2022 a group of Harpers Ferry residents and voters sued the two state officials in the Circuit Court of Kanawha County. They argued the Act is a special law barred by Article VI, sections 39 and 39a of the West Virginia Constitution, that its classifications violate equal protection principles under Article III, section 10, and that transferring control over projects in their town away from the municipality negates their rights to self-rule and to vote in municipal elections. The circuit court dismissed the complaint on March 29, 2023, and the Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed in 2024. Writing for the Supreme Court of Appeals on November 13, 2026, Justice Wooton affirmed. The court held that the Act "does not target specific people or entities" and grants benefits to up to five large projects that private entities choose to locate in small communities, so it is not a special law. It found the population and cost thresholds rationally related to the Legislature's stated goals of encouraging tourism development in small municipalities and supporting large projects. It found no constitutional right to self-rule, noting that municipalities have only the powers the Legislature grants and that the Legislature may modify or withdraw them, and held that the Act does not affect anyone's right to vote. The court declined to decide whether an earlier Jefferson County ruling against a citizens' group barred the claims. Chief Justice Bunn dissented and reserved the right to file a separate opinion; one justice was disqualified, and a judge sat by temporary assignment.
live-409: The Westborough Shopping Center on Route 9 in Westborough, Massachusetts, is scheduled for a foreclosure auction on December 8, 2026 at 11 a.m. in the Staples parking lot, MassLive reported, citing the listing by auctioneer Paul E.
