live-410: F-Star Socorro, L.P. and affiliated companies filed Chapter 11 petitions in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas on November 4, 2025, according to the ElevenFlo case summary and the court docket. The group, which developed a Ritz-Carlton project in Arizona and also owned industrial and commercial property around El Paso, filed amid a liquidity crisis and a dispute with lender Madison Realty Capital. The debtors allege Madison stopped funding construction and manufactured defaults on the Arizona project; Madison had scheduled a foreclosure on the Arizona collateral. The Texas side of the business, which the docket calls the Commercial Property Debtors, is now on its own track. On September 25, 2026, the court authorized the sale of four El Paso County properties to Madison through a $90 million credit bid, subject to closing conditions, and separately approved a $180 million replacement financing facility from Farallon along with the use of cash collateral. On November 13 the court conditionally approved the disclosure statement for the Commercial Property Debtors' plan, which lets voting begin and leaves final approval for a combined hearing with confirmation. Under the plan, the $120 million senior mortgage DIP facility and the $60 million mezzanine DIP facility would become exit loans dollar for dollar, with no cash payment. Allowed general unsecured claims would be paid in full from a claims reserve, without postpetition interest; insider and affiliate claims would receive senior interests in a plan trust, and parent equity would receive junior interests. Funding the reserve and meeting the exit-financing conditions are among the conditions for the plan to take effect. Ballots and confirmation objections are due December 7, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central Time, and the combined hearing is set for December 16. A dispute over the clawback guaranty in the September sale order is set for hearing on November 19. Conditional approval is a procedural step, so objections to the disclosure statement and the plan remain open for the combined hearing.
live-411: The Pennhurst property covers about 124.6 acres at 1205 Commonwealth Drive in East Vincent Township, Chester County, in the township's Industrial Mixed Use District. Penn Hurst Holdings DE LLC applied for conditional-use approval for data center buildings, an office building and related improvements. The Philadelphia Inquirer described the plan in May as 1.9 million square feet in three two-story buildings, with a power generation and battery storage field. On May 21, 2026, the township's Board of Supervisors unanimously rejected the application. According to MyChesCo, which cited reporting by Spring-Ford Press, the supervisors concluded that the proposal did not qualify as a planned commercial development under the zoning ordinance. The Inquirer reported that the board found the application did not fully meet the applicable zoning criteria, and that the developer's lawyer said an appeal would follow. Penn Hurst Holdings filed its land use appeal in the Chester County Court of Common Pleas in June, arguing that the supervisors misread the ordinance's provisions on permitted uses, zoning standards and transferable development rights. Two sets of would-be parties asked to join the case on the township's side: the owners of an adjoining farm of about 130 acres, who cited their downhill position, stormwater runoff, deeded access rights over roads serving the property and effects on their livestock and crops; and East Vincent Advocacy, a resident-led 501(c)(4) nonprofit that reports more than 950 members, about 80 percent of them township residents. The developer argued that the farm owners had not formally established party status in the township proceedings and that a group owning no property in the township could not stand in for affected owners. The township's solicitor supported the farm owners' request, and the advocacy group noted that it had held party status in the township hearings. At a hearing on November 10, 2026, Judge Nicole Forzato granted both requests. "I do believe there is a direct, substantial interest," she said, according to MyChesCo. The ruling decides only who may participate; it does not address whether the project complies with the zoning ordinance, and the application remains denied. The developer asked for 30 days to file an amended brief, and the judge directed counsel to propose a briefing schedule by November 18. No further hearing date has been set.
live-412: The Exton Square Mall is a nearly 1 million-square-foot enclosed center that closed this summer, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported. live-413: Water's Edge at Wind Gap, LLC seeks to redevelop its 51-acre property in Moore Township, currently a golf course, into an industrial development with two warehouses, according to the Commonwealth Court's opinion. The zoning ordinance requires that 60% of existing woodlands be preserved, and the developer asked for a dimensional variance to preserve only 55%. The Zoning Hearing Board denied the developer's preliminary land development application in a March 17, 2023 decision. The Northampton County Court of Common Pleas affirmed on March 4, 2024 on three grounds: a steep slope provision, a requirement to build traffic improvements to Jones Road, and the variance. In an opinion filed December 31, 2025, the Commonwealth Court affirmed on the steep slope requirement, reversed the requirement for Jones Road improvements, and found the developer had shown unnecessary hardship because the woodland rule conflicts with another provision of the ordinance on this property. It remanded for the Board to decide whether the variance would alter the character of the neighborhood or be contrary to the public interest. On remand the Board found that the total woodland area is 4.18 acres, that the developer proposes to disturb approximately 45%, or 1.88 acres, and that the 5% variance accounts for approximately 0.21 acres of additional disturbance. It found that removing those large, mature trees would take away a visual buffer in a neighborhood that is almost entirely residential. In an unreported memorandum opinion by Judge Matthew S. Wolf filed November 16, 2026, the court affirmed. The developer argued that the findings lacked record support, that its engineer testified the development would improve landscape screening, and that the property is in an industrial zone. The court pointed to the developer's own plans, which show the woodlands screening adjacent residential lots, and to the engineer's testimony that the existing trees are at least 40 to 50 feet tall. The Board was not obligated to credit the engineer's testimony that the variance would allow sufficient screening, the court said, and the developer's failure to satisfy each variance factor required the Board to deny the request.
live-414: The City of Umatilla and Umatilla County filed a petition on Nov. 11, 2026, in Umatilla County Circuit Court seeking to compel the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality to resume the permitting process for data centers, the Hermiston Herald reported. The filing responds to Gov. Tina Kotek's Oct. 9 direction that DEQ pause the processing and issuance of air and water permits for new or expanded data center facilities until July 1, 2027. According to the Hermiston Herald, the petitioners say DEQ "has a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty" to process pending National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit applications in a timely manner. Elkhorn Media Group reported that the filing argues DEQ must review pending applications on their individual merit, and that the city and county ask the court to compel the agency to do so and complete the process with reasonable promptness. The filing claims the pause has already caused the city to lose approximately $2.5 million per year in contracted payments on completed but unoccupied data center buildings, the Hermiston Herald reported. It also says the suspension jeopardizes future bonding revenues pledged to the city's $19.8 million police station bond and threatens to drive away more than $1.2 billion in additional private investment. Neither report includes a response from DEQ or the governor's office to the petition.
live-415: A federal lawsuit filed to stop construction of a 22-story tower at the Marina Safeway in San Francisco no longer names the developer, The San Francisco Standard reported on Nov. 13, 2026. In an amended complaint filed that Wednesday, Nov. 11, neighbors and two advocacy groups removed Align Real Estate, Safeway and parent company Albertsons as "real parties in interest." The city and PG&E remain defendants. The Standard reported that the case is before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín. According to the Standard, the amended complaint accuses city officials of "deliberate indifference" to the risk of toxic exposure from the construction site, and the plaintiffs still seek to force PG&E to investigate and clean up any contamination beneath the site, where the utility used to operate a steam plant. The plaintiffs also claim that the Safeway building, constructed in 1959, has been listed on the Register of Historical Resources since 2015, which the Standard reported would disqualify the project from fast-track approval under AB 2011. The city's approval letter said the building was determined ineligible for the Register in 2015 and in 2020, the Standard reported, and the developer's attorneys argued in an Oct. 27 letter to planners that the building was never listed. Align told the Standard it is moving forward with 848 homes; the new building's ground floor is slated to have a 63,000-square-foot Safeway. KQED reported in September 2026 that the suit was filed in federal court in San Francisco and named Align, the city's Planning and Public Health departments, PG&E and Albertsons. NBC Bay Area reported that it was filed by the YesAND Foundation and Neighborhoods United SF along with several Marina residents. The Standard reported on Nov. 1 that the developer's attorneys had moved to dismiss.
live-416: According to the opinion, FWREF Nashville Airport, LLC agreed in October 2019 to sell an existing Hilton-branded hotel near the Nashville airport to UNI Nashville Airport Hotel, LLC for $79,000,000, with a $1,750,000 earnest money deposit and a January 3, 2020 closing date. The agreement recited that fluctuating land values, the economy, governmental regulations and the market for real estate loans made the seller's damages from a failed closing extremely difficult to ascertain, and that the earnest money was a reasonable estimate the seller could retain as liquidated damages. The parties then signed twenty-four amendments, each adding earnest money deemed earned by the seller and non-refundable, extending the closing date or deposit deadlines, and ratifying the agreement. The price rose to $82,125,000, the agreement was assigned to SH Nashville, LLC, and the deposits reached $18,917,500. The purchaser learned on October 21, 2020 that a new Hilton-branded hotel on airport grounds was scheduled to open in late 2023, which it said was a surprise. It was unable to close by January 11, 2021, and the seller gave notice that the agreement had automatically terminated. The purchaser sued on April 22, 2022 for a declaration that the seller's retention of the earnest money was an unenforceable penalty, and the seller counterclaimed for breach of contract and attorneys' fees. The Davidson County Chancery Court stayed discovery and granted the seller summary judgment. The Court of Appeals reversed, reasoning that contract language stating the amount was a reasonable estimate was not sufficient. In an opinion by Justice Dwight E. Tarwater, joined by four other justices, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals. It held that the parties' agreement creates a presumption of enforceability and that the burden of showing a penalty lies with the party seeking to avoid the provision. The court rejected the purchaser's argument that the aggregate sum was unreasonable on its face, noting that the deposits grew incrementally with each extension and that the seller lost the ability to seek out other purchasers each time. It found no abuse of discretion in the denial of discovery, including discovery the purchaser sought for an economic duress defense, and upheld the dismissal of the purchaser's conversion claim. The case was remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.
live-417: The case was decided on the pleadings, and the appeals court took the facts from Jackson & Jackson, LLC's counterclaim and treated them as true for the appeal. The property is approximately nine acres with improvements at 5670 West Alexandria Road in Madison Township, Butler County, Ohio. The opinion says the zoning does not permit commercial uses, but that over the years the property was used for a variety of commercial functions. Jackson & Jackson, which provides commercial electrical and emergency response services, bought it on November 22, 2021 for $270,000 and began parking trucks and equipment there and using existing office space. On or about May 9, 2023, the office of the Zoning Inspector for Butler County served a notice of zoning violation. On August 17, 2023, the Butler County Board of Zoning Appeals denied the company's variance application. The Butler County Zoning Inspector then sued in the Butler County Court of Common Pleas for an injunction, and the company counterclaimed against the inspector and the Butler County Board of Commissioners. The County moved to dismiss, arguing that the Section 1983 claim was filed more than two years after the company took title, that all of the claims had to be brought as a mandamus action to compel appropriation proceedings, and that the company failed to exhaust administrative remedies. The trial court dismissed all of the counterclaims. The Twelfth District affirmed in part and reversed in part on November 16, 2026. It held that the Section 1983 takings claim was subject to the four-year limitations period in R.C. 2305.09(E), and that the company was not required to appeal the zoning board's decision before challenging the constitutionality of the zoning resolution. It upheld dismissal of the count that asked for a declaration of a taking without requesting just compensation. On remand, Count Two remains dismissed, and Counts One and Three may be pursued.
live-418: According to the opinion, the Township of Parkman conveyed a 0.2596-acre piece of its public square to BTE Properties, L.L.C. on January 22, 2018. The deed said the conveyance was subject to a restriction from the original grant of the square to the township, under which the land was to be used as a public square or commons unencumbered by any building or structure. BTE then consolidated nearby properties into a 2.6298-acre commercial lot that included the parcel. On December 12, 2023, ABC Development L.L.C. agreed to buy land containing the parcel. The opinion says the deed restriction created an exception to title, and on March 1, 2024 the two companies amended the purchase agreement to make the purchase contingent on that exception. On April 16, 2024 they filed a quiet title complaint in the Geauga County Court of Common Pleas asking that the 1843 use restriction be declared invalid and unenforceable. The trial court granted summary judgment to the township. The Eleventh District affirmed on November 16, 2026. BTE argued that the restriction bound only the township trustees and their successors in office, not later private holders, and that the township waived or abandoned it. The majority held that the township did not waive or abandon the restriction by selling the parcel where the deed specifically incorporated it and BTE had actual notice. The dissenting judge wrote that he would reverse and enter judgment for BTE.

live-420: The Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania on November 17, 2026 affirmed an Allegheny County Common Pleas Court order overruling IBIS Kennywood, LLC's preliminary objections to a condemnation notice from the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. According to the opinion, the owner's property in West Mifflin is improved by a large regional shopping center with a grocery store, a gas station with a convenience store, and retail shops. The trial court overruled the objections on October 1, 2021; the Commonwealth Court later vacated that order and sent the case back for the trial court to decide whether the plot plans complied. On September 19, 2024, the trial court again overruled the objections and referred the matter to a Board of Viewers for an assessment of damages. On appeal, the owner argued that the plot plans failed to show the location of the temporary construction access, the temporary and permanent utility relocation easements, the design of the main access driveway and the power pole relocation easement. The Commission responded that its plot plans fully complied with the Code and that design changes made as the plans moved to final form did not change the type or extent of the taking. The court agreed with the trial court that the plans show the area of the partial taking and concluded that the Commission complied with the notice requirement.
live-421: A Colorado state court has placed Panorama Corporate Center in Centennial in receivership, BusinessDen reported on Nov. 18, 2026. live-422: A federal judge has turned down a request by the incoming Pulaski County judge to become a party to a data center developer's challenge to a county ordinance. live-423: The Business Court of Texas, Fourth Division, on November 17, 2026 denied a motion to dismiss filed by San Antonio Housing Facility Corporation, which the opinion describes as a nonprofit public-facility corporation affiliated with the San Antonio Housing Authority, known as Opportunity Home. According to the opinion, the housing corporation and Cadence McShane Construction Company LLC are parties to a joint venture agreement for construction of Horizon Pointe, an affordable-housing apartment development in San Antonio. Cadence sued on August 17, 2026, seeking declarations about the allocation of project funds and the housing corporation's rights to inspect Cadence's records, and pleaded that more than $5 million is in controversy. A few weeks later, the opinion says, the housing corporation sued Cadence in the 57th Judicial District Court of Bexar County for fraud and breach of contract, seeking $4,999,999.99 in contractual damages. Cadence pleads that the Horizon Pointe partnership agreed to pay $45 million for the project and that the housing corporation has accused it of taking more than $7.7 million in profits, more than federal law permitted. The housing corporation argued that the value of the case is set by its own Bexar County petition. The court disagreed, writing that the housing corporation "has it backwards" and that jurisdiction is decided on the pleadings in the suit before it. Even accepting the housing corporation's valuation of Cadence's first two requests at $4,999,999.99, the court said, the record-inspection declarations are separate requests and there was no evidence they are worth less than two cents. Each side accused the other of forum shopping: the housing corporation said Cadence filed minutes after mediation failed, and Cadence said the housing corporation capped its damages one cent below the minimum. The court said neither argument affected its analysis, and that neither party had raised whether the Business Court has dominant jurisdiction over the district court.
live-424: Sachem Capital Corp. reported in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, dated November 16, 2026, that a group of investors who purport to hold interests in IRG Master Holdings, LLC and related entities filed a complaint on November 3, 2026 against the company and certain of its affiliated entities in the Superior Court of California for the County of Los Angeles, Case No. 26STCV34893. live-425: Clark County commissioners voted on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, with no discussion, to appeal the Badlands tax judgment to the Nevada Supreme Court, KTNV reported in an article posted October 21, which said the appeal had not yet been filed. KSNV reported on October 29 that the county formally filed its notice of appeal that week; neither outlet gives the filing day. live-426: A request to rezone roughly 1,402 acres in Lenox Township, in eastern Macomb County, to light industrial use is on hold after a judge issued a restraining order, The Detroit News reported. According to The Detroit News, Macomb County Circuit Judge Michael Servitto issued the order on the grounds that the township did not give proper notice and withheld information from the public. live-427: Burlington Coat Factory of Puerto Rico LLC sued Empresas Puertorriqueñas de Desarrollo Inc., its landlord at Mayagüez Mall, on Nov. 16 in federal court in Puerto Rico, according to News is My Business. Burlington seeks the $1 million allowance, additional damages, interest, costs and attorneys' fees. live-428: The Des Moines Register, in a story republished by Yahoo News, reported that Project 1551 filed a lawsuit on Sept. 28 in Polk County court to break JCPenney's lease at Valley West Mall. Threshold Capital, which announced Sept. 29 the closing of its purchase of the 856,000-square-foot mall and its 58-acre site, is redeveloping the property through Project 1551. The developer argued it is no longer possible to operate the mall and that the lease signed in 1974 is an unreasonable obstacle to redevelopment. live-429: The Texas Court of Appeals, Third District, at Austin affirmed a Williamson County district court judgment requiring the City of Jarrell to perform a 2008 development agreement with BE Theon East Partnership No. 3, Ltd. According to the opinion, the agreement concerned an undeveloped 24.4-acre property that BE Theon owned near the intersection of Ronald Reagan Boulevard and Interstate 35. BE Theon agreed to let the city annex the property, and the city agreed to provide sufficient water and wastewater capacity and approach mains within three years after the completion of Ronald Reagan Boulevard at its intersection with the interstate. The city passed an annexation ordinance in 2009. The opinion says BE Theon sent the city a letter in August 2019 with the capacities it considered sufficient, the city did not respond, and the city has not provided water or wastewater services to the property. BE Theon sued in January 2020 seeking specific performance or, alternatively, damages. In November 2025 the trial court granted BE Theon's motion for summary judgment and ordered the city to invite and award bids for construction of water and wastewater utilities to the property with capacities no less than those in the August 2019 letter. On appeal the city argued the agreement was void from the start, that the judgment violated the separation of powers, and that the proper remedy was disannexation. The court held the city had not preserved its reserved-powers or separation-of-powers arguments because it did not raise them in response to the summary judgment motion. It concluded the agreement's terms were sufficiently certain to create a binding contract, noting that the parties had performed for over a decade as though a valid contract existed and that BE Theon used the city's Unified Development Code to calculate capacities. The court also rejected disannexation as the exclusive remedy, saying the case does not involve involuntary annexation, and held that Subsection 212.172(j) of the Local Government Code allows specific performance for a party with a valid contract under Subsection 212.172(c). It found no fact issue on when the road intersection was completed.
live-430: The case arises from a Labor Law and negligence action over injuries a worker sustained in a fall from a ladder while doing electrical work at a commercial property owned by Huron Group, Inc. According to the decision, Huron brought a third-party action against Ellicott Development Company, which was the worker's employer and the property management company Huron contracted with to maintain the building. Ellicott counterclaimed for contractual indemnification under the parties' management agreement. The court noted that when the agreement was made, the same individual was president and majority owner of both companies. Supreme Court, Erie County, in an order entered April 2, 2025, granted Ellicott summary judgment on its counterclaim and denied Huron's motion for summary judgment dismissing the counterclaim. The Fourth Department unanimously modified the order by denying Ellicott summary judgment on the counterclaim, and otherwise affirmed. The court concluded the management agreement falls within the plain language of General Obligations Law § 5-322.1 (1), which voids agreements tied to building construction, repair or maintenance that indemnify a party against liability for bodily injury resulting from its own negligence. But the clause is not automatically void: the statute's prohibition does not apply without a finding of negligence against the party seeking indemnity. Because triable issues of fact remain about Ellicott's negligence, the court said it could not yet determine whether the provision violates the statute. The panel declined to adopt the interpretation in Westport Ins. Co. v Altertec Energy Conservation, LLC, a 2011 Second Department decision, saying the statute's language is neither doubtful nor ambiguous.
live-431: The Arkansas Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of a challenge to the Benton County Planning Board's 20 March 2024 decision approving a site plan for Contentment on Beaver Lake, LLC to operate what the opinion calls a "glampground" or "glamping site" on 209 acres near Beaver Lake. live-436: The Texas Court of Appeals for the Fifth District at Dallas affirmed, in a memorandum opinion filed November 16, 2026, an order appointing a receiver over two apartment complexes in Dallas. According to the opinion, FS CREIT Finance WF-2 LLC and FS Rialto 2021-FL3 Issuer, Ltd. hold first-priority liens securing loans exceeding $53 million against the Bella Vida and CDMX apartment complexes. The loans matured on September 9, 2025, the appellants did not pay, and the loan documents authorized the lenders to seek a receiver upon default. The appellants are Nitya Capital, LLC, Nitya AM, LLC, KPM Multifamily, LLC, The Residence at Bella Vida, LLC and The Residence at CDMX Apartments, LLC, along with the properties in rem. Before the loans matured, the City of Dallas had sued alleging numerous health-and-safety violations at the properties, and the trial court granted temporary injunctive relief requiring remediation. live-437: The Louisiana Court of Appeal, Second Circuit, on November 18, 2026 affirmed a judgment of the First Judicial District Court for Caddo Parish that upheld the Shreveport City Council's approval of a special use permit for a proposed data center at Resilient Technology Park, off Greenwood Road. According to the opinion, Bohler Engineering applied to the Shreveport/Caddo Metropolitan Planning Commission on October 17, 2025 for a special use permit covering seven buildings of 400,000 square feet each on approximately 254 acres zoned light industrial. live-439: The Texas Court of Appeals for the Fifth District at Dallas, in a November 13, 2026 memorandum opinion by Justice Emily Miskel, affirmed in part, reversed in part, rendered judgment in part and remanded a dispute between the City of McKinney, its Board of Adjustment and Cowtown Redi Mix, Inc. over a concrete batch plant. The appeal came from the 401st Judicial District Court in Collin County. According to the opinion, Cowtown built the plant under city-approved site plans and permits. The city enacted an ordinance on April 16, 2019 rezoning the area, which made the plant a legally nonconforming use, and an ordinance on November 5, 2019 setting procedures to amortize and terminate nonconforming uses. It later ordered Cowtown to cease operating the plant after a seven-year amortization period, in an order sent on or about September 30, 2020. A 2022 amendment to the city's noise regulations barred operating power equipment in certain areas between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. On competing summary-judgment motions, the trial court declared that Cowtown had a vested right under Chapter 245 of the Local Government Code, that the rezoning ordinance was void for lack of notice and that a noise provision was unconstitutionally vague, while rejecting Cowtown's retroactivity and settlement-agreement claims. The appeals court reversed the vested-rights declaration and rendered judgment that Cowtown take nothing on its Chapter 245 claims, relying on its precedent that "the operation of a business is not a 'project' as a matter of law." Cowtown had argued its situation was unique, saying it incurred $3 million in construction costs for a single-use facility that would have to be torn down; the court said those distinctions did not change the rule. On notice, the court found that neither side conclusively proved whether the city sent the notice required by section 211.007 and remanded that claim because fact issues remain. The court overruled Cowtown's two cross-issues. It held Cowtown had not conclusively established that the Board of Adjustment's order is an unconstitutional retroactive law, noting the city gave Cowtown a seven-year period to continue its nonconforming use. On the settlement agreement, the opinion says the trial court rejected the claim in part because Cowtown was not a party to that agreement. The court also reversed the declaration that section 70-121 of the noise ordinance is unconstitutionally vague, rendered judgment denying that claim, and reversed and remanded the attorney's fee award.

live-441: The Michigan Court of Appeals on November 18, 2026 affirmed Muskegon Circuit Court rulings in a dispute between Northern Biomedical Research, Inc., a tenant, and its landlord, NBR Investment Properties, LLC. The opinion is unpublished and per curiam. The trial court had granted summary disposition to Northern Biomedical on liability and said the landlord must complete the sale of the property at the appraised purchase price. According to the opinion, the landlord leased 65,000 square feet of the property to Northern Biomedical, and the lease gave the tenant an option to purchase the property, exercisable by written notice at any time during the term when the lease was not in default, at a price set by appraisal. Northern Biomedical exercised the option by letter on July 1, 2021. The appraisal found the best use of the property was a warehouse, reduced the value by $1.1 million as an estimated cost of removing the laboratory, and reached a net appraised value of $8.87 million. The landlord conveyed its dissatisfaction and asked to extend the closing date to obtain a separate appraisal; Northern Biomedical refused, and the landlord refused to close. Northern Biomedical sued, and the landlord counterclaimed, alleging among other things that the tenant assigned the option without consent, to 1210 Pontaluna, LLC, and paid rent late. The appeals court held that Northern Biomedical was not in default when it exercised the option. It found the tenant's earlier sharing of an unsigned copy of the lease with a third party breached the confidentiality provision, but concluded the tenant was not materially "in default" because the lease tied default to notice from the landlord and a chance to cure. It held the appraisal was a condition subsequent to the option's exercise, that the assignment may have breached the lease but not substantially, and that the landlord had not shown "qualified" appraiser meant anything other than licensed and in good standing. It also rejected the landlord's due-process challenge to specific performance. On the tenant's cross-appeal, the court held that Northern Biomedical's rental of another space was a consequential damage, which the lease waived for both parties, and that the trial court did not err in considering expenses the tenant avoided because the purchase was not completed.

live-444: The Delaware Supreme Court on November 16, 2026 affirmed the Court of Chancery's judgment in a dispute over loans secured against three properties in Bakersfield and one in Fresno, California. In a short order, the court, sitting en banc, said the judgment should be affirmed for the reasons stated in the Court of Chancery's April 8, 2026 post-trial opinion. According to the Chancery opinion, NICbyte and Wishon Row LLC formed a joint venture, NIC Wise RE LLC, on June 6, 2022, with NICbyte owning 95 percent of the membership interests. BW Industries, which owned and managed Wishon Row, sold the properties to NIC Wise subsidiaries, and NIC Wise then leased the properties back. The opinion says the joint venture agreement precluded Wishon Row from entering into a financing or encumbering the properties without NICbyte's consent. It says Bitwise issued StarTop a $10 million note on January 13, 2023, that StarTop closed on a $5 million loan on March 15, 2023, and that the total loan amounts were aggregated to $20.4 million. NICbyte, NIC Wise and four subsidiaries sued on June 20, 2023, seeking declarations that the StarTop loan documents are void and unenforceable, and StarTop counterclaimed to enforce the loans. The Chancery court wrote that before trial it had found StarTop, through its principals, engaged in spoliation of evidence, deleting thousands of documents. After a two-day trial, it found that StarTop intentionally destroyed evidence and imposed an adverse inference that there was no apparent authority to enter into the loans; it also found no actual authority. StarTop argued that Section 6.1 of the joint venture agreement left it "fully protected" in not inquiring further into that authority, and the court rejected the argument. The court held the plaintiffs entitled to a declaration that the loan documents are invalid and cancelled as they relate to any right to enforce against them or the properties, granted permanent injunctive relief, and ordered StarTop to pay $423,781 in fees and expenses tied to the spoliation motion.
live-445: 73 Dun One, Inc. is a tenant under a lease it signed in May 1994 for premises on a commercial property in Berlin Township, New Jersey, where it operated a franchise then known as Dunkin' Donuts. The lease gave the tenant a right of first refusal to purchase the premises on the landlord's receipt of a bona fide written offer from a third party, and required it to pay its share of the real estate taxes. The tenant and the property's other tenants were later notified that the leases and management had been assigned to Gould Holdings, and Gould Holdings then purchased the property. The tenant sued for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, specific performance and unjust enrichment. The defendants counterclaimed over underpaid real estate taxes; according to the opinion, the tenant continued to pay only $1,102.87 a month from 2003 through a portion of 2023, and in July 2023 it stopped making payments to Gould Holdings. The Chancery Division in Camden County granted summary judgment to the defendants and dismissed the complaint, and on July 22, 2025 entered an order fixing the taxes and prejudgment interest owed: $13,029.48 for 2023, $24,020.81 for 2024 and $8,408.09 to bring 2025 current. In an unpublished per curiam opinion decided November 19, 2026, the Appellate Division affirmed the summary judgment. It held the right of first refusal is triggered only by a bona fide written offer to purchase the premises, that the provision applies only to the premises and not the property as a whole, and that no bona fide offer was made for the premises alone. The court noted that the parties cited, and its own research found, no controlling authority directly addressing the issue. On the tax award, the court said there is no genuine dispute that the tenant must pay outstanding real estate taxes and prejudgment interest, but the record did not show which lease provision the trial court relied on or how it calculated the amounts. It remanded for the limited purpose of having the trial court make findings of fact and conclusions of law on the taxes and interest for 2023 to 2025, and did not retain jurisdiction.

live-452: The Appellate Division, Fourth Department, decided the case on November 20, 2026, in an original proceeding under EDPL 207. Target Corporation, which the court says operates a retail store in Irondequoit just west of the site of the shopping center once known as the Medley Centre and the Irondequoit Mall, asked the court to annul COMIDA's determination condemning certain of its contractual rights. The respondents are COMIDA and One Medley Center, LLC. The opinion says COMIDA sent notice of the public hearing, with an accompanying letter, by certified mail and Federal Express to the address Target had given the tax assessor for billing purposes. No one appeared for Target at the hearing, and the only people who spoke supported the condemnation. The court noted it is undisputed that the notice itself did not carry the statutory warning that a later challenge may rest only on issues raised at the hearing, but the accompanying letter did, in bold, underlined capital letters. Target argued that the notice was insufficient because it did not state the public use to be served or describe the property rights sought, and did not include the warning. The court rejected those arguments, holding that section 202 requires notice of the hearing's purpose, time, date and location, not a description of the project, and that the notice and letter together were sufficient to give the warning; it noted that Target cited no authority for disregarding the letter. WXXI News reported in May 2026 that the dispute concerns a reciprocal easement agreement, that Target asserted in court filings that the condemnation was improper and done in bad faith, and that COMIDA sought dismissal on the ground that Target had the opportunity to raise objections at the condemnation hearing and did not. The Fourth Department did not reach Target's substantive contentions, because Target did not appear at the hearing, and it confirmed the determination without costs.

live-454: The Nevada Supreme Court's order of affirmance, filed November 20, 2026, concerns a vacant parking lot on the Las Vegas Strip that Siegel LV North Strip Tolleson LLC purchased subject to a Parking Easement Agreement (PEA). The order says the PEA grants the owner of the adjacent property, EC 215 Las Vegas LLC (called Silver City in the order), and its patrons access to certain portions of the lot. Silver City owns a strip mall with retail and restaurant tenants. Siegel put up a chain-link fence around the lot's perimeter and installed gates requiring Silver City's driving patrons to enter a QR code to park for free. Silver City sued, alleging the fence and gate system violated the PEA, and moved for a preliminary injunction requiring its removal. After an evidentiary hearing, the district court granted the injunction on July 10, 2024. It denied reconsideration on April 28, 2025, but clarified that Siegel was only required to remove the portion of the system subject to the PEA. On appeal, Siegel argued that the PEA does not guarantee unobstructed access and that the evidence did not support a finding of irreparable harm. The Supreme Court held that Siegel had not shown reversible error: the district court had determined only that Silver City's interpretation was more persuasive for purposes of preliminary relief, and Siegel's argument that the PEA affords some access did not establish that the system is consistent with the access rights granted. On irreparable harm, Silver City said leaving the system in place could jeopardize its contractual relationships with tenants, including its obligations to provide their customers parking access; the court said such harm extends beyond calculable lost revenue and that Siegel identified no specific alternative modifications the district court overlooked. It rejected Siegel's reliance on crime and homelessness risks because Siegel bought the lot fully aware of those concerns, and affirmed.
live-455: Kings Mountain Land Development Partners, LLC sued the Catawba Indian Nation on October 3, 2024, alleging continuing trespass, recurring trespass, conversion, breach of a stormwater easement, breach of a temporary construction easement and unfair and deceptive trade practices, and seeking injunctive relief. According to the opinion, which treats the complaint's allegations as true only for purposes of the appeal, the tribe bought a 17-acre parcel from the company in 2018 and opened a temporary casino there in July 2021, and the company later conveyed a second tract to the tribe for use as a surface parking lot. The parties signed a temporary construction easement agreement, an easement agreement and an agreement of restrictive covenants, in which the tribe agreed not to build a parking structure or garage on that tract for twenty-five years. Each agreement contains a limited waiver of the tribe's sovereign immunity for any claim "directly or indirectly related to" the agreement or the transactions it contemplates. Carolina Journal reported that the company sued over disagreements about the tribe's use of easements to build the casino and a parking deck. The tribe moved to dismiss every claim except the two easement claims, arguing the rest were barred by sovereign immunity except to the extent they relate directly or indirectly to the easements and fall within its waiver. On July 9, 2025, the trial court dismissed each claim, in whole or in part, except the claims pertaining to the easements. It concluded that a claim is not related to an agreement unless it is based on the agreement's express rights or restrictions, and it found that only eighteen allegations in the complaint could support a claim within the waivers. The company appealed. Judge Toby Hampson wrote for the majority, Carolina Journal reported. The court held the appeal could proceed although the order dismissed the complaint only in part, saying it was bound by an earlier Court of Appeals decision that the grant of a motion to dismiss based on sovereign or governmental immunity is immediately appealable. On the merits, the court said nothing in the plain language of the waivers requires a claim to be based on the express rights or restrictions in an agreement, and that the trial court's order did not decide what claims, if any, fall within the waivers. It vacated the order and remanded for the trial court to interpret the complete language of the waivers. The tribe had argued that federal law requires a court to construe the waiver strictly in its favor; the majority said its review followed state law principles of contract interpretation because the agreements were made with a private actor. Chief Judge Dillon concurred. Judge Tyson concurred in part and dissented in part, writing that the trial court properly dismissed the company's tort and statutory claims, that the company is not a sovereign and had not shown a right to immediate appellate review, and that the appeal should be dismissed. The dissent notes that the tribe's counterclaim for unjust enrichment remains before the trial court. Carolina Journal described the ruling as a 2-1 decision.

live-457: The Palo Alto Daily Post reported that Simon Property Group filed a lawsuit against the companies behind Zaytinya, a Mediterranean restaurant that opened at Stanford Shopping Center in December 2025. live-458: The Appellate Division, in an unpublished per curiam opinion by Judges Natali and Jablonski, affirmed a September 12, 2025 order of the Law Division in Monmouth County dismissing the complaint of Planet Shred Records Management LLC and Planet Shred LLC with prejudice. The complaint asserted claims for declaratory relief, breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, wrongful eviction, and violations of the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act. The trial court concluded those claims were barred by a September 27, 2024 consent judgment entered in an earlier landlord-tenant action. According to the opinion, the earlier action sought $101,598.96 in additional rent, late charges, and interest. Under the consent judgment, the tenants agreed to pay a reduced sum of $51,032.28 and to vacate by March 31, and the defendants obtained a judgment for possession with removal not to be carried out before April 1, 2025. The tenants filed the new suit in July 2025. The tenants argued on appeal that the consent judgment was entered under duress and economic coercion. The court was unpersuaded, holding that the consent judgment unequivocally operated as an accord and satisfaction because it resolved the parties' known claims arising out of the tenancy. It also said the complaint and the motion record did not plead facts sufficient to establish duress or economic coercion, a breach of the implied covenant, or a Consumer Fraud Act violation, and that repleading would not cure those deficiencies.
live-459: The Hawaii Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Ginoza, reviewed the dismissal of a suit by Haleiwa Town Center, LLC, which leases the Haleiwa Town Center from the Trustees of the Estate of Bernice Pauahi Bishop, also known as Kamehameha Schools. According to the opinion, the tenant's First Amended Complaint alleges that the landlord tried to shift its kuleana access obligations onto the tenant, made conflicting representations about whether a historic lane was on the tenant's property, and encroached on the tenant's property during construction. The only lease provision the complaint relies on is the quiet enjoyment provision. The Supreme Court said the trial court was required to accept the allegations as true and held that the complaint asserts viable claims for breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. The Supreme Court held that the tenant's unfair competition claim was properly dismissed. It also held that the Circuit Court should have allowed the tenant to file its proposed Second Amended Complaint, which adds factual allegations supporting the two surviving claims. On fees, the court held that because there is no prevailing party at this stage, the Intermediate Court of Appeals erred by vacating the Circuit Court's denial of the landlord's request for fees and costs and by awarding the landlord fees and costs on appeal. The court vacated the appeals court's judgment in part and remanded the case to the Circuit Court.
live-460: According to the opinion, the petitioners had operated a scrap metal recycling business on the Van Nuys parcel since at least April 2017 under a lease that is not in the appellate record. In September 2023, Metro sent them written notice of its intent to acquire the premises to construct the East San Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit Project. The owner conveyed the property to Metro by a grant deed recorded on January 23, 2025. Metro then sent three successive 30-day notices to vacate and, on October 6, 2025, filed an unlawful detainer action seeking immediate possession. Its complaint alleged that any leasehold interest ended when Metro acquired the premises for public use. Three days later, Metro filed an eminent domain complaint to acquire improvements located on the premises. The tenants demurred. The trial court, Judge Shirley K. Watkins, overruled the demurrer, and the tenants petitioned the Court of Appeal for a writ of mandate. They argued that the Eminent Domain Law requires a condemning entity to secure possession through that law, that the statute ending a lease when leased property is acquired for public use does not terminate a lease so as to authorize an unlawful detainer action, and that Metro had to follow the prejudgment possession procedure. The Court of Appeal rejected each argument and denied the petition. It concluded that the trial court correctly rejected the claim of exclusive eminent domain jurisdiction over premises acquired by purchase, that Metro's purchase extinguished the tenants' possessory interest as well as their duty to pay rent, and that the prejudgment possession statute does not apply where the acquisition occurred without the need for an eminent domain action. The court noted that the tenants did not argue their lease contained provisions displacing the Eminent Domain Law, and that their demurrer did not seek dismissal for deficient notice under the California Relocation Assistance Act. The court vacated its temporary stay of the unlawful detainer proceedings, effective when the opinion becomes final, and awarded Metro its costs.
live-461: The First Department's November 24, 2026 decision reviewed a judgment of Supreme Court, New York County (Justice Lyle E. Frank), entered October 8, 2025, awarding plaintiff Escrown LLC $587,238.40 against Arepas NYC Corp. and its co-defendants. The court unanimously modified the judgment to vacate the award of prejudgment interest in the amount of $126,186.48, remanded for further proceedings, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. It noted that the defendants had not filed a notice of appeal from the September 17, 2024 order granting summary judgment on liability, but said that in any event the trial court properly found the defendants liable for breach of the lease. On liability, the court said that although Real Property Law § 223-a implies a right to rescind a lease for failure to give possession, the statute expressly permits the parties to waive its application, as they did in the lease, and that the lease's liability disclaimer for failure to give possession did not render the lease obligations illusory. The court said the defendants did not establish any intentional conduct by the plaintiff that precluded the tenant's use of the premises: the plaintiff's work in the premises was contemplated by the lease, and the pandemic-related construction delays were largely outside the landlord's control. The court also said damages were not precluded by the plaintiff's refusal to provide the keys until the defendants provided the requisite insurance. The court held that the plaintiff was entitled to full enforcement of the guaranty until at least 36 months after the rent commencement date, and that the trial court properly declined to limit damages against the guarantor under New York City's guaranty law, because the defendants acknowledged that they never took possession of the premises. It also upheld the award of the broker's fees the plaintiff incurred in reletting the premises. The prejudgment interest award was a different matter. The court said the representative from the plaintiff's managing agent's office testified at the damages hearing that he had not personally calculated the interest charged and did not know whether the calculation was made based on multiple periods or one final interest calculation. The $126,186.48 in interest, the court noted, was more than 20% of the total $596,904.79 contract damages requested at the hearing. On remand, the court said, the interest award should be supported by evidence showing how the calculation was made, at what intervals the interest rate was applied, and whether any interest was compounded.
live-462: According to the Second District's opinion, Bearcreek Farms contracted to buy real property at 2 E. Center Street in Germantown, Ohio, from S.L.S. Partnership and its partners. The tenant, JSR, operated a bar there, and the purchase agreement said the property was sold subject to lease agreements. After closing, Bearcreek believed a commercial bar, a freezer and a steel kitchen hood had been conveyed in its purchase. JSR apparently claimed it owned the items as trade fixtures that the purchase agreement did not identify as part of the sale. Bearcreek sued for a declaratory judgment that the items were fixtures it owned and, alternatively, for breach of contract against the sellers. The trial court dismissed the claims against the sellers. It reasoned that the agreement's trade-fixtures box was empty, so the parties did not intend to convey trade fixtures or other personal property, and that classification of the items had no bearing on whether the sellers breached. Bearcreek then dismissed JSR so the ruling could be appealed. The appeals court, in an opinion by Judge Mary K. Huffman, disagreed. It held that the items had to be classified to resolve which party was the rightful owner, and that Bearcreek's allegations were sufficient at the pleading stage on the purchase agreement, the deed's general warranty covenants and declaratory judgment. It reversed and remanded, and said the result may be the same once the items are classified after discovery, on summary judgment or at trial.
live-463: CASD Council Watch, a newsletter covering local government in Pickens County, South Carolina, reported in late November 2026 that the City of Easley has begun eminent-domain proceedings to acquire a property owner's right to approve changes to a shared driveway needed for a Target development's proposed access road. live-464: The Appellate Court of Illinois, Third District, filed the order on November 24, 2026, in an appeal from the Circuit Court of Du Page County, where Judge Robert G. Gibson presided. Justice Davenport delivered the judgment. According to the order, Sigma Ventures, LLC authorized its tenant, Associates in Sleep Medicine, LLC, with which it shares common ownership, to construct a building on Sigma-owned land. In May 2016, Associates in Sleep Medicine contracted with general contractor Foxfield Construction, Ltd. to build a two-story office building, under a contract requiring $1.8 million in payments over the course of the project. The order says Foxfield recorded a mechanic's lien against the premises for $473,589.10 in June 2017 and sued in October 2017 to foreclose it, also alleging breach of contract and, in the alternative, quantum meruit. Associates in Sleep Medicine and Sigma denied the complaint's material allegations and countersued; their surviving counterclaims include one seeking a declaration that the lien was invalid and Sigma's slander-of-title count. The circuit court granted summary judgment against Foxfield on the lien foreclosure count, holding the lien invalid because Foxfield's sworn contractor statements did not strictly comply with the Mechanics Lien Act. In August 2025, Foxfield moved to certify that ruling for immediate appeal under Rule 304(a), and the circuit court granted the motion. The appeals court did not reach the merits. The single question Foxfield raised was whether an architect furnishes "services" under the Act such that leaving the architect out of its sworn statements invalidated the lien. The court said the circuit court did not explain why a later reversal of the lien ruling would require a retrial, that a reversal would not disturb the adjudication of the surviving counts, and that other counterclaims allege defects that, if established at trial, could independently support the lien's invalidation. It held that the certification was an abuse of discretion, vacated it and dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
live-465: The Times-Tribune of Scranton, in an article carried by Yahoo News, reported that Brooklyn-based Cornell Realty Management filed a land-use appeal on a Thursday in Lackawanna County Court; the article appeared the following Monday evening, which places the filing on Nov. 19. live-466: According to ElevenFlo's docket summary, the debtors filed on February 2, 2026 in the Northern District of Texas, and the court ordered joint administration of 161 cases. live-467: The Superior Court of Delaware decided the case on November 24, 2026, in a memorandum opinion by Judge Danielle J. Brennan. According to the opinion, Lofton Enterprise Group executed a commercial lease for the property at 2 S. Congress St. in Port Penn on December 13, 2022, to expire May 31, 2027, with Port Penn Fire Company, which then owned the property; the lease was never recorded in the office of the Recorder of Deeds. Port Penn later sold the property to IBR Properties, LLC, which maintained the lease. The opinion says IBR executed a mortgage with Wilmington Savings Fund Society on March 27, 2023, and that the mortgage fell into default. The lender filed a foreclosure action against IBR on December 27, 2024, and a default judgment was entered on February 7, 2025. Global Tradings purchased the property at a sheriff's sale on July 9, 2025, did not execute a new lease with Lofton, and filed its ejectment complaint on October 23, 2025. Lofton argued that the Superior Court lacked jurisdiction because the litigation concerns a lease, and that a lease is a contract and not an encumbrance and so survives a sheriff's sale. The court held that it has jurisdiction because a complaint for ejectment is an action at law. It held that because the lease was never recorded, the mortgage takes priority, and that the subordinate lease was extinguished upon the completion of the sheriff's sale. The court granted the writ of possession.
